#2967. Yankees reach agreement with old friend on two-year deal to bolster bullpen

The Yankees have reached an agreement with an old friend on a two-year deal pending a physical to bolster their bullpen.

The team have agreed with right-handed free agent reliever Jonathan Loáisiga for two years, according to Nicaraguan reporter Levi Luna

Randy Miller of NJ.com reported earlier this week that the Yankees had offered Loáisiga a one-year deal worth more than his only other offer, a one-year, $5 million offer from the Diamondbacks. Loáisiga was seeking a three-year deal in the $18 million to $20 million range.

Luna also reported that "The Mets came in slightly higher with their offer for Loáisiga." The Dodgers and Phillies had also shown interest.

Bolstering the bullpen is GM Brian Cashman's No. 1 priority and he has now re-signed lefty Tim Hill re-signed and extended a $23.15 million qualifying offer to closer David Bednar, which he accepted.

Coming off another injury-plagued season in 2025, Loáisiga settled for a minor-league deal with the D'backs last January that included a $1.5 million salary in the majors. He proved to be a bargain, going 7-3 with a 2.42 ERA over a career-high 67 appearances.

Loáisiga averaged 97.9 mph on his sinker, while allowing 1.9 walks per nine innings and a barrel rate of 3.5%.

Loáisiga, 32, started his major-league career pitching with the Yankees from 2018-25. He had a breakout season in 2021 when he was 9-4 with a 2.17 ERA in 57 outings, but he was on the injured list 10 times as a Yankee.

Loáisiga wanted to sign with someone before a probable work stoppage begins Dec. 1 at 11:59 p.m. ET.

"I know they want him to sign before the lockout," a source close to the pitcher told Miller. "The Diamondbacks' offer was weak and they were very clear telling him, 'We want to lower our payroll.'"

Loáisiga picked Arizona because he thought his career would benefit from pitching a full season in a warm-weather city and in the NL West, which is loaded with pitcher-friendly ballparks.

Loaisiga wanted at least a two-year deal so he could get to 10 years' service and qualify for a full pension. He's currently at eight years and 22 days.

"Two years is important to him because he wants to secure the 10 years," the source said.

As of 2026, a player with 10 years of service time qualifies for a full pension that pays $290,000 annually if the start date is at age 62. Retired players can get a reduced rate starting at age 45.

Randy Miller of NJ.com contributed reporting.

#2965. Commerce approved sales of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies, Rep. Mast says

The subagency of the Commerce Department that regulates and enforces exports approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies including Alibaba and Tencent as of May 2026, according to documents released Thursday by the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

Some of those approvals, made by Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, included sales to companies designated by the Department of Defense as "Chinese Military Companies," according to the documents. From December through May, companies had made 3.4 million requests for sales of U.S. AI chips to China, the committee reported, citing those made by Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices.

"Over the past month, the administration's handling of chip export controls has put our national security and technology edge at risk. The Bureau of Industry and Security has failed to enforce the rules, and Congress must now conduct rigorous oversight of the administration's policies," Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said at a meeting of the panel Thursday at which members voted to release the documents.

Spokespersons for Nvidia and AMD said their companies comply with U.S. export control laws.

Nvidia argued it was following the Commerce Department regulations that were in effect at the time.

A spokesperson from the Bureau of Industry and Security said it shared information with Congress on both approvals and denials of licenses for Nvidia's H200 and comparable chips. "Licensing decisions are the product of deliberation and consultation among multiple U.S. Government agencies," the spokesperson said.

"The review and licensing process spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes. Despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China," Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo told CNBC.

On Tuesday, Nvidia reported $2.4 billion in quarterly revenue from H200 and related chip sales in China. In total, customers based in China and Hong Kong made up about 9.5% of all revenue.

"AMD complies with applicable U.S. export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations," AMD said through a spokesperson.

The approval of 879,000 AI chips is "not that many," Bernstein Senior Analyst Stacy Rasgon told CNBC, adding that this news is not surprising.

"It doesn't sound to me like they're approving everything they got willy nilly," Rasgon said of the Commerce Department. With 879,000 approvals out of 3.4 million requested AI chip sales, he added, "There was a process in place, and it sounds like they approved about one out of every four."

Despite a rapid succession of China export controls on AI chips that started under the Biden administration in 2022, Nvidia and AMD both re-engineered some chips to comply and be sold legally in China. And in December, Trump said Nvidia could ship H200s, its older generation Hopper chips, to "approved customers in China" if the U.S. got a 25% cut of sales.

The U.S. then licensed Nvidia H200 sales to Alibaba, Tencent, ByteDance and other Chinese companies, although sales were limited because Beijing didn't approve large-scale imports, chip analyst Patrick Moorhead of Moor Insights & Strategy told CNBC last week.

H200 sales numbers remained low due to those restrictions on China's end. Nvidia said H200 shipments to China made up less than 1% of data center revenue for the quarter that ended in July.

"In the grand context of the size of this market and how much they're shipping, it's a rounding error. It's tiny," Rasgon told CNBC.

The committee cited the Export Control Reform Act as justification for releasing the data. The panel said the law allows it to declassify and release export data if it "determines that the withholding of the following information is contrary to the national interest."

The license requests released by the Foreign Affairs Committee include requests to sell to major firms including ByteDance, Tesla (Shanghai) and Baidu.

The release of documents comes in the wake of Jensen Huang's resignation from the chip supplier Nvidia after news surfaced that he had several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy that led to concerns about Nvidia chips being diverted to China.

In the weeks since, Republicans and Democrats in Congress have called for legislation to be passed that would impose stricter export controls on the sale of advanced AI chips to China and other adversaries.

"The license information we are disclosing today will help inform the American public about how BIS has handled licenses for Nvidia H200 and equivalent AMD chips to China. The public has the right to know how these decisions were made," Meeks said.

Mast said two of the firms listed in Nvidia license applications to BIS — Maginfra and New Matrix — are suspected "smuggling fronts." The New York Times reported in November that both companies had empty offices and had ties to companies under national security sanctions.

"Both are fake companies. If BIS approved the sale of these chips to these firms, obviously that is of tremendous concern to us — especially given that President Trump made clear last year that the sale of any AI chips to China will have very real national security conditions," Mast said at the Thursday meeting.

Maginfra and New Matrix did not reply to requests for comment.

Shares of AMD fell Thursday after the investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging the company "has its own China problem." The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers."

CNBC did not independently verify this information.

Fallout from the Huang scandal on Capitol Hill has intensified in the last week, as lawmakers question the degree to which the former head of Nvidia's relationship with the suspected Chinese spy could have jeopardized national security and American AI dominance.

Huang is due for a closed-door transcribed interview with the House Foreign Affairs panel and two other committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter is scheduled to appear before the panels Dec. 2.

Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., announced on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had also agreed to testify.

Lutnick has come under fire over his relationship to Huang and for his failure to take action on Megaspeed, the Singaporean company where Alice Huang, with whom the former Nvidia CEO had an affair, was an executive until 2025. U.S. investigators suspect Megaspeed diverted Nvidia chips to China.

Amid that criticism, the Commerce Department on Monday issued an interim final rule to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies to lease Nvidia's advancing computing power from data centers in third countries.

The rule was "written by and at the direction of" the Treasury Department and the White House National Security Council, BIS said in a press release.

— Megan Cassella, Daren Fonda and Kif Leswing contributed to this report.

#2964. Penny Hardaway Names 4 Active NBA Players Who Belong In The All-Time Top 10

Former NBA star and current Memphis Tigers head coach Penny Hardaway appeared on Thursday's episode of the Run It Back show, where co-host Chandler Parsons posed an interesting question. Parsons asked Hardaway whether he feels it's fair for the NBA's all-time top 10 list to change as basketball evolves.

"I think it is fair to change it because we have different eras of who was dominant," Hardaway said. "Obviously, you never take away the greats; you can't. But you got to give the young guys an opportunity. I mean, there were a ton of great players that would be arguing that you're putting certain guys in this era in over them.

"But at the end of the day, you got to respect [Nikola] Jokic for how many times he's won MVP," Hardaway continued. "You got to respect Giannis [Antetokounmpo]. You got to respect Steph [Curry]. You got to respect all these guys that are really dominant in their era because it's about your era. And I'm not mad at all when they start trying to adjust it and change it a little bit."

Many former players would take issue with today's players getting in the top 10. Hardaway, who played 14 seasons in the NBA, is among the few who give this generation their due respect. As for how many active players the 55-year-old thinks belong in the top 10, the answer is four.

"I say [Kevin Durant]," Hardaway said. "I say Steph for sure. Those two. And then you got to add Jokic in there somewhere. I mean, he was dominant in his time, whether you like it or not. He's dominating this era."

Hardaway notably didn't mention Philadelphia 76ers superstar LeBron James, which led to Parsons bringing him up as the fourth one.

"Oh, we know LeBron is in the old era and the new era, the next era," Hardaway said.

James is probably the only lock in the all-time top 10 among active players. The 41-year-old is widely regarded as one of the two greatest players of all time and is in that GOAT debate with Michael Jordan.

James has won four titles, four Finals MVPs, four MVPs, one scoring title, and one assists title. He is the NBA's all-time leading scorer and recently climbed up to third in assists. James is in the midst of his 24th season, and his longevity is simply mind-boggling.

Speaking of longevity, Kevin Durant is also going strong with the Houston Rockets in his 20th season. Durant has won two titles, two Finals MVPs, one MVP, and four scoring titles. He might be the most complete scorer we have ever seen, but he isn't usually found on top-10 lists due to his infamous decision to join Stephen Curry and the Golden State Warriors in 2016.

Durant was long seen as the second-greatest player of his generation, but Curry has now surpassed him. The Warriors superstar has won four titles, one Finals MVP, two MVPs, and two scoring titles. Curry is the unquestioned greatest shooter of all time, and Shaquille O'Neal believes he should be in the GOAT conversation.

Now, while Durant and Curry might be somewhat controversial picks, they're not as controversial as Denver Nuggets superstar Nikola Jokic. Jokic has been the best player of the 2020s and has won one title, one Finals MVP, three MVPs, one rebounding title, and one assists title. While those three MVPs are impressive, only winning one title is held against him in these conversations.

Former NBA head coach George Karl doesn't blame Jokic for that, as he slammed the Nuggets for ruining his chances of becoming an all-time top-10 player. They have lost a lot of key pieces since winning the title in 2023, and it'll be a surprise if the Serb wins another as long as he stays in Denver.

Hardaway could have potentially been in these conversations, too, but knee injuries meant he didn't fulfil his potential. He finished third in MVP voting in just his third season, and one wonders what might have been.

#2963. Tokenization platform Securitize gains 10% postmarket on Q3 results, move into asset-backed finance

Tokenization platform Securitize climbed about 10% postmarket after reporting third quarter growth alongside increased operating expenses, and announcing an expansion into asset-backed finance through a strategic acquisition.

Miami-based Securitize, which made its public market debut in July, operates in the relatively new corner of the crypto equity universe involved in institutional tokenization infrastructure. Tokenized assets on the platform grew 9% in the third quarter, to $4.8 billion, from the same period a year ago. Aggregate transaction volume rose 20% from a year ago, to $4.3 billion. Revenue of $11.5 million was up 28% from last year.

The growth came as bullish sentiment around tokenization gained traction throughout the third quarter, ahead of the Security and Exchange Commission formalizing the long awaited Innovation Exemption on Sept. 17, which created a temporary pathway for trading of certain tokenized stocks and strengthened the regulatory outlook.

Profitability is still meaningfully below year-ago levels, due in part to costs associated with going public over the summer, as well as the scaling up of the tokenization business at an active time for the entire sector, Securitize CEO Carlos Domingo told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Securitize reinforced "certain areas of the company like finance, compliance, legal [and] cybersecurity," which increased corporate costs "compared to a year ago when we were privately held," Domingo said. "We're in in a very good position. The adjusted EBITDA … is improving significantly from previous quarters."

Securitize reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of $2 million, compared with positive adjusted EBITDA of $3.6 million a year ago, better than a $5.5 million loss in the second quarter. The company posted a 183% increase in operating costs and expenses.

Also on Monday, the Securitize board authorized a $50 million share buyback and announced the acquisition of River One, an institutional asset-backed financing platform developing technology to connect stablecoin capital with traditional lending markets. Terms were not disclosed.

Securitize sees an opportunity to modernize the $9 trillion market for asset backed finance by using stablecoins to finance real world assets, generate yield and tokenize investment positions and credit products, Domingo said.The acquisition also marks an expansion beyond Securitize's core niche markets at a time when tokenization's competitive landscape is growing, with traditional asset managers like BlackRock and Franklin Templeton, and established financial market infrastructure providers like DTCC and Broadridge, entering the industry.

"We have been very active in tokenized funds, treasuries [and] yield … And we've been obviously recently very active in tokenized stocks, so this adds another piece of the puzzle in the emerging tokenization space for us to capture revenue growth."

#2962. LeBron James sues makers of 'Bron' app over unauthorized use of his nickname and AI-generated likeness

Former Lakers star LeBron James is suing a company and its founders for using his nickname as the name of a sports-betting analytics app and using unauthorized AI-generated images in his likeness to advertise the product.

According to a civil lawsuit filed Tuesday in U.S. District Court of New York by James and his LBJ Trademarks LLC, the San Francisco-based developer PlayVision Inc. named its app "Bron" in an attempt to benefit from James' name and star power "without any connection between the word and Defendants or any feature of their app."

"The word 'Bron' has no dictionary definition and no special meaning in the context of sports analytics, wagering, or artificial intelligence," the complaint states. "Rather, in the context of anything sports-related, it refers to only one man — LeBron James."

Read more: LeBron James says 'family is safe' after arrest of alleged stalker outside Brentwood home

The Times on Thursday reached out to PlayVision and fellow defendants Anish Gupta (co-founder and CEO) and Marc Zoghby (co-founder and CTO) through the company's email address and did not immediately receive a response. The Associated Press reports that requests for comment sent Tuesday to Gupta and Zoghby's email accounts were also not immediately returned.

In early November, PlayVision released a video advertisement for the Bron app that featured a player "with physical traits that mimic Mr. James, down to his identifiable tattoos," according to the complaint,. The player is shown mainly from behind, with a partial side view of his face also displayed at one point, while using the app.

He wears a basketball jersey that features the name "Bron" and the number 23, which is the jersey number James has worn during most of his 24 years in the NBA (including his current stint with the Philadelphia 76ers).

Read more: Swanson: One frigid night against the Jazz doesn't change the fact the Lakers are legit

"The Ad catapulted the Bron App from obscurity to controversy, with the Ad gaining a million views within a day—exactly as Defendants intended," the lawsuit states, adding, "When Mr. James's counsel sent a cease-and-desist letter to Defendants, they used it as an opportunity to gin up additional publicity, taking down the Ad while teasing 'a new name' without delivering one..."

On Monday, Gupta posted a video to his LinkedIn page that featured clips of people discussing and, at one point, chanting "Bron AI." The post promoted the relaunch of the Bron app under a new name later in the week.

"We found Bron. Apparently, the lawyers found it too," Gupta wrote. "Find out our new name Wednesday. 10 AM PT."

The new app's name, which was introduced on the same day as James' lawsuit was filed, is "Evie."

Read more: Stephen Curry calls out Gilbert Arenas, others over comments about wife Ayesha. Here's the latest

"Defendants' latest post underscores that Defendants' entire marketing campaign has been in bad faith, referencing the public backlash against their Ad and daring Mr. James to sue," the complaint states. "Defendants are not winding down their misconduct. They are milking it, stringing out the controversy one video teaser at a time for as long as it keeps the Bron App in the headlines."

#2960. The Tech Download: Anthropic charmed Wall Street. But one big uncertainty hangs over the business

Anthropic's historic debut on Thursday saw the company defy a wider tech selloff, as investors paid a premium for the stock.

The five-year-old company, which raised $81.3 billion as part of the listing, is one of the first opportunities for public markets to value a pure play AI lab.

Many see the IPO as a possible savior of the AI trade after a shaky few months, but one big uncertainty hangs over the company's future prospects.

"One of Anthropic's biggest challenges will be securing enough compute to support their steep growth trajectory," Gil Luria, D.A. Davidson, head of technology research, told me.

Access to the huge quantities of compute the company needs to continue developing and deploying models is a big challenge for Anthropic, which didn't respond to a request for comment for this piece, to navigate. It also comes at a time when there's growing public opposition to major data centers and delays to some AI infrastructure projects.

Anthropic has said it has entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements for compute and infrastructure worth around $900 billion. The company expects to incur roughly half of that cost before the end of 2030, with the rest between 2031 and 2045. Around $186 billion of that spend is tied to deals that can be terminated or subject to conditions like securing financing, facilities or regulatory approvals.

There have been signs of hurdles for access to some of that capacity.

Lambda missed a deadline to secure a facility lease for a $34.9 billion agreement, Anthropic said in a filing earlier this month. Nscale disclosed that it had yet to secure binding financing commitments for its Anthropic contracts, which are worth up to around $44 billion. Lambda didn't respond to a request for comment and Nscale declined to comment.

"In both cases the financing risk falls on the neoclouds and their lenders, not on Anthropic," Nick Patience, AI lead at Futurum Group, told me. But, he added, the "real question is whether that capacity arrives on time."

Anthropic has cloud infrastructure commitments with Amazon and Google worth more than $100 billion each extending into the 2030s. It also could end up spending more than $100 billion with SpaceX to access AI compute.

So, no shortage of big-money deals for graphics processing units, or GPUs, access.

But even if some of the smaller deals collapse or take longer to get off the ground than expected, it could slow Anthropic down.

"Demand is running ahead of supply, so missing capacity turns into lost revenue very quickly," said Patience.

Margins could suffer too, he added, as a result of increased costs of short-term compute commitments.

Anthropic has said that long-term capacity is significantly cheaper than short-term commitments, which it would need to turn to when "customer demand or research needs exceed this long-term capacity."

Capacity constraints will be a challenge Anthropic has to navigate.

"Throughout 2027-2028 we are expecting the firm to remain compute constrained, using a mixture of short-term compute to augment longer-term deals with the hyperscalers coming online," Malik Ahmed Khan, senior equity analyst at Morningstar, told me.

Some slippage in terms of AI infrastructure delivery is likely, said Patience, but a "serious shortage is not, because its biggest suppliers are also its biggest investors and have every reason to keep it supplied."

#2957. Ranking the Penguins best trade assets

On Wednesday, Pittsburgh Penguins general manager/president of hockey operations Kyle Dubas pointed out the biggest problem with the 2026-27 season is the team's lack of consistency. He specifically talked about how they show flashes of strong play for brief moments, can not sustain it, and then keep losing games as a result.

The team responded on Thursday night against the St. Louis Blues by demonstrating exactly what he was talking about in a 5-2 loss. After a first period that was one of their best of the season, they followed it up by playing a rather lifeless 40 minutes to close out the game, getting outscored 5-1 during that time.

This is important because Dubas also pointed out that if the season continues on that same trajectory, some changes are going to have to be made. That means trades. Along with that, the returns are likely to be more long-term and futures based.

It is not surprising, and it is the next step and likely escalation of a rebuild that has already been underway for a couple of years now.

The Penguins reportedly tried to get a start on that earlier this month with a rumored trade involving Rickard Rakell and the Chicago Blackhawks. According to Elliotte Friedman, the apparent return was going to be one of Chicago's first-round picks in 2027 (belonging to Florida or Edmonton), veteran forward Teuvo Teravainen and a prospect. Quite honestly, that is more than I would have expected for Rakell, and it is likely a sign of Chicago's desperation more than anything else.

Rakell, however, utilized his no-trade protections and nixed it (as is his right to do).

So now that all of that is out there, and this seems to be the path we are headed down, let's look at the Penguins best trade assets and rank them. This is not a ranking of who is most likely to be traded. It is a look at which players would bring the most value back in return if they were to be traded.

1. Sidney Crosby. I don't think Sidney Crosby is going to get traded. It is ultimately going to be his decision on if he goes and where he goes, and even though his agent put out a really vague statement on Thursday, I just can't see it going down this path.

Or more accurately, I don't see it going down this path.

I think it's more likely that Crosby simply retires after this season.

He's not playing the way he expects or wants to play, and he doesn't strike me as the type of player that is going to want to hang on if he can't reach the level he expects of himself. He also doesn't strike me as the type of player that wants a season long farewell tour and the attention that comes with it. When he retires, he's just going to do it (I think).

He also doesn't need to follow the Ray Bourque path and latch on to a contender so he can finally win something. He's already won. A lot. He doesn't have to prove anything to anybody, answer to anybody, or complete a Hall of Fame resume.

If I am wrong about all of that, and if he by some chance he went to the Penguins and said, "I'd like to play in Montreal, or play alongside my buddy in Colorado," I don't think Dubas would hesitate to make it happen.

Not only out of respect to Crosby, but also because he just seems like he's ready to turn the page on this era.

Even though Crosby is 39 and not having a particularly good season, he's still Sidney Crosby, and he would still warrant some kind of a significant return. Probably better than any other realistic trade option on the team. For that reason, he goes at the top of the list, even if I don't think it actually goes in that direction.

2. Erik Karlsson. I don't like the season Karlsson is having, and even though the point total is still fine, his drop in play is one of the biggest factors in the Penguins' regression from a year ago. He was their MVP and best player during the 2025-26 season, and one of the reasons for their surprising success. He channeled his Norris Trophy/Hall of Fame level and played like the player the Penguins always expected him to be. It was just about points or scoring, either. It was about dictating the pace of the game, having everything run through him, and just being a difference-maker in all three zones.

It is simply not there this season, for whatever reason.

Having said that, he's still going to have some value to a contender. He plays a premium position, he can still generate offense, and there's no term on his contract beyond this season, so any team trading for him isn't going to have to be overly concerned about his long-term outlook. He would be a hired gun at this point, and probably a good one in the right situation.

I'd expect a first-round pick and a mid-level prospect.

3. Tommy Novak. I'm going to put Novak high on this list because I think there's a lot of value with him. Not franchise-changing trade value. But definitely good value. For one, he's just a good player, and he's having a really good season. He also has an extremely cheap contract and has the positional flexibility to play on the wing or at center. He can play in the top-six. He can play on the third line. He can play on the power play. He can carry the puck. He can make plays. He can do a lot. I think a lot of teams would like him and what he does, and they could probably get a surprisingly strong return for him if they moved him.

I also get the sense the Penguins like him. A lot.

They might not LOOK to move him, but I'd be willing to bet people would call, and I'm not sure they would hang up the phone. He also has no trade protections in his contract, which would remove any complications.

4. Evgeni Malkin. Everything I wrote up above regarding Crosby applies here the exact same way. I don't think he's going to ask out. Even though his trade protections are small, I don't think the Penguins are going to aggressively look to move him unless he does ask out. I do think there would be some sort of a market for him given the offense he can still produce. I just don't know how much value.

Patrick Kane and Brad Marchand were two veteran wingers traded at the ends of their contracts. Both essentially went for a conditional second round pick that would be upgraded to a first rounder based on playoff performance (which worked in Marchand's case but did not in Kane's). That would seem about a ballpark for a potential Malkin trade in 2026, if all the other factors came together.

5. Rickard Rakell. I am still skeptical of the market for him, even with the report of Chicago trying to get him. I think that speaks more to the desperation of the Blackhawks than anything else. As I wrote over the summer, mid-30s wingers with term remaining on their contract are not always attractive trade targets. But that could change as the season moves along and contenders start to get a better idea of what they need and who is actually available. It could also start to change if Rakell keeps scoring more and playing the way he has over the past couple of weeks. As we saw recently, he does have some say over where he goes.

6. Bryan Rust. I like the idea of Bryan Rust on a contender, and I like the idea of a contender wanting a player like Rust. He is as solid as they come, can play up and down the lineup, is not really out of place in any situation, and has a knack for playing his best in the biggest moments. General managers love players like that. He is also one of the few veteran players on the roster that is currently without any trade restrictions on his contract.

The problem: He's 34 years old with a year remaining on his deal (the whole mid-30s winger with term thing) and is going to miss 10-20 games every year, or be playing through something. He just is. You can't ignore that reality. And I think all of that would be reflected in what any potential return looks like.

7. Blake Lizotte. Depth centers that can kill penalties and are signed to cheap contracts can have more value than you might expect, but I still don't think it would be be anything more than a few lottery tickets. I could easily see a second-rounder, though.

8. Sam Girard. I don't think he's a bad player by any means, and as a pending unrestricted free agent he is almost certain to be on the trade block. I just don't think he's bringing back anything significant. Maybe a second-round pick.

9. Justin Brazeau. Fine depth player. Cheap contract. Big guy with some skill. General managers, again, love that sort of thing. Maybe a couple of mid-round picks.

10. Trevor van Riemsdyk. He would need to play more and show he can still be a solid defender, but he has enough of a track record that there might be some market for him by the trade deadline.

11. Andrei Kuzmenko. This is just an unfortunate situation with the way it has played out. I understand what the Penguins were trying to do. Take on a cheap, one-year reclamation project and see if you can get some production out of it to flip it at the deadline, or get a surprisingly good year for another potential playoff run. Anthony Beauvillier. Anthony Mantha. Same idea. I don't blame anybody for the way it's worked out because sometimes life just sucks. I just don't think there's a trade market.

12. Kris Letang. I actually don't think he's been all that bad this season. He is clearly not prime Kris Letang, and there have been some tough moments, but he's been fine. I just don't see teams lining up to take the 39-year-old version of him with another year at $6.1 million against the cap remaining.

They are not trading Ben Kindel. They are not trading Sergei Murashov. There is no good reason to trade Egor Chinakhov at this point. Ville Koivunen and Rutger McGroarty are the type of players that are probably going to get more of a look as the season goes on, and especially if veteran plays get moved. Same thing applies to Elmer Soderblom. I'm going to be honest, I have no idea where to slot Connor Dewar in any of the above tiers. I don't know that Arturs Silovs is going to have a big demand, and you still need somebody to play in net.

#2955. Senate passes BAAJA permitting reform bill backed by AI, energy sectors

The Senate on Thursday passed a long-sought bill to ease the nation's environmental permitting laws and overhaul electrical transmission regulations, a crucial step toward boosting construction for the energy and technology industries.

Senators voted 62-33 to pass the bill, which split Democrats just weeks after they flipped enough seats from Republicans in the midterm elections to give them majorities in both chambers of Congress in January. The bill, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, is projected to lower energy costs for consumers while weakening some environmental laws to speed up the permitting process.

The vote offers a window into the fissures forming in the Democratic Party as it prepares to assume full control of Congress in January and tries to address the affordability crisis that catapulted it to power.

More Democrats voted against the permitting measure than voted for it. Still, more than a dozen — including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y. — voted to pass it over the objections of climate groups and tribes to get the bill across the finish line.

"It's going to be legislation that's really going to make the biggest difference for the next 100 years, especially bringing down carbon emissions once this president is gone," Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., told reporters on Thursday before the vote. Gallego supported the measure.

The bill's Senate passage is a key step to it becoming law, but it would also need to clear the House before heading to President Donald Trump's desk.

Democratic supporters of the bill touted its cost benefits as a win after they ran campaigns on affordability, and pointed to a massive glut of clean energy the bill could bring onto the grid. Opponents lamented rollbacks to the nation's bedrock environmental protection laws favored by the fossil fuel industry and Republicans, and warned the measure could offer carte blanche authority to the data centers undergirding artificial intelligence.

"No big, bipartisan bill is going to be perfect for everyone, but we have a real opportunity to make electricity more affordable for families. Working people can't afford to wait another few years for us to get this done," Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., the incoming chair of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and an author of the bill, said in a statement to CNBC.

Heinrich brokered the agreement with his counterpart Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, along with Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., and Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., the top Democrat and Republican on the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee.

"Earlier this month, Americans sent a clear message: They want Congress focused on making their lives more affordable. That's precisely what this permitting reform bill will do," he said.

Getting to a final vote was acrimonious. Senators amended the package in the weeks leading up to the vote to address concerns from Native American tribes, which objected to changes in their participation in permitting.

"I'm not going to sit around and let these data centers scar our treasures," Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., told reporters Thursday about the push for his amendment, which would have blocked data centers from being built on public lands.

Clean energy and fossil energy groups both cheered the bill's passage in the Senate.

As negotiated, the bill would benefit both renewables and fossil fuels. Artificial intelligence and the broader tech industry also stand to benefit — despite the bill's provision forcing hyperscalers to pay for upgrades to the grid — as power-hungry data centers demand more electricity.

The American Clean Power Association, a group that represents renewables, said it was "a clean energy bill that will modernize America's energy systems and lower consumer prices."

The American Petroleum Institute, which represents the oil and gas industry, called the bill a "major breakthrough on historic permitting reforms that would deliver more affordable energy for consumers, cut costly delays, and build much-needed critical infrastructure."

Renewables would benefit largely from the bill's electricity transmission component, along with measures aimed at blocking Trump from cancelling already-permitted wind and solar projects. New solar and wind projects are often bottlenecked by a lack of transmission able to deliver power to the grid.

Rhodium Group, an economic research firm, estimates the bill would allow an additional 17 to 249 gigawatts of clean energy to be built by 2040. Natural gas exports would rise 8% to 15% beyond a 76% to 145% rise already accounted for under current policy. Greenhouse gases would be reduced by 5 to 148 million metric tons annually in 2040.

"A lot of Democrats are involved and supportive in this deal because expanding grid capacity would integrate a lot of clean energy," said Rob Gramlich, the founder and president of Grid Strategies, an energy consulting group. "Republicans are maybe less interested in that benefit, but they do care about economic growth and serving new large loads. And I think members on both sides of the aisle are pretty well aware that we're doing much less grid investment here in the U.S. compared to other countries."

Gramlich added that "you can't get to 60 to 80% of our grid from renewable energy without a significant expansion of grid capacity."

However, the Natural Resources Defense Council was among the opponents.

"The House should not pass a bill that gives President Trump a blank check to reward oil and gas companies and data center developers," the organization said in a statement. "Lawmakers should oppose this bill and try again next year to pass legislation worthy of the American people, not for the fossil fuel industry and data center companies."

The bill now heads to the House, where Republican leadership is expected to attempt to pass it. Trump also supports the deal.

But as in the Senate, Democrats are expected to be divided.

"Democrats promised to lower bills, cut pollution, and protect ratepayers," said Rep. Scott Peters, D-Calif., a longtime champion of permitting reform. "Voters are giving us a chance to show we mean it. BAAJA does all three. We should pass it before the end of this Congress."

House Natural Resources ranking member and likely incoming Chair Jared Huffman, D-Calif., meanwhile, urged Democrats to say no to the permitting bill.

"Don't believe the lie that this terrible bill, exactly as drafted, is the last, best and only chance to ever do permitting reform," he said. "We can produce a better deal."

#2953. Scouting the Enemy: Las Vegas Raiders

The Denver Broncos battle the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday. It's a big division rivalry matchup for Broncos who are coming off their bye week. After starting their season 3-0, the Raiders have dropped six of their las seven games and are 4-6 on the season. Here is a deeper look at their Week 11 opponent.

2025 Las Vegas Raiders Regular Season Review

The Pete Carroll experiment in Las Vegas lasted just one season. The Raiders finished dead last in the AFC West with a 3-14 record. After his dismissal, the Raiders hired Klint Kubiak to be their next Head Coach.

2026 Las Vegas Raiders Offseason Additions and Departures

After a disappointing '25 season, the Raiders embarked on a tremendous overhaul this offseason. Both their offense and defense were awful. They added a handful of players on offense early on in free agency including center Tyler Linderbaum and wide receiver Jalen Nailor.

On defense, they overhauled their linebacking corps bringing in former Georgia Bulldog teammates Nakobe Dean and Quay Walker to man the middle of their defense. They also added edge rushers Kwity Paye and Malcolm Koonce to bolster their pass rush. Additionally, the Raiders traded for former Buffalo Bills defensive back Taron Johnson to shore up their secondary.

Head Coach Klint Kubiak and General Manager John Spytek were busy this past April making ten selections in the 2026 NFL Draft. Quarterback Fernando Mendoza, taken with the top pick, is poised to start his second career game with the Broncos. The Raiders found two starters on Day 2 with defensive back Treydan Stukes and offensive lineman Trey Zuhn. On Day 2, they made high upside picks with cornerback Jermod McCoy and running back Mike Washington Jr. who have seen a decent amount of reps this season.

Offensive X-Factor: Quarterback Fernando Mendzoa

Tight end Brock Bowers was going to get the nod here. However, Bowers injured his ankle against the Seattle Seahawks in Week 10. While the ankle injury won't land him on injured reserve, Head Coach Klint Kubiak stated he will be day-to-day and did classify it as significant.

With that in mind, I'll turn to rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza as their offensive X-Factor for the game. Last week against the Seahawks, Mendoza made his first start of his NFL. He struggled and completed just 17 his 29 pass attempts for only 143 yards. However, he did get his first career touchdown with 10-yard quarterback draw in the first quarter of the matchup.

The Raiders' offensive line had just allowed 11 sacks all season before the Seahawks game, but their defense was able to drop Mendoza for six sacks. This is a game where Denver's defensive front seven needs to play at a high level. I consider it a favorable matchup for Defensive Coordinator Vance Joseph and his players. If they can rattle the rookie signal caller and force him into bad decisions, I really like their chances on Sunday.

Defensive X-Factor: Edge rusher Maxx Crosby

For a moment earlier in the spring, Broncos Country was elated with the news that premier edge rusher Maxx Crosby would be heading out of the division to join the Baltimore Ravens. However, much like the Daiyan Henley trade, the deal was nixed due to a failed physical. So now, he is back for his eighth season with the Raiders.

At 29-years-old, Crosby has cemented himself as one of the league's best defenders. He has earned five-straight Pro-Bowl designations and has been a two-time All-Pro dating back to the 2021 season. In ten games this season, Crosby has 34 tackles, 9 tackles for loss, 21 quarterback hits, and 5 sacks.

During the bye and earlier this week, Head Coach Sean Payton emphasized that blocking up front, whether it's against the run or the pass, is one of the huge things Denver's offense needs to accomplish to finally hit their stride in the second half of the season. Going up against Crosby will be a big challenge for them. We will see if the offensive line is up to the task.

How the Broncos can achieve a victory over the Raiders

ICYMI: Yesterday, I wrote how the Broncos can achieve their eighth victory of the season over the Raiders. Overall, I feel confident about Denver's chances. The extra week of preparation should help them out, plus going up against a rookie quarterback in his second start should help matters. I believe the Broncos will achieve a decisive double-digit victory over the Raiders.

Hart's Prediction: Broncos 30, Raiders 16.

#2952. Memphis Grizzlies showing Warriors the new generation

The Golden State Warriors are landing in Memphis tonight caught in a freefall, but context is everything. Steph Curry's Dubs sent Grit and Grind home in 2015 and Ja and Jaren home in 2022. Now Memphis is on its third version, and it's already won at Chase Center. Tonight the Warriors get their second look at these Grizzlies, this time without Steph.

Grit and Grind reached the 2013 conference finals and were up 2-1 on the Warriors in 2015 before Golden State took the next three. The Ja and Jaren teams won 56 games in 2021-22, lost to the Warriors in the second round, and were done after a first-round sweep by OKC in 2025.

Then they opened the season with six straight wins, and the rebuild turned into the surprise of the NBA.

The face of the surprise is a familiar one. Ty Jerome, the same guy Steve Kerr called a "godsend" as a two-way player in 2022-23, went from 6.9 points per game in Golden State to leading Memphis at 25.4. In the Nov. 2 overtime loss to New Orleans he dropped 40, including 23 after the third.

And without Draymond in the paint, can Golden State keep Boozer off the offensive glass?

#2951. AI can help find holiday deals — but it's not great at spotting scams, experts say

Artificial intelligence shopping tools can help consumers compare prices and find gift ideas, but experts say shoppers still need to verify unfamiliar retailers and sellers before buying.

Scammers can use AI to make fake stores, product photos and reviews look convincing. It can also make creating and deploying websites easier, said Leyla Bilge, global head of scam research at cybersecurity company Norton.

"The biggest impact right now we're seeing in AI is on coding," Bilge said. Scammers can register "thousands and thousands of fake e-shops online," she said, which increases the chances shoppers will encounter one.

A Norton survey of 1,000 U.S. adults found that 16% of respondents had been scammed while shopping online during the holidays. Of those victims, 88% lost money, with an average loss of $394. The survey was conducted from an opt-in online panel between Sept. 10 and 21 by Dynata on behalf of Norton's parent company, Gen.

Here's a look at more stories on how to manage, grow and protect your money for the years ahead.

Scams can have impacts beyond financial losses. In a survey of 3,110 U.S. adults released in June, the Global Anti-Scam Alliance found that 82% of respondents had encountered a scam in the past year. More than half, 59%, said the scam affected their mental well-being.

More than half of GASA survey respondents said they had experienced repeat scams.

If you put your address or phone number in an AI tool that turns out to be fraudulent, "you might get reached out to again with a much more sophisticated, much more targeted and personalized attack and scam," Bilge said.

Among respondents who had used an AI shopping assistant or agent, 56% said it had recommended or completed a purchase from a retailer they didn't recognize, the Norton survey found.

An agent focused on finding the lowest price may steer a shopper toward an unfamiliar seller, so experts say shoppers shouldn't treat its recommendation as vetted.

"You absolutely need to check with the retailer directly," said Matt Schulz, chief consumer finance analyst at LendingTree and author of "Ask Questions, Save Money, Make More."

Bilge said many shoppers make purchases on their phones through social media, sometimes with a single click, leaving them little time or incentive to assess where the link goes. Then, some still buy even if they're unsure of the site's legitimacy.

The Norton survey also found that 35% of Americans had bought from a website or seller they thought might be a scam because the deal seemed too good to pass up.

Before buying from a seller or retailer, consumer experts recommend these steps:

While AI can narrow gift options and find the lowest prices, experts say shoppers should verify the store before handing over payment details — and, when possible, pay by credit card. Keep order details and receipts, too.

The FTC says cardholders can dispute charges in certain cases, such as when merchandise never arrives.

— CNBC's Stephanie Dhue contributed reporting to this article.

#2949. Paul George flips the script — and the bird — in Philadelphia return

Paul George flips the script — and the bird — in Philadelphia return originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

PG-13 was rated R in his return to Philadelphia.

The middle finger Paul George directed toward one baseline fan only reinforced that rating.

Tuesday night was expected to revolve around Jaylen Brown and Jayson Tatum sharing an NBA court as opponents for the first time. Instead, the other headliner in the summer's blockbuster trade stole the show.

George scored a game-high 36 points in Boston's 123-101 win over the Sixers. He shot 14 for 22 from the floor, made six of his 11 three-point attempts and scored 14 consecutive Boston points in the fourth quarter.

The game was tied at 79 with 3:19 remaining in the third quarter. Boston outscored Philadelphia 44-22 from that point forward.

The Celtics went nine minutes and 20 seconds without making a two-point field goal during the second half. Instead, they made nine consecutive field goals from three, the second-longest such streak by a Sixers opponent over the last 30 seasons.

Payton Pritchard opened the fourth with consecutive threes. George followed with eight straight points, helping the Celtics begin the quarter on a 14-0 run that turned a competitive game into a rout.

George's return carried a complicated history. His two seasons with the Sixers were repeatedly interrupted by injuries, but he also played a significant role in their most memorable playoff run in years.

Last spring, George helped the Sixers overcome a 3-1 deficit to eliminate Boston in seven games. He averaged 17.4 points and shot 55 percent from three during the series.

Tyrese Maxey was happy to see his former teammate Tuesday, even if he disliked what followed.

"It was good to see Paul," Maxey said. "I love him, love his family. … He gave us everything he had while he was here. We know what he did in the playoffs last year. Great person, great family, and we'll see him again."

Maxey then added one important qualifier.

George instead scored from nearly everywhere.

"He had some open threes. He had some pull-up threes. He had some middies," Maxey said. "He played within the game, too. That's what Paul does. He plays within the game. He takes what the defense gives him, and we gave him too many open looks tonight.

"PG, we know what PG does. We shouldn't even be allowing him to get up 11 threes, and that's on us."

Nick Nurse watched George attack the Sixers in several ways.

"He really had it going," Nurse said. "He'd post up, and-one, fallaways. He went down the lane, high archer off the glass, and-one. He scored in about every way he could tonight."

George heard boos during his return and said the arena carried the atmosphere, though not quite the intensity, of a playoff game.

"This building can be very electric as well," George said. "It was fun. It was fun to play in this environment."

One interaction extended beyond the usual reception for a returning player.

During a stoppage, the ball rolled toward a fan seated along the baseline. George said the fan looked directly at him before dropping the ball instead of returning it.

"There was a fan being an a–," George said. "The ball rolled to him. He looked me dead in my eyes, dropped the ball on the ground as if I'm a dog to go fetch or go get it, instead of passing the ball to me like a normal fan would do.

"And so, yeah, then I rolled him a middle finger in return."

#2948. What's ahead for AI financing after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang departs

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the company's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.

Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the company. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent chief executive.

Nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand. That could all change.

"Although we expect the company to fulfill all of its previously announced commitments, we believe that going forward, it may be more difficult for the company to negotiate new multi-party investments among ecosystem partners at the same scale it has done up to this point," Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider said in a note Thursday.

The news of Huang's resignation comes after investors were already concerned about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.

Tech bond yields have risen and spreads have widened on credit default swaps, most notably in lower-rated names. Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier.

On Friday, the yield on Nvidia's 4.5% bond due in 2031 sat at 5.717%, nearly 5% higher week to date. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

Tech stocks slumped Friday with the Nasdaq 100 closing down 1.2% as markets continued to digest the Nvidia news. Yields on hyperscaler bonds ticked slightly higher on Friday, signaling the broader concern about AI debt lingers.

It's the smaller AI companies that could ultimately see an impact if Nvidia makes any changes to its AI financing. The company had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, according to its last quarterly financial filing in July.

Neoclouds CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN are all in Nvidia's portfolio. Their shares were down sharply Thursday.

CoreWeave, which has become the poster child for AI debt fears, saw its bond yields retreat after its quarterly earnings on Tuesday eased investor concerns. The yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 was 14.79% on Friday after climbing to 16.7% last week. The spread on its five-year CDS also dropped more than 17% week to date, although it remained above 1,000 — which is generally considered a sign of distress.

It remains unclear how Nvidia's support for those companies may change, said CreditSights analyst Andy Li.

"We don't know what the ultimate strategy for Nvidia is going to be coming out the other side," he said.

"However, I think directionally, just given the fact that Jensen was so crucial in selling the Nvidia story and being a very aggressive deal maker, it's likely that a lot of this creative deal-making and circular financing and equity and credit support is going to moderate," he added.

CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC Wednesday, before Huang's departure, that Nvidia "is not one person."

"There are thousands of people over there that interface with thousands of people at my company every day. They integrate on the technology. They integrate on the physical infrastructure. They integrate on the networking," he said in an interview with "Squawk on the Street." "They have been a great partner for us for years. They will continue to be a great partner for us."

Bob Lang, founder and chief strategist at Explosive Options, doesn't see any big changes in terms of Nvidia's relevance or its ability to finance for now. As CFO, Kress was involved in the financing deals, and the search for a permanent CEO is going to take some time, he noted.

The real issue is just how much money the company will want to lend for AI financing, rather than, say using its hundreds of billions in free cash flow for other purposes, like share buybacks, capex, or acquisitions.

"Big companies like Nvidia and Meta, they're holding all the cards," he said. "When they decide that the game is over, that's it — it's going to be curtains for some of these smaller companies."

— CNBC'S Kif Leswing and Isabel O'Brien contributed reporting.

#2947. Panthers vs Ravens: Matchups to watch

The Carolina Panthers notched a key divisional win over the New Orleans Saints last Sunday. They sit alone at the top of the NFC South with a one game advantage over both the Saints and Bucs. Both of those teams have very difficult road games against NFC North foes. Meanwhile the Panthers are playing host to the Baltimore Ravens, who are having a season from hell and just loss to the previously winless Los Angeles Chargers. It was the Ravens' fifth straight loss. And now they're embroiled in controversy because their starting cornerback said his own team's city was "best at making criminals." He's been suspended for those comments and won't be playing on Sunday.

It's a great spot for the Panthers to create some space and the teams that are chasing them. There are some spots where they can really take advantage and help themselves get that much needed win.

The Ravens made a desperate trade for former Eagles center Cam Jurgens as they were ravaged by injuries at that spot over the course of the season. Walker has had his fair of struggles at left tackle this season, and he's going to be the primary adversary for Hendrickson in this game. #2946. How the Lakers' Quentin Grimes wants to maintain his hot shooting, even off the bench

When Lakers public address announcer Derrin Horton introduced Quentin Grimes in the starting lineup Wednesday, the easy-going Lakers guard was met with an unusually loud ovation. Dropping a career-high 47 points with 10 made three-pointers less than 24 hours before warranted such a reception.

Grimes has used a recent promotion to the starting lineup to fuel a career scoring binge. But his official place in the starting lineup could be short-lived when Austin Reaves returns from a left heel bruise that's kept him sidelined for three games. No matter if Grimes gets his name announced at the beginning of the game or comes off the bench, he wants to maintain his rediscovered rhythm.

"I feel like we all respect each other's games, we know what everybody can do," Grimes said Wednesday after he scored 20 points in the Lakers' loss to the Utah Jazz. "JJ [Redick] gives everybody credit to go out there, no matter who it is, to be themselves, so I feel like whenever we get back whole I'll still be able to keep playing how I've been playing."

The Lakers ruled Reaves out for Friday's NBA Cup game against the Sacramento Kings at 7 p.m. at Crypto.com Arena. The guard, who was injured during the third quarter against Milwaukee on Nov. 11, did on-court work Wednesday morning before the Lakers' game against the Jazz, and Redick said it went "well" but didn't have any further idea about Reaves' timeline for return.

In the three games without Reaves, Grimes has flourished, averaging 29.7 points, 6.3 rebounds and 2.7 assists while shooting 57.4% from the field and 63.3% from three-point range.

It's not just the "statement" night in which he joined Kobe Bryant as the only Lakers players to make 10 or more three-pointers in a single game. In five starts this season, Grimes is averaging 24.8 points and shooting 55.3% from three compared with 5.9 points and 24% three-point shooting off the bench. The Lakers are 4-1 in games Grimes has started.

Lakers guard Quentin Grimes, shooting over Jazz center Jaxson Hayes, scored 20 points on Wednesday. (Eric Thayer / Los Angeles Times)

Grimes credited his recent success to finding a rhythm after a slow start to the season in which he was eight-for-33 shooting from three in the first 11 games before missing two games because of a sprained right pinky. During his career, Grimes has averaged 14.3 points per start compared with 8.5 points coming off the bench with 59.6% and 57.8% true shooting percentage, respectively.

Grimes has made a career out of shape-shifting. The 25th pick in the 2021 draft once was just trying to crack the New York Knicks rotation as a three-and-D player. With Dallas, where he played briefly with Luka Doncic, and Philadelphia, he had the ball in his hands more often, jumping between the starting lineup and the bench.

Now with two dynamic scorers in Doncic and Reaves, the Lakers are searching for new ways to let Grimes shine.

"A big part is like for him if he's gonna play off-ball, he needs to feel like he's touched the ball and he feels like he's in a rhythm," Redick said. "So, again, this is a new team, and we're feeling out a bunch of stuff for each individual guy. Our job as coaches is try to maximize each player and maximize the group, and there's a learning curve to that."

Grimes, whose relationship with Redick started in 2023 when Grimes visited Redick to work out one summer but accidentally wandered into his future coach's neighbor's house in the Hamptons, has cherished the open line of communication with the coaching staff.

"It's a good problem to have: a coach that wants to get you the ball, wants to get you into a rhythm, stay in that rhythm that I've been in," Grimes said. "So I feel like it's a good thing. He's really good at what he does. We're rolling right now. So I have no doubt he'll be able to keep me in this rhythm once we all get healthy."

Read more: Swanson: One frigid night against the Jazz doesn't change the fact the Lakers are legit

Grimes was thought to be a strong contender for an opening day starting role next to Reaves and Doncic. But the Lakers started wings Matisse Thybulle and Ziaire Williams first along with center Walker Kessler, and then inserted 6-foot-8 forward Jake LaRavia in Williams' place when the Lancaster native missed three games because of a left foot injury.

Redick has said previously he liked the balance of those lineups: Reaves and Doncic for offensive punch, two perimeter, defensive-minded wings to back them up and hit open three-pointers and Kessler to anchor the middle.

The Lakers' lineup with Doncic, Reaves, Thybulle, LaRavia and Kessler still ranks second in net rating among five-man groups that have played more than 50 minutes together.

Instead of focusing on the starting unit, Redick wants to keep tinkering with lineups to find more minutes with neither Doncic nor Reaves on the court. Coaches think those moments could help other players get into the rhythm on their own so that during the second half when the staff is deciding which lineup will finish the game, everyone will be in a good flow.

"I think with this group and the way this group [is], it's just an egoless group," Redick said. "We're going to be able to be flexible with the starting lineup and flexible with matchups."

#2945. Intuit to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion

Tax software maker Intuit said Thursday that it has agreed to sell marketing subsidiary Mailchimp to Italian technology consolidator Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion in cash and stock. The deal is set to close in early 2027, according to a statement.

The sale is a costly retreat for Intuit, which paid $12 billion for Mailchimp in 2021 in a push beyond its core tax and accounting businesses. Five years later, the software maker is unloading the email-marketing company for less than one-third of that price after Mailchimp became a drag on its overall revenue growth.

The deal is the latest instance of Bending Spoons picking up a once promising technology asset. The company bought productivity software startup Airtable in September for 10% of what it was once worth.

The Bending Spoons portfolio also contains AOL, Brightcove, Eventbrite, Evernote, Meetup, Vimeo, and WeTransfer.

In August Intuit started running Mailchimp as a distinct operating segment. The move was meant to give investors more transparency as the company tried to manage the unit for profitability, Sandeep Aujla, Intuit's finance chief, said at a September company briefing.

Also on Thursday, Intuit announced stronger-than-expected earnings and revenue for its fiscal first quarter, which ended on Oct. 31. The company reported $2.91 in adjusted earnings per share on $4.35 billion in revenue. Analysts polled by LSEG were looking for $2.70 per share and $4.31 billion in revenue.

While Intuit's revenue increased 12% year over year, Mailchimp revenue declined 1% to $313 million. Analysts polled by StreetAccount had expected $314.4 million.

Management called for $22.88 to $23.12 in adjusted earnings per share for the 2027 fiscal year, with $23.081 billion to $23.365 billion in revenue. Analysts polled by LSEG had predicted $23.62 in adjusted earnings per share on $23.43 billion in revenue. Intuit shares tumbled 15% in extended trading.

The company said Mailchimp should produce $1.256 billion to $1.266 billion in fiscal 2027 revenue, which would be down 1% to flat year over year. In August Aujla said Intuit anticipated Mailchimp's higher effective prices offsetting increased client churn. Mailchimp was founded in 2001. Rivals include Klaviyo, which went public in 2023.

Berkshire Hathaway invested $600 million in Bending Spoons when the acquirer went public in July, and in October Bending Spoons said Berkshire invested another $330 million.

#2944. Cutting pressure in half and beating Cover-0: Washington’s OL is finding answers at the right time - Daily Slop

Editor's note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy!

"Teams noticed that we had a 14-point lead, that they got us off the field and then put points on the board when they had the ball," Allegretti said. "That Week 5 game influenced a lot."

The Commanders faced a similar trend last season. They entered Week 6 against the Bears at 3-2 but without injured starting receivers Terry McLaurin and Noah Brown. Washington then struggled when Chicago pressed its perimeter receivers at the line of scrimmage, daring them to win downfield. The strategy showed promise. Dallas deployed its version the following week, beginning a stretch of four consecutive Commanders losses by at least 21 points. Injuries aside, Washington never solved the press-coverage problem.

This time, Washington may be finding answers before the latest defensive trend becomes another season-long issue.

There is no gentle way to say it: Dexter Lawrence has been a problem for every offensive line he has faced this season. The three-time Pro Bowler arrived in Cincinnati via trade this past spring and has looked fully rejuvenated in his first year with the Bengals. Through ten weeks, Lawrence holds an 87.6 PFF overall grade — second among all interior defensive linemen in football — with a 89.6 pass-rush grade that ranks first at the position. He has racked up 22 total pressures, four sacks, three hits, and 15 hurries. Teams have been double-teaming him on nearly 80% of his pass-rush snaps, and he still wins.

Which is exactly why the center situation matters so much heading into Monday night. Lucas Patrick missed last week with injury but returned to practice Wednesday, though Dan Quinn stopped short of declaring him the starter. That leaves the door open for Nick Allegretti, who stepped in against the Giants on Thursday night and delivered one of the offense's cleaner weeks in terms of protection and communication. The offense visibly flowed better — fewer high snaps derailing Daniels before plays even started, and cleaner interior windows for the run game to operate through.

The question now is whether Washington rolls with what's working or returns to Patrick in a spot where continuity matters. Lawrence's ability to collapse the pocket from the inside forces quick decisions and kills run lanes. If whoever is playing at center cannot get a hat on Lawrence consistently, the Bengals will dictate tempo all night. The Commanders know this. What they decide at center will be one of the biggest pregame storylines on Monday.

To read more of this Commanders Roundtable article, CLICK HERE

The schematic turnaround addresses a recurring early-season issue for Washington, transforming pass protection from a liability into a platform for downfield efficiency. Establishing reliable pass blocking allows the offense to dial up vertical concepts with Burks while keeping Daniels protected in the pocket. The win solidifies Washington's offensive identity following an inconsistent start.

By the numbers: Washington's pressure rate dropped from 46% (seventh-worst in the NFL in Week 5) to 23% in Week 10 (third-best mark in the league). Daniels has completed 138 of 213 passes for 1,499 yards with 10 touchdowns and two interceptions in 2026 through seven games. Sinnott has caught five passes for 48 yards and one touchdown in 2026 through nine games.

One of the biggest turnarounds from the Commanders tie back in Week 5 against the Giants and their win over the Giants on Thursday night was the plan of attack against Cover-0. In Week 5, the Giants spammed Cover-0 blitzes throughout the second half and overtime and the Commanders just couldn't handle it. They continually attempted to take shots down the field to try and hit explosive plays rather than just finding a simple quick solution.

Daniels was seeing those blitzes a lot better and it showed in the most critical moment.

Having thrown two late interceptions, it looked like the Commanders season was over, but the defense bailed Daniels out and gave him another opportunity, which he wasn't going to pass up. On third and four with under a minute remaining in the game, the Giants of course show Daniels another Cover-0 blitz. This time, Daniels doesn't adjust the protection, but instead signals to Stefon Diggs in the slot to change his route. In the first game, when Daniels saw Cover-0, he often checked into a shot play to try and attack the blitz and throw a big touchdown over the top of it. But clearly this time they were looking to play smarter, and it worked out much better for them.

Daniels adjusts Diggs route, having him run a slant against the slot corner. When he snaps the ball, the defense comes on the blitz, but the defensive tackle to the right side of the line pops up and drops out into coverage, trying to take away a hot throw over the middle. Daniels just checked into a hot throw over the middle with Diggs running a slant, so that could potentially be a problem. But Daniels does a great job adjusting his throw to beat that defensive lineman dropping into coverage.

Diggs runs a great route, beating the corner with a nice stutter move before sharply cutting across his face to get inside. The throw from Daniels has to be slightly behind him because of that defensive lineman dropping into coverage, but Diggs does well to adjust to the pass and make the grab. Diggs breaks a diving tackle from the slot corner and gets some help from fellow receiver Van Jefferson, who helps block the other nearby defender. With both defenders out of the picture, Diggs runs uncontested into the end zone for a 32-yard game-winning touchdown.

It goes to show that you can still score a big touchdown against Cover-0 without having to try and take a deep shot constantly. As I said back in Week 5, I don't mind that their philosophy against Cover-0 is to go on the attack, in fact I quite like it. It offers you one-on-one matchups and I like that they feel like they can take shots with those matchups. But they clearly went too far in Week 5 in trying to throw bombs down the field. This game proved there's more ways to go about it. Winning a one-on-one doesn't have to be 20 yards down the field, it can be a quick slant like this when you have Stefon Diggs or Antonio Williams in the slot. With it being Cover-0, if you win that one-on-one quickly, there's every chance the receiver can run freely after the catch and score as there's no safety help over the top.

So credit should go to David Blough and Jayden Daniels for making that adjustment. It's a shame they couldn't have made it back in Week 5 because they would have won that game too if they had, but it paid off for them this time around and it meant that the Commanders have just about kept their season alive.

"We're headed in the right direction," Robertson said. "But that's why everybody don't run it except the Vikings."

The Commanders' defense has faced another top offense this season: the San Francisco 49ers. The 49ers scored 20 points and gained 303 yards in the first half. But, faced with more Washington blitzes after halftime, they managed only a field goal and 105 yards. Quarterback Brock Purdy completed just one-of-four passes and was sacked twice.

The second-half performance represented the sort of improvement Washington needed — and will need against Cincinnati. Over their last three games, the Commanders rank seventh in scoring and eighth on third downs. They were 25th in yards and on third down and 31st in scoring over the first seven weeks. And they've now allowed 23 points or less in four consecutive games for the first time since 2022, when they recorded 10 in a row.

The Commanders' defense has been at its best when it's attacking. That doesn't mean Washington has to blitz all the time, but that mindset must remain.

Generating splash plays — sacks, tackles for loss and turnovers — requires taking risks. Being timid won't save the Commanders from the Bengals.

To read more of this Washington Post article, CLICK HERE

Chase, Higgins, and Brown vs. Washington's Secondary

The Cincinnati offense does not have a weak link. Tee Higgins is playing the best football of his career, averaging career-highs in receptions and yards per game through ten weeks. At the halfway point of the season, he was on pace for 104 catches, over 1,700 receiving yards, and ten touchdowns — numbers that belong in the MVP conversation. Ja'Marr Chase, as always, is a matchup nightmare. Through the first part of the season, the duo combined to give Joe Burrow the most dangerous one-two punch in the AFC, and Chase Brown adds a receiving dimension out of the backfield that stretches linebackers horizontally. Cincinnati leads the NFL in net passing yards per game at 298.3.

Washington's secondary enters this game four weeks into being fully healthy as a unit — Trey Amos, Amik Robertson, Nick Cross, Jeremy Reaves, and Quan Martin are all active and communicating together — and they have improved as a unit each week. The turnovers have been a genuine bright spot. But this is a different level of test. This is not a pick-your-poison situation; this is a pick-your-poison-and-then-the-other-one-also-poisons-you situation. The Commanders cannot take Chase or Higgins away without gifting the other a favorable matchup.

Washington has to accept that Cincinnati is going to move the ball and score. The assignment is not to shut them down — it's to stay disciplined, contest every throw, avoid giving up a lot of chunk plays of 20-plus yards, and generate turnovers. Force the Bengals to eat nine-play drives instead of two-play touchdowns. Take away the explosive play.

The No. 61 overall selection is giving up just 50.0 percent of his targets and an 85.2 passer rating when targeted. Amos looks assured in coverage, and his presence has given the Commanders a highly productive cornerback trio alongside Amik Robertson and Rasul Douglas.

Running back Jacory Croskey-Merritt (groin) was listed as a full participant in Thursday's practice after having his 21-day return-to-practice window opened from injured reserve earlier in the week. Williams's first target against New York came on third-and-one from the Giants' 31 in the third quarter. Jayden Daniels hit him short to the right, and Williams took it to the house to give Washington a 17–14 lead. His other catch, an 11-yard gain on first-and-10, came after the Giants took the lead back in the fourth. He got one early-down opportunity, and it moved the chains.

I've been asking for more of that since the 49ers game. Williams ran 35 routes that night, but all four targets came on third down in the fourth quarter. He caught three, and each moved the chains. Against the Eagles, he had seven targets, five catches for 54 yards and a second-and-10 conversion. David Blough has made room for him on the field. The play that kept the Washington Commanders' season from falling off a cliff will be replayed because of the ending. Stefon Diggs had already caught Jayden Daniels' pass; he had already broken away from two New York Giants tacklers when he arrived at the goal line at MetLife Stadium, completely in the clear. The clock ticked down. Diggs turned his back to face upfield, then performed a reverse plunge into the end zone for the game-winning touchdown.

Among the players Flowers trained then was Vernon Davis, the former Maryland star who was in his third year as a standout tight end for the San Francisco 49ers. Diggs was a kid. But he was also an immediate presence — even at 14, with NFL players in the room.

"I always felt like no one could outwork me, or there was no one close to me when I was working out," Davis said. "But when Steph came, that all changed. His work ethic, his energy, everything was just next-level."

"He's very disciplined," McLaurin said. "He's very detail-oriented — day in, day out, rep in, rep out. He likes to talk s—. He likes to have fun. But there's work behind all that."
