Okonkwo's performance this season is fully in line with the first four years of his NFL career in Tennessee, but he was supposed to be more than that for the Commanders. There was hope that he could take another step forward at age 27 to become a major part of Washington's passing game. Okonkwo himself told the Commanders' website that "this is the place where I can finally unleash."

It hasn't happened. Okonkwo has never matched the three touchdowns (on only 32 catches) or 14.1 yards per reception he had as a rookie in 2022. He's having another season of reasonable but relatively inefficient production. His 69% catch rate isn't terrible, but it's still below average for tight ends, and the same goes for his average of 9.7 yards per reception. Okonkwo also hasn't found the end zone yet for Washington, but he'll probably end up with a touchdown or two before the season is over. It's just a little disappointing because the Commanders hoped for more.

What has gone right? The Commanders are tied for ninth in plays gaining 20-plus yards; their percentage of plays (6.4) that gain that many yards overall is their best since 2016. Plus, their percentage of pass plays (15.5) is their highest since 2017. Keeping Daniels healthy after he missed two games for a dislocated elbow has been huge.

What has gone wrong? Game management. Washington has committed too many pre-snap penalties, ranking fourth in false starts and third in delay of games. In a Week 5 tie versus the Giants, the Commanders mismanaged the last play, in part because the play wasn't communicated quickly enough. The run game has been ineffective.

Key to second half: Daniels' growing comfort in the system and developing a consistent run game. Daniels has started five consecutive games for the first time since his rookie season two years ago. In a new system, that should result in growth. But the Commanders must develop a run game, otherwise Daniels will have to provide high-level play to win. — John Keim

The 2026 Eagles offense has been one of the worst in franchise history, and it continues to get worse throughout the season. They are last in total offense, averaging 260.2 yards per game. Philly is also tied for 31st in points per game (16.4), 28th in rushing yards per game (88.6), and 27th in passing yards per game (171.7).

Eagles are practicing patience with Sean Mannion because they have to (for the time being)

[P]layer development, play calling, and decision-making are things he can control, and those have not gone well. The rookies had slow starts, and players who needed bounce-back seasons, like Dickerson and Barkley, haven't been able to get there.

Philly's offensive line has been the biggest problem in the Mannion tenure, with the group looking like the worst it's been in nearly three decades.

Eagles fans wanted to see a change in the offense, but there is really no one on the staff that would be any better than what Mannion is doing. Sure, Josh Grizzard and Parks Frazier have play-calling experience, but they were not great when they were doing it in the past, so how would they do any better?

Mannion has leaned heavily on three-wide receiver formations, playing 11 personnel at 78 percent, tied with the Titans for the league's highest rate. That's one reason they also haven't run the ball well; most of their receivers can't block.

Mannion's offense was supposed to be predicated on multi-tight end formations, but Dallas Goedert missed two games and has been nursing his sore knee, playing just 56% of snaps. TE Johnny Mundt, signed to help in run blocking, hasn't blocked well at all. The Eagles are trying to get rookie second-round TE Eli Stowers on the field more, but he's also not an effective enough blocker to help boost the run game and neither is TE Grant Calcaterra.

Mannion must show something, anything, to illustrate why the Eagles were so thrilled to hire him despite no prior play calling experience, and why he was once referred to as an "evil genius."

Philadelphia Eagles: There were warning signs this season could be a bit rough for the Eagles. But nobody could have foreseen a 2-7 record with an active seven-game losing streak and a starting quarterback who wasn't even in the building for training camp. It's hard to blame the team for how bad it's been, given the circumstances. Jalen Hurts is out for the season, a key player retired mid-season and there's a long list of injuries, including Saquon Barkley and DeVonta Smith.

after years of bad defenses, the hope was that things would turn around in 2026, but they haven't. Under defensive coordinator Christian Parker in his first season in the role, the Cowboys are just as bad, if not worse, than they were defensively under Matt Eberflus in 2025, which was the worst defense in team history.

Parker, who again is calling plays for the first time, has now essentially been demoted. What makes it worse is that Dallas is still letting him keep the defensive coordinator title, but Pettine is now the man that will make all the calls on game day. Keeping that title on him but taking away a huge part of his responsibility is humiliating.

The organization would have been better off just firing Parker and going their separate ways.

Nobody is saying that this is the case, but stripping Parker of play-calling duties and giving them to Pettine after a month makes it seem like the move to bring him in wasn't to help, but rather take his job. The Cowboys praised the hiring of Parker all offseason long, yet they only gave him two months before publicly shaming him.

[The whole] situation is a terrible look for the Cowboys, and it speaks volumes as to why they've been a laughing stock around the league for quite some time.

Is the best case scenario still winning the NFC East for these Cowboys?

[W]ith the context we now have through ten weeks, beating a Commanders team that went on to beat the Giants team the Cowboys are still chasing at home is a decent result. But nobody will forget that Jayden Daniels was knocked out of the game, and nobody is getting away with moving the goalposts a country mile for this season along with that. From potential playoff contenders to happy to be in the mix with the… 5-3-1 Giants? I'm not buying it, and oh by the way the most glaring and obvious thing the Giants do better than the Cowboys to start having instant success is coach better under their new leadership.

The team is so up and down, even from play to play. They will have a strong defensive stop on one play, maybe a sack or a run stuff, then give up a big gainer – usually, it seems, on third and long. And the offense is not exempt. They will have several good plays, then a couple of dropped passes or a breakdown in the blocking scheme, and Bryan Anger or Brandon Aurbrey will have to come out. And if things weren't bad enough, Aubrey is showing signs of having the yips, missing kicks we used to take for granted.

I can't recall a time where both the present and the future feels so shaky for the Cowboys, or trust in the leadership that can get an organization through shaky times is so low. After all, Pettine has only been here since October, and now he's calling plays? I don't know if we're even grasping how much of a structural failure it takes to get to that point in any season.

There are six games left in Indianapolis' season. That's about the most positive takeaway. Harsh and sardonic as that might read, the Colts looked like a defeated team throughout the majority of this game. With much of the most talented players on the roster having been traded or injured, the remaining Colts have the appearance of squad wanting to go home for the holidays and never come back.

The offense, in particular, was dreadful, netting just 167 yards, eight first downs and going 1 of 11 on third down. Much-maligned quarterback Daniel Jones will likely get skewered, and probably deservingly so, but Jonathan Taylor, the most positive face of the franchise, had an equally horrendous game. Jones was 12 of 27 for 144 yards, an interception and a dismal 45.9 rating. He was pressured on 66% of his dropbacks in the first half and 56.7% for the game. Taylor averaged 1.9 yards per carry on 11 attempts for a grand total of 21 yards. Granted, comparing quarterback play to running back play is hardly apples to apples, but each player is working with the same complement of talent around him. To place the blame on one player at this point is foolish. Jones looked professional early, guiding the Colts to a 3-0 lead on the game-opening drive. Yes, the Colts led this one, 3-0. #2943. LSU president orders RJ Luis benched amid SEC expulsion threat

The RJ Luis Jr. drama came to an inevitable and ignominious end Thursday, Nov. 19, as the LSU guard is to be benched by Will Wade at the behest of LSU President Wade Rousseau after playing in one game on Wednesday, Nov. 18.

Luis, who played under the protection of a court order, scored 11 points for the Tigers in his season debut against Louisiana-Monroe, which ended in a 79-67 LSU win. Luis was added to the roster Tuesday, Nov. 17, with Rousseau saying in a statement:

"LSU is a member institution that will act in accordance with that order. The conference has confirmed it will do the same and has stated in writing that it 'will abide by the terms of the preliminary injunction while it remains in place and will not impose penalties or fines on LSU if (it) places Mr. Luis on its men's basketball roster."

Hayes: LSU played chicken with the SEC — and finally blinked. Was it worth it?

'Really gross': Dan Hurley rips NCAA basketball eligibility crisis, blames coaches

In a course reversal Thursday, Rousseau said: "In my role as President of the LSU System, after further review, I have instructed LSU Men's Basketball Coach Will Wade to not play RJ Luis."

In a statement, Luis' lawyer Elliot Abrams said there were threats of expelling LSU from the SEC if Luis continued to play.

"The SEC's decision to threaten a member with expulsion if it plays an eligible student-athlete is reprehensible and seriously harms a young person who was caught in the middle of a power struggle having nothing to do with him," Abrams wrote in a statement to USA TODAY Sports.

District Attorney Tony Clayton, another of Luis' attorney's, told The Daily Advertiser, part of the USA TODAY Network, that Luis told him to give up the fight.

Luis declared for the 2025 NBA Draft and was in the Jazz and Celtics organizations, but joined a lawsuit to get another year of eligibility after being waived before the start of the 2025 season.

Wade didn't elaborate on his decision to play Luis after Wednesday's game.

"I'm going to refer to our university's statement from yesterday," he said. "I'll be happy to answer any questions about how he played, but going to refer in terms of anything about his eligibility and rostering him to the university's statement yesterday.

"Everybody who played tonight is eligible."

LSU went through this same situation with football, when Dae'Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris were cleared to play by the courts, added to the roster, and ultimately later removed. Expulsion talks arose during that time as well.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: LSU president orders RJ Luis benched amid SEC expulsion threat

One study, published Thursday by researchers at Boston University and Banner Health, was based on a small sample of former American football players who donated blood while alive. #2939. Kushner says Russia 'comfortable' with idea of NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine

U.S. envoy Jared Kushner has said Russia may accept NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine, adding that President Donald Trump wants to bring an end to Russia's full-scale invasion "with Europe by his side."

His comments come shortly after Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping held historic trilateral talks on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, a meeting that did not appear to result in any concessions on Ukraine or European security.

"I think we've got the Russians comfortable with that concept where any security guarantee for Ukraine would be based on Article 5," Kushner said alongside European leaders at a news conference in Germany on Thursday, referring to the part of NATO's treaty that enshrines the principle of collective defense.

"I think that that comes with at least what the Russians are saying, which is their intention is, when this war is over, to not have another war in the future," he added. Kushner, who is Trump's son-in-law, was at the conference in Berlin alongside fellow U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff.

They have led the Trump administration's efforts to end Russia's nearly five-year-long war with Ukraine.

Article 5 defines an attack against one NATO member as an attack against all members. The alliance calls it a "unique and enduring principle that binds its members together, committing them to protect each other and setting a spirit of solidarity."

Ukraine has long held ambitions to join the alliance. Russia has previously said that if Kyiv joined NATO, it would cause problems for many years.

It was not immediately clear what form potential security guarantees would take, or whether Russia or Ukraine would accept them. Russia's Foreign Ministry, Ukraine's Foreign Ministry and NATO were not immediately available to comment when contacted by CNBC on Friday morning.

"From America's perspective, giving an Article 5-like security guarantee is a really, really big deal and I think that that is something that President Trump is open to, but obviously it has to be in America's interest to do that," Kushner said.

Russia launched a wave of missile and drone attacks on Ukraine's energy and transport infrastructure overnight, damaging three bridges in Kyiv and killing at least three people, authorities said.

Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said via Telegram on Friday that Kyiv's Podilskyi, Darnytskyi and Southern crossings had been damaged by missile strikes, with experts currently assessing the damage.

Russia's Defense Ministry said it had carried out a "massive" strike on several Ukrainian cities, targeting enterprises of the country's defense industry and warehouses used in the production and storage of missiles and drones.

Putin vowed on Thursday that Russia would respond to Ukraine's attacks on the Kerch Bridge, adding it would be "much more painful." The bridge, which links Russia to occupied Crimea and is one of Putin's signature projects, was damaged by repeated Ukrainian attacks this week.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Tuesday described it as an "unprecedented operation" several weeks in the making, with Ukraine's defense forces, security services and weapons manufacturers involved.

#2938. Bears’ Caleb Williams Focused on Bouncing Back After Four-Interception Game

Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams' four-interception performance against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Week 9 was uncharacteristic of the ball security he had displayed throughout his NFL career.

The bigger question now is how Williams responds to that performance and bounces back over the remainder of the season. That will be especially important as the Bears enter the second half of the season with a challenging stretch of games remaining on their schedule.

Williams described two of the interceptions as "funky" and acknowledged that one was a bad decision, but the four-interception performance was still frustrating for the Bears quarterback, with his biggest disappointment stemming from feeling like he had let his teammates down.

"The biggest thing is, the frustration comes from the feeling of, for me, personally, I always don't want to let my teammates down," Williams said. "That's always big for me, and in those situations, I feel like did. That's the frustrating part that lingers."

Even after throwing four interceptions, Williams still led the Bears on a late-game drive that put them in position to win, setting up the field goal that sealed the game.

That ability to respond is something that Bears offensive coordinator Press Taylor has seen Williams demonstrate time and again, particularly in high-pressure situations. His history of delivering in critical moments has given the coaching staff confidence in how he handles adversity and moves forward from difficult performances.

"That's something that's been his thing, you know, late in last year, you think of the late game plays he's able to make," Taylor said. "He's demonstrated that over and over, so as you see it over and over and continue to reveal itself, then you're going to trust him more and more with that type of situations. And every game is really a learning opportunity for all of us to learn how everybody responds to certain situations."

Even with the four interceptions against Tampa Bay, Williams' career interception rate remains unmatched in NFL history among quarterbacks with 1,000 or more pass attempts. It's a testament to the level of ball security he has maintained throughout his young NFL career, and why one rough performance doesn't change the bigger picture.

With the bye week giving him time to step away from the field, Williams has shifted his focus from the frustration of the performance toward what he can learn from it and apply moving forward.

"I've moved on from it," Williams said. "It's more of a, how can I get better? What can I be better at? Just finding ways to be more consistent."

That starts with turning the page and shifting the focus to the New Orleans Saints. The Bears have remained committed to taking the season one game at a time, with the goal of going 1-0 each week rather than looking too far ahead.

For Williams, that means applying what he learned against Tampa Bay while keeping his attention on the opportunity in front of him.

#2935. Parsons’ return imminent but doesn’t solve Packers’ biggest problem

For all of the Green Bay Packers' issues through ten games of the 2026 season, getting to the quarterback generally hasn't been one of them. The Packers' defense ranks fourth in the NFL in sacks this year, with pressure helping the team rank second in interceptions and fifth in overall passer rating against.

Now the cavalry appears set to arrive. Micah Parsons is on his way back, seemingly with the intent of playing next Wednesday against the Los Angeles Rams, and his presence will only further bolster the team's ability to get after the quarterback. It remains to be seen how he will be deployed — expect a light workload for the next few games, perhaps with him only playing on passing downs — but his return should provide an emotional lift as well as a physical one for a defense that's already playing well.

As that last phrase suggests, though, the defense isn't really the Packers' problem right now. That is of course the offensive line, where some recent front office decisions have helped set the table for a catastrophic season up front. One can't help wondering if this team would be functioning better had Elgton Jenkins been kept around for one more year; had the team not invested so much money in Aaron Banks; had Anthony Belton — wait, the front office drafted him as a guard and he's been thrust in at tackle by circumstance and the coaching staff, so that one probably isn't on the front office.

And then there is that coaching staff. From a poor overall offensive game plan last week against Minnesota to players seemingly having no idea what they're doing on a play-to-play basis, the offensive coaches should have spent their few off days in a shortened bye week doing some serious self-evaluation.

So, while Parsons' return is an exciting storyline for the Packers, it almost feels like we're adding the whipped cream on top of an excellent pumpkin pie while smoke is billowing out of the oven as the turkey burns. So let's get that main course under control, yeah?

Packers cut Pierre Strong to clear roster spot for Micah Parsons' imminent return | Packersnews.com ($)Strong's release is all but assuredly a move to open a roster spot for #1, and we should probably expect Strong to return to the practice squad if he clears waivers.

When you get basically nothing out of a 4-year, $48 million deal (Nate Hobbs) and a 4-year, $77 million contract (Aaron Banks), it's going to set you back significantly.

Brian Gutekunst vindicated as former Packers struggle in new homes | Packers WireStill, it's not all bad for the front office. Using PFF grades (with the usual caveat on that), nearly every player that the Packers let walk this offseason is having a career-worst season. And the one who isn't, Kingsley Enagbare, is being outplayed by his replacement, Barryn Sorrell.

Packers LB Isaiah McDuffie 'just doesn't flinch' | Packers.comThe team's position coaches spoke earlier this week, but the big comments were about Parsons. From Demarcus Covington: "As he's been getting ready to play, whenever that is, he's always been in the classroom with us the whole time, and he's done a really good job with that leadership portion, helping us out throughout the week, film study with the guys and then also just giving his evaluation within the meeting room."

I won't mince words: suspending a player when he's already on injured reserve is an embarrassing look for the NFL. Yeah, you're taking three game checks, but when it comes to sending a message about actions having consequences, this message falls pretty flat.

#2931. Nate Ament, former Tennessee star, scores career-high 18 points for Bucks

The Milwaukee Bucks were once again haunted by the past.

One day after facing ex-star Giannis Antetokounmpo for the first time in Miami, former Milwaukee players Damian Lillard and Jrue Holiday came to Fiserv Forum and helped the Portland Trail Blazers beat the Bucks,124-114, on Nov. 19.

A very positive sign for the Bucks is Nate Ament looking comfortable on offense.

The 13th overall pick in the 2026 NBA Draft had a career-high 18 points.

"Very confident, I think," Ament said. "Kind of just learning the offense and learning the players I'm playing with.

"Learning the spots I can attack and just the decision-making. How quick that's come for me. If I'm going to shoot it, shoot it. If I'm going to drive, drive. Kind of reading the defense and knowing what I'm going to do before I catch it."

When Ament was in college at Tennessee last season, he only lost 12 games all season. So it's been an adjustment to get used to the losses piling up.

"It's been very tough," Ament said. "Very tough."

"And we've walked about it a lot. (Burries) said he's never lost more than two games in a row in his life. So it's been crazy. In the end, I think it will good for us. Just learning how to (win) and how to respond to losses."

#2930. Is a bottom in for the Nasdaq-100? Charts to watch

(See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.)

Is the Nasdaq-100's recent bounce a sign that the bottom is in? We're going to look at several charts to help answer that question.

First, let's remember how we got here. In September, the NDX broke out from a bullish cup-and-handle pattern, producing a 33,200-upside target. That breakout quickly failed, however, and gave way to a bearish pattern that broke down aggressively two weeks ago.

The decline brought the index relatively close to its 26,350 downside target before the current rebound began.

Zooming out, it's telling to see where the bounce originated. Three important forms of support converged in the 25,000-26,000 area:

This confluence of support helped encourage buying after a roughly 15% decline.

For perspective, we also see what larger drawdowns of 20%, 30%, 40%, and 50% would look like … a lot worse.

The following chart tracks NDX drawdowns from 52-week highs going back to just after the financial crisis. Only a handful of declines exceeded 20%, and three produced relatively quick reversals: late 2018, the Covid lows in 2020 and April 2025.

Historically, buying into declines of approximately 15%–25% has generally paid off, even when additional downside occurred first (yellow highlights).

The chart also highlights previous declines of 10%–16% in green, putting the current pullback into perspective.

The major exception was 2022, when the NDX eventually declined nearly 36% over approximately 10 months ... a much worse outcome, which many investors are concerned could happen again now.

That raises the key question: Are we experiencing another routine correction, or the early stages of a larger bear market?

One important clue will be how far this bounce progresses.

Any rally that fails to reclaim the previous highs could establish a significant lower high. Additional lower highs would provide stronger evidence of a developing, longer downtrend.

We saw this in March 2022, when that first sharp rebound effort failed to reach the previous high before a much more severe decline followed.

The bottom line: The current bounce is encouraging, particularly given where it originated and knowing how well buying prior 10-20% drawdowns has paid off.

From here, it's all about the follow through.  We don't need to see new highs right away, but any rally from here that's met with another wave of strong selling could reignite downside momentum.

#2927. Some FHA borrowers pay mortgage insurance for a decade or more. There's an industry push to change the rules

Homeowners with conventional loans who pay mortgage insurance typically can shed that expense — meant to protect a lender against loss if the borrower defaults — once they've built sufficient equity in their home. But that's not how it works for those with a Federal Housing Administration loan.

A fresh push to change the rules governing mortgage insurance for FHA loans came this week, after the Department of Housing and Urban Development released a report to Congress on Monday showing that the FHA's mortgage insurance fund remains financially strong. Its capital ratio — a measure of its financial cushion against potential losses — was 10.29% as of Sept. 30, down from 11.47% a year earlier, but still more than five times the 2% minimum required by Congress.

"The program's financial strength provides an opportunity for targeted changes that improve affordability for borrowers while preserving the long-term stability" of FHA's insurance fund, said Bob Broeksmit, president and CEO of the Mortgage Bankers Association, in a statement released after the report was issued. The trade group was one of a handful of organizations that put out statements calling for changes.

The push, which revives a longstanding mortgage industry request, also comes several weeks after President Donald Trump issued an executive order that included calling for the launch of a federal pilot program that would cancel mortgage insurance on certain conventional loans once borrowers meet equity requirements.

The order would apply generally to future loans backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac — two government-sponsored enterprises that purchase qualifying mortgages from lenders and resell them as bundled securities. It wouldn't apply to FHA loans.

FHA mortgages are issued by private lenders but insured by the federal government, which protects lenders against losses if a borrower defaults. The loans are designed to make homeownership more accessible, particularly for borrowers with limited savings for a down payment or with lower credit scores.

Affordability challenges persist in the housing market, with elevated home prices and mortgage rates putting homeownership out of reach for many prospective buyers. Existing homeowners are also facing rising costs alongside their mortgages, including property taxes and homeowners insurance amid overall high inflation.

About 83% of new FHA purchase loans went to first-time homebuyers in the most recent fiscal year, according to the FHA report to Congress. Altogether, the FHA insured more than 8.4 million mortgages as of Sept. 30.

The median age of first-time buyers is 40, according to a new report from the National Association of Realtors.

FHA loans also require borrowers to pay mortgage insurance regardless of the size of their down payment. Under current rules established in 2013, FHA borrowers with a down payment that's less than 10% of the loan must pay mortgage insurance premiums for the duration of the loan. Those who put 10% or more down pay that insurance for 11 years.

Borrowers generally pay both an upfront mortgage insurance premium and an annual premium, which is typically divided into monthly payments. The upfront premium is usually 1.75% of the base loan amount and can be financed into the mortgage. For many borrowers with 30-year FHA loans, the annual premium is 0.55% of the outstanding loan balance.

Conventional mortgages generally don't require mortgage insurance unless the loan is for more than 80% of the home's value. In 2022, the premium typically ranged from 0.58% to 1.86% annually, according to Fannie Mae.

If those borrowers have to pay mortgage insurance, they can typically request its removal once they've built 20% equity in the home, or it is automatically canceled when their loan drops to 78% of the original value.

The mortgage industry has floated two different proposals.

One would reduce the rate that applies to FHA mortgage insurance. For example, the Mortgage Bankers Association recently suggested a rate reduction of 20 basis points, which would lower the standard 0.55% rate to 0.35% for new borrowers.

For example: On a $350,000 mortgage, a 0.55% rate generally translates into $1,925 annually, or about $160 monthly, at the start of the loan. As the principal owed slowly goes down over time through a borrower's monthly payments, so does that mortgage insurance amount.

At 0.35%, the annual premium would be $1,225 at the start of the loan, or $102 monthly — a difference of $58 per month.

The FHA last cut that rate in 2023, when it was reduced from 0.85%. At the time, HUD estimated that affected borrowers would save an average of $800 annually. However, in the FHA's new report to Congress, the agency noted that the 2023 cut has reduced the fund's revenue, contributing to a decline in its capital ratio.

The other industry proposal would implement auto-cancellation of premiums once the loan balance fell to 78% of the home's original value at purchase — in other words, the same as for Fannie- and Freddie-backed mortgages.

"Cancellation prevents the squeeze for borrowers who have paid down their loans and shouldn't be paying for coverage they have outgrown," said Michael Farrell, president of the National Association of Mortgage Brokers, a trade group that generally has supported the cancellation proposal.

"NAMB believes that cancellation at 78% protects the [FHA insurance fund], because premiums can restart if the [capital] ratio ever falls to 2%," Farrell said.

FHA mortgages received that treatment from 2001 through 2013, but the agency eliminated it to shore up its insurance fund after financial reserves deteriorated over time following the housing market crash, which led to the 2008 financial crisis.

Whether the proposals will go anywhere this time is uncertain. HUD, which oversees the FHA, did not respond to a CNBC email seeking more information.

#2926. How Columbus Crew turned it all around to set up MLS playoff showdown vs. Messi

It wasn't working. Issa Tall had to admit that. Well, he didn't really have to. The results told the story for him.

The Columbus Crew didn't win in its first five MLS matches. By the World Cup break, 15 games in, they'd only added two more. There needed to be changes, and they needed to be big.

In May, he fired coach Henrik Rydström, his first coaching hire as the Crew's chief soccer officer, though he was quick to point out he was involved with previous hires including bringing in Wilfried Nancy. He spent big in the summer, revamping the Crew's attack and adding pieces while bidding farewell to some regulars. Ten players arrived, and eight went out.

The Crew turned the boat around, going from worst in the Eastern Conference to closing the season on a six-game win streak and having won eight of their last nine. That was enough not only to jump out of Thursday's wild card match but to set up a First Round playoff series with Inter Miami, the reigning champion led by Lionel Messi. They also pushed to the U.S. Open Cup final, falling to St. Louis City in a penalty shootout.

All of it led Tall to believe he made the right decisions, moving on quickly from the coach he thought was the right man for the job.

"Some people could've waited the full year. Maybe it would've been safer, but that's not me. That's not us as a club. That's not even the way we play!" Tall told USA TODAY Sports ahead of the playoffs. "You see how we are bold and are not afraid of taking risk. At the end of the day, it wasn't even a risk necessarily. It was necessary for our players, for our club as a whole and I think ultimately we made the right decision to do it at that time."

Tall still stands by Rydström as a good coach, something he's proving while leading Hammarby in Sweden which currently sits atop of the table after running off five consecutive wins. But he wasn't the right fit for the Crew in the post-Nancy era.

The Crew turned to Courtois, a former Crew academy and MLS Next Pro coach who continued the idea first expressed on the field so successfully by Nancy's teams. The squad might not have been the entirely right squad, either.

Tall turned to a scouting network led by Mark Nichols, bringing in a proven MLS veteran in Santi Rodriguez, Chile national team forward Gonzalo Tapia, securing a loan deal for Moroccan winger Anass Zaroury and signing designated player Brais Mendez, a Spanish attacker whose arrival from Real Sociedad brought to mind that of Cucho Hernandez. While Mendez is at a different stage of his carer than Hernandez was, he turned into a star in Columbus, showing his full potential in MLS after frustrating stints with Watford and loans in Huseca, Mallorca and Getafe.

Those new players bolstered a core that had been depleted by player movement but still included veteran defender Steven Moreira, homegrown center back Sean Zawadzki, fullback Mo Farsi - formerly a futsal specialist who the current Crew staff helped turn into an outdoor stalwart - and is backed by U.S. goalkeeping hopeful Patrick Schulte.

After the Crew's past success, particularly signings under Tim Bezbatchenko that led to MLS Cup wins in 2020 and 2023, plus a Leagues Cup title in 2024, Tall knew similar results would be expected from him when he took over in the summer of 2024. It's a challenge he welcomed, saying demanding fans and an expectant ownership group means he's in the right type of environment.

"To be in a place where there are standards and there are expectations? It's a blessing," he said. "It's a challenge because it's hard to top what we've done in the past - and I felt like I was part of that. I'm no stranger to the success we've had but blessing to have such a clear identity a clear style of play and that we are still to this day seen as a model club in MLS. It does add pressure, but it's welcome pressure because it shows that people care."

The fans have enjoyed the turnaround but may not be placated with another piece of silverware this year.

While the Crew have hit on seemingly every player signing, Tall was quick to remind that even teams with successful track records can point to players who didn't fully click with their club. No matter how much data and how many analytics numbers are run, how many character references are checked, how much game film is scouted, Tall said sometimes a player gets into the building and doesn't work with the existing group.

That's why he also is at work on the winter strategy, looking to equip the current group with what it needs to not just make the playoffs but contend for a title.

"There's more to come," he said. "I think this is just the beginning. Literally, they came this summer, and it took time to click. We're able to qualify playoffs, you have a big one coming up this weekend and then there's a spring season that we look forward to."

Of course, there could still be a title run this year if the Crew can extend the winning streak it ended the season with.

"We know we're the underdog. They're ranked second for reason, and we're ranked seventh for reason, but at the same time as much as we respect them and obviously we know who they have in their squad we have a lot of respect for them but we're not afraid of them," Tall said, pointing to a road draw and a home win against Messi and Co. during the regular season.

Whether or not the Crew are able to end Miami's title defense, Tall is confident that the team now is on the right path. If that changes again, he's ready to make the tough choices to course correct.

#2925. White House replaces cyber director Sean Cairncross amid widespread tech outages

White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross is leaving his post, with Pentagon CIO Kirsten Davies set to serve as acting director after a week of high-profile U.S. technology outages.

The role, which advises the president on cybersecurity and coordinates U.S. cyber policy across federal agencies, has been handed to Davies, the Pentagon's chief information officer, on an interim basis. A permanent national cyber director must first be nominated by the president and then confirmed by the Senate.

Axios first reported Cairncross' exit, citing two White House officials who said President Donald Trump's chief of staff, Stephen Miller, pushed for his departure. One official told Axios that Miller thought Cairncross "lacked the strong cyber credentials to perform the job."

The White House and the Office of the National Cyber Director did not immediately respond to a CNBC request for comment. A White House official confirmed Cairncross' departure to NBC News and CBS News on Thursday.

It comes after a series of technology outages, including a nationwide aviation ground stop, a worldwide Microsoft Outlook outage and a reported blackout of the National Security Agency's classified communications network.

The White House has insisted that there are no indications of a coordinated cyberattack, state-sponsored activity or malign actor behind recent tech outages.

Davies addressed her responsibilities in the new position and thanked Miller and Trump for their confidence late Thursday.

"Our nation stands in the crossroad of analog, digital, and quantum technologies, our American way of living increasingly interconnected. Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come … but only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on," she wrote on X.

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio both congratulated Davies on her appointment.

#2924. Anthropic defies the odds, holding record IPO despite ‘massively disruptive’ market

The moment felt impossible.Between Jensen Huang's shocking exit from chip giant Nvidia, voters' rebuke of artificial intelligence in this month's midterm elections, and rising interest rates that threatened to stymie plans for a multitrillion-dollar infrastructure buildout, there seemed to be no way Anthropic could carry out an initial public offering.Anthropic's response? Let's go!"Very few companies would've attempted it in this environment," said Byron Deeter, a partner at Bessemer Venture Partners, which counts Anthropic as its biggest investment ever, in an interview. "These things collectively have been massively disruptive, yet the team stuck to its true north and got the largest financing in IPO history done, and it's just remarkable."

Anthropic's stock jumped 17% in its Nasdaq debut on Thursday, closing at $97.17 per share and giving the Claude creator a market cap of roughly $1.8 trillion. That makes it the seventh-most valuable U.S. company, despite being less than 6 years old.

Earlier in the day, the second floor of the Nasdaq was decorated in orange, Anthropic's signature color. Founders and backers were given Claude lapel pins that served as their ticket to the bell ringing, which was followed by a champagne toast ahead of the opening. With the first trade, the stock shot up to $111.50.

The previous afternoon Anthropic raised $81.3 billion, topping Elon Musk's SpaceX for the largest IPO on record.

It was a wild feat, and Anthropic backers breathed a sigh of relief. Days earlier, Altimeter Capital's Brad Gerstner, whose firm put in an order for $5 billion of stock in the IPO, acknowledged that the election results, the semiconductor sell-off and the Huang scandal created "a very bad backdrop" for the offering. Nvidia shares are headed for their seventh straight weekly drop, losing 38% of their value over that stretch.

Malcolm Ethridge, managing partner at Capital Area Planning Group and a CNBC contributor, pointed to the high levels of volatility in the market as a real risk to going public. The Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) is up 46% this month, including a 16% surge on Thursday, to over 28.4.

Ethridge said that with the VIX above 25, most companies would consider "shelving" an IPO. But Anthropic decided, "this is our window," Ethridge said.

In the face of stout headwinds, investors told CNBC that the combination of Anthropic's historic growth rate (1,200% year over year), its adjusted operating profit and its openness to constructive feedback from Wall Street contributed to this week's gravity-defying moment.

"Just truly, truly market redefining," Iconiq partner Will Griffith, an Anthropic investor, said in an interview. "The ability to achieve this growth, at this scale, in this short of a time frame, this efficiently — the world has never seen that before."

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei co-founded Anthropic in 2021, after he and a handful of other researchers defected from OpenAI, now its chief rival, to pursue what they viewed as a safer approach to AI. The company captivated the corporate world with its Claude AI models and products, which fueled its unprecedented rise.

With tens of billions of dollars flooding in over the past few years from private investors and tech giants, Anthropic was able to secure the computing power needed to train frontier AI models and serve customers with an expanding portfolio of services.

Anthropic executives, including CFO Krishna Rao, used those funding rounds as opportunities to build goodwill with the market, particularly when it came to pricing. The company opted not to squeeze every last dollar out of the ecosystem, preferring, in Amodei's words, to "underpromise and overdeliver."

"This isn't a company that's focused on optimizing price," Deeter said. "They could have priced the IPO higher. At every financing they have chosen to leave some money on the table."

Anthropic has also worked to prove itself as a company that can deploy capital responsibly. Of the more than $140 billion that the company has raised, it's only spent around $10 billion, which helped to reassure investors that it could weather a potential storm.

The company confidentially filed its prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, and OpenAI, followed days later. But by August, OpenAI executives signaled that the ChatGPT maker was targeting a 2027 debut, as a series of security incidents rattled the industry and opposition to data centers swept the nation.

The market, stung by rising oil prices and the Federal Reserve's plan to raise interest rates, soured on the AI trade and lost its appetite for IPOs. Biometric ring maker Oura, Australian AI data center operator Firmus and SK Hynix's U.S.-based Solidigm subsidiary all postponed or abandoned plans to go public.

Gerstner said Altimeter reduced its exposure to the broader AI trade to the lowest in three years. Meanwhile, the firm aimed to put five times as much into Anthropic's IPO as it had invested in any prior initial share sale, Gerstner told CNBC.

Anthropic began testing the waters with investors in August, before kicking off its official roadshow last week. It was all taking place while many AI stocks were melting down.

Having successfully reached the public market, Anthropic now has a boatload of much-needed cash on hand as it continues to spend aggressively on compute capacity.

Assuming underwriters exercise their option to buy all the shares available to them, Anthropic's fundraise would total $93.5 billion in the IPO, topping the $85.7 billion raised by SpaceX. Add to that another $26 billion from a parallel share sale to a handful of tech companies, and the more than $130 billion in cash and equivalents on Anthropic's balance sheet at the end of September.

It's only been one day for Anthropic as a public company, but the AI lab's financial standing is about as solid as anyone could have hoped.

"Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so, only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing," Amodei said in a speech at the Nasdaq on Thursday. "If we can show it's possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same."

— CNBC's Leslie Picker and Jordan Novet contributed to this report.

#2921. Bitcoin's regulation bull case is played out. What could drive crypto gains moving forward

Crypto investors are hunting for the next positive catalyst after U.S. crypto regulation — a long-time market driver — fizzled in 2026.

Bitcoin traded around $61,500 on Friday, a more than 50% decline from its all-time high above $126,000 reached in October 2025. The broader digital asset market has struggled after the Clarity Act, a crypto market structure bill, failed to advance in the Senate in September.

Investors now see Wall Street's embrace of blockchain technology — particularly tokenization — as the next trend to give bitcoin a boost.

"Every single traditional firm is now looking at digital assets," BitGo CEO Mike Belshe told CNBC last week in an exclusive interview from the fintech-focused Cantor Convergence conference in Miami Beach. That includes BlackRock, the world's largest asset manager.

He pointed to statements from the asset management giant's CEO, Larry Fink, who said the next major evolution in global finance is the creation of digital representations of every stock, bond, fund and real-world asset onto a shared blockchain ledger.

"I think the biggest catalyst we're seeing right now is actually very much in motion and it's happening, which is capital markets are moving onchain," eToro CEO Yoni Assia told CNBC in an exclusive interview from the conference. He pointed to the SpaceX IPO as an example, which had derivatives trading on eToro before the IPO.

"First day of trading, we distributed it to our retail clients, and it started trading 24/7, and that's all because capital markets are now copying crypto markets and are sitting on the same rails," Assia said. "Crypto markets have always been 24/7, they never sleep, and now what we're seeing is that capital markets are copying crypto markets using the same technology so stocks are moving onchain, they're being tokenized."

Assia said that supportive regulation in the U.S. from agencies, including the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, is also helping adoption of crypto.

He pointed to the CFTC earlier this month clearing the way for crypto-style perpetual futures tied to individual stocks to trade on regulated U.S. exchanges for the first time. Assia also highlighted the SEC's move to issue an order in September, creating a regulatory pathway for certain trading venues to trade tokenized representations of publicly traded U.S. stocks.

"Blockchain technology is now starting to power what's happening in capital markets," Assia told CNBC. "That is the one of the biggest changes we're going to see in capital markets for many, many years."

"We're talking about hundreds of trillions of dollars that are going to be tokenized and move onchain and at the same time, I do believe that will support prices of bitcoin and other blockchains as well," he continued.

The industry is also watching whether inflation will ease and geopolitical tensions will subside in the new year, which could lower broader macro risk currently hampering the industry.

Last month, Strategy's Michael Saylor said he thinks bitcoin's next bull market is already underway.

ARK Invest CIO Cathie Wood told CNBC the investment management firm's $1.5 million bull case price target for bitcoin by 2030 still stands. She also said that it wouldn't surprise her if bitcoin reached its all-time high again before the end of 2027.

"Our macro forecast has inflation breaking down considerably," Wood told CNBC in an exclusive interview at Cantor Convergence. "I think the elections have increased our confidence there because the war [in Iran], one way or the other, is going to end."

She added that "bitcoin has weathered so much bad news," including the $6.3 billion Binance hack and the "distraction" of AI which, "many people would say is sucking the oxygen away from bitcoin."

The maturation of the artificial intelligence trade could provide an opportunity for bitcoin to find new inflows.

Wood said that ARK Invest believes bitcoin has found its low and stressed that cybersecurity is "top of mind right now," which could provide yet another opportunity for crypto markets to rebound.

"I think if the Bitcoin and crypto world coalesces and makes investors feel that they've got their arms around security and actually understand that there might be more security issues in the traditional financial system, I think we're going to see a wave of support," Wood said.

#2920. Karl-Anthony Towns letting his Knicks play speak loudest in face of uncertainty

MINNEAPOLIS — In his own words, this should be an uncomfortable situation for Karl-Anthony Towns.

Regardless, it's produced some of the best basketball of his career.

Before the season, when Towns still was publicly pushing for a contract extension from the Knicks, he said he wanted his long-term future settled "so I can feel as comfortable as possible." Without a new deal, he said, "there's no comfortability to be had."

Karl-Anthony Towns rises up for a rebound during the Knicks' win over the Raptors on Nov. 17, 2026, in Toronto. NBAE via Getty Images

That new deal, of course, never materialized, as the Knicks shut down all extension negotiations for the season while navigating owner James Dolan's mandate to stay under the second apron. It left Towns in that uncomfortable situation.

He's responded by making a loud statement to Knicks brass with his play.

"I got a job to do, at the end of the day," Towns said before the team's game against the Timberwolves on Thursday. "I gotta come here and put that jersey on and do what's best for my brothers and the guys they have in my locker room. So, I'm just here to do my job."

Towns entered Thursday night's game averaging 21.2 points, 3.9 assists and a league-high 14.1 rebounds while shooting 54.5 percent from the field and 40.0 percent from 3-point range.

Karl-Anthony Towns looks to make a pass while being defended by Collin Murray-Boyles during the Knicks' road win over the Raptors on Nov. 17, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

He has been by far the most consistently strong performer through the Knicks' rocky first few weeks of their championship defense.

He's shown no signs of letting that discomfort affect him. If anything, it is fueling him.

"I gotta put that jersey on and put the best performance out there for my teammates," Towns said. "So, that's all I really think about."

Towns' standout performances came just as he returned to Minnesota, where he spent the first nine years of his career.

He didn't want to opine Thursday about whether winning a championship with the Knicks validates the move for New York and means it won the blockbuster trade with the Timberwolves, which sent Julius Randle and Donte DiVincenzo back to Minnesota.

But at this point, it's a clear Knicks win.

Karl-Anthony Towns looks to make a move on Collin Murray-Boyles during the Knicks' road win over the Raptors on Nov. 17, 2026. Dan Hamilton-Imagn Images

But it doesn't make being back any less emotional for Towns, who still has a painting of him and his mother and father hugging that the Timberwolves gifted him. They were the last team he played for before his mother passed away during the COVID-19 pandemic.

"I still have so much love for this place," Towns said. "It doesn't go away. I think it's actually grown as I've been away. I think that, even for me and my dad, we were just driving around the city and just going to places. We went to eat at a spot we love to go here. It always hits home. This is the last place that I got to play basketball with my mom. I got to see the kids be young before now. Jolani, my niece, who was in my rookie of the year photo actually in here, she was a baby, and now she's in high school. It's a different part of life, but it's a part of life that I really enjoy."

Thursday was the third time Towns returned as an opponent. But it was the first time as a champion.

"It's always great to be home and to be back here," Towns said. "Nine years of my life, some amazing years, amazing moments. Yeah, it's special to be back. Obviously, it's bittersweet to come back with a championship because I wanted to win it here so bad for the city, for Minneapolis, for Minnesota, for all the people who haven't seen an NBA championship here. But it's great to be able to come back and to be able to see friends, people I call family here."

#2919. Lions vs. Buccaneers preview, prediction: On Paper

For the first time in several weeks, the Detroit Lions hold the top spot in the NFC North. But in order to hold it, they'll have to take down a sneaky-good Tampa Bay Buccaneers team. They may be 3-6 on the season, but as you'll soon see, they are doing a lot of things very well, and present a tough matchup for any team. There's a reason why they have a positive point differential, despite having two times the losses than wins.

I'll break it down further in my Detroit Lions vs. Tampa Bay Buccaneers preview and prediction: On Paper.

The Lions' passing attack remains pretty steady and reliable, despite the fact that Jared Goff has now thrown an interception in three straight games after not throwing a single one through his first six contests. For the year, the Lions rank:

In short, the Lions have been playing like a near top-five passing offense pretty much all season.

Goff is at his best when his offensive line is pass blocking for him, and the front has done a pretty good job this year. Detroit is allowing just a 30.8% pressure rate (fifth best) and 6.4% sack rate (15th), while ranking fourth in pass block win rate (58%) and second in PFF pass blocking grade (76.8).

Relevant this week is how Goff performs against the blitz, seeing as Tampa blitzes at the second-highest rate in the NFL. This year against the blitz, the Goff ranks:

The Bucs have shut down nearly every single opponent this year in the passing game, outside of—oddly—Deshaun Watson. For the year, they rank:

Obviously, these stats are pretty darn good, but with lower success rates and yards per attempt than EPA and passer rating, there's at least a little indication that some of these stats are being propped up by Tampa's ridiculous 16 interceptions (most in NFL) and 5.2 interception rate (highest). While the Bucs deserve credit for those interceptions, a 5.2% interception rate is unbelievably high. The highest interception rate for an entire season over the past 10 years is 4.7%. There's a good chance this is unsustainable.

Regardless, this is still a top-10 pass defense and shouldn't be overlooked.

As mentioned earlier, the Bucs have the second-highest blitz rate (43.9%), yet their pressure rate ranks just 24th (33.2%) and their sack rate is 25th (5.0%) per NFL Pro. That said, they are improving as the season goes on. Of their 17 sacks on the season, 11 have come in the last four games.

Really, their pass defense is led by a strong secondary. Cornerbacks Jacob Parish, Zyon McCullom, and rookie nickel Keionte Scott are having outstanding seasons.

Player to watch: Rueben Bain Jr. vs. Blake Miller. Who isn't excited about first-round rookie on rookie action? Bain and Miller were taken two spots apart, and both have had ups and downs in their rookie season. Bain is starting to put some things together after a slow start to his career, while Miller has seen more good than bad.

Advantage: Lions +0.5. With all due respect to DVOA, I think the Bucs' numbers are a little artificially inflated by high interception rates. I still think it's going to be a slog for the Lions to put up big numbers, but I won't be surprised if they can patiently dink and dunk their way down the field.

Every week, the Lions' run game gets a little more consistent and explosive. For the year, Detroit ranks:

What's even more promising is that the high stuffed rate that had been plaguing this rushing attack is finally starting to settle down. Right now it sits at 18.6%, which is still 10th-highest, but it's on a downward trajectory. Similarly, their power success rate is much better now. After Week 8, the Lions were converting on just 59% of short yardage situations (24th). Now they're at 68% (12th).

It's been a marriage between good blocking and Jahmyr Gibbs being outstanding. The Lions rank second in adjusted line yards (4.99), seventh in run block win rate (75%), and fourth in PFF run-blocking grade (77.0).

Meanwhile, Gibbs has forced 16 more missed tackles than any other player and is averaging 3.6 yards after contact per rush (11th).

Put it all together and Detroit is both extremely consistent down to down (see: success rate) and explosive (second-most 10+ yard runs in the NFL).

The Lions may have met their match this week. The Bucs haven't allowed over 100 rushing yards since Week 1, and only two opponents all year have managed 4.0 yards per carry or more against this unit.

It's hard to pick holes in the data here. Tampa is legit. They don't give up big plays (only 16 rushes of 10+ yards, third fewest). The defensive line ranks well in run-stop win rate (eight), adjusted line yards (seventh), and second in PFF run-defense grade.

Player to watch: Josiah Trotter. The second-round rookie linebacker has been outstanding for the Bucs' defense, ranking 19th in PFF run defense grade among qualifying linebackers. He leads the team in tackles (76) and PFF run stops (14).

Advantage: Draw. It's elite vs. elite, and both teams have shown they can win those kind of matchups. Detroit ran all over the elite Vikings' run defense, while the Bucs completely shut down both the Falcons and Bears strong rushing attacks. I can't pick a side here.

Bold and italicized data were starts by Jalen Daniels.

The Buccaneers' passing attack has been a disaster this year, and it's hard to figure out why. For the year, they rank:

It's been a disaster year for Baker Mayfield. Beyond just the injuries to his thumb and feet, Mayfield has just not looked the same as the game-changer he had been for the previous few years. Accuracy has been a problem, ranking 27th of 31 in completion percentage over expected (-3.3%). His PFF passing grade of 54.8 is 31st out of 37 qualifying QBs.

But his receiving corps hasn't been much help, either. There just doesn't seem to be any chemistry between quarterback and receiver.

Pass protection, however, has been acceptable. Tampa ranks 16th in pressure rate allowed (36.4%), 11th in pass-block win rate, and sixth in PFF pass-blocking grade (73.7). However, they have the second-highest sack rate (10.1%), suggesting both Mayfield and Daniels have struggled to escape pressure when it arrives.

For now, I'm assuming Mayfield plays in this game, but if Daniels has to go, it's good news for Detroit. The rookie quarterback has an even worse CPOE (-5.7%) and worse passer rating (74.9 vs. 63.4).

I want to believe that the Lions' pass defense is getting better, but it's really hard to know. They've faced some very mediocre quarterbacks all season, and the numbers are certainly improving, but I can't yet say it's good. Even the data from the last two weeks comes with significant asterisks because of Malik Willis' injury and Drake Maye exiting one series into the game.

Compiled on top of that are the injuries to Jack Campbell and Aidan Hutchinson, but the returns of Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph are a factor, too, and there is just so much noise with the data here that it's hard to make sense of anything.

Detroit has climbed out of the basement in a hurry, and if you were to just look at Detroit's stats out of the bye week (Weeks 7-10), they're even better:

But, again, how much is this impacted by strength of opponent?

Pass rush will be a big question moving forward without Hutchinson. He was responsible for 52 of the teams' 199 pressures—with Alim McNeill (39), Skyler Gill-Howard (19), DJ Wonnum (19), and Derrick Moore (15) next in line. Will the Lions just roll with those players, or increase their blitz rate, which currently just sits at 30.9% (16th)?

Player to watch: Derrick Moore. The Lions' second-round rookie defensive end has four sacks in his last two games, and is bound to have a ton more opportunities moving forward with Hutchinson out. In the past four weeks, Moore has posted a 68.5 PFF grade, ranking 37th out of 117 edge rushers.

Advantage: Lions +1. I still have a healthy amount of skepticism regarding the Lions' pass defense, but what they have proven without a doubt over the past month is that they can hold bad pass offenses down. That's what the Bucs are.

Tampa has been outstanding running the football this year, particularly as of late. They've rushed for over 100 yards in six straight contests and finished with at least 4.5 yards per carry in five of those six games. For the year, they rank:

The offensive line can be great at times, but their overall stats are more average than outstanding. They're 14th in adjusted line yards, 16th in run-block win rate, and 15th in PFF run-blocking grade.

The stars of the show, without a doubt, are the running backs. Both Kenny Gainwell and Bucky Irving are outstanding at creating yardage on their own.

+1.2 rushing yards over expected per rush (third in NFL)

According to Pro-Football-Reference, Irving's 16 broken tackles leads the league.

Despite the very low DVOA ranking, the Lions' run defense has passed both the eye and statistical test over the past five games. For the year, Detroit ranks:

So what is dragging them down so much in DVOA? A few things. They haven't faced particularly good rushing attacks all season. By rushing yards per game, the Lions have faced just a single team (Bills) ranked 15th or higher this year. And while they own a great success rate, they've been terrible in short-yardage situations, allowing conversions on 86% of power runs (32nd). Those high-leverage plays are almost solely responsible for Detroit's low DVOA ranking. Because Detroit looks great in adjusted line yards (third), stuffed rate (sixth), and run-defense PFF grade (fourth).

Personally, I think they're a lot better than DVOA suggests, but will admit that the Bucs will present the second-biggest challenge of the season.

Player to watch: Irving. He's extremely capable of carrying defenders, but it's worth noting that the Lions are outstanding at tackling. They have PFF's best tackling grade in the league (81.6) and the fewest missed tackles, per PFR.

Advantage: Bucs +0.5. I think this could go in either direction, but because the Lions haven't been tested like this in months—and they'll be without Campbell and Hutchinson—I'll give the slight edge to the Buccaneers.

I'm tempted to throw out last week's prediction entirely because so much of my preview was about the huge advantage the Patriots' passing offense had. When Drake Maye was lost on the opening possession, that edge was completely erased. Now, the Lions still did a good job in coverage, but it's hard to believe that game would've looked anything like that if Maye had stayed in the game.

Still, it counts. I got the winner right, but missed on the Vegas line. On Paper is 7-2 overall and 4-5 against the spread.

In the comment section, we had one prediction that was outstanding on just about every level:

Congrats, ascofield68! Here's your prize.

Do you have trouble sleeping? Do you spend time in the middle of the night worrying about all the "what ifs" in your life? Well, enjoy this new white noise option on your phone:

The Lions come out with a +1 advantage, but I think it's worth pointing out how no team as more than a +1 advantage in any of the four matchups. Just about every single aspect of this game is a coin flip, and my confidence level is very low in any predictions this week. Add in the fact that Mayfield is likely playing through injury, the Lions will be missing Hutchinson but getting back Joseph, and there are just so many factors in this game that make it so difficult to predict.

Still, I'm expecting a low-scoring, tight battle. Lions 20, Buccaneers 16.

#2918. Jensen Huang's — and Nvidia's — legal exposure balloons

The still-unraveling scandal of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's extramarital affairs and the tech giant's potential role in its advanced semiconductor chips ending up in China present a legal minefield for Huang and Nvidia.

Federal and state prosecutors and Nvidia employees may target Huang and the company in court, where some shareholders have already taken action.

That's on top of a rapidly growing pile of probes by Republicans who control Congress now and Democrats who will have majorities in both the House and Senate come January.

"It's not going to get any better for Jensen Huang; it's going to get far worse," said Salvatore Graziano, a New York securities litigation attorney at Bernstein, Litowitz, Berger & Grossmann. His firm is looking at shareholder lawsuit opportunities against Nvidia and Huang.

[Huang] "faces the Department of Justice, the Securities and Exchange Commission and private litigation," Graziano said. "The criminal exposure is very serious. The SEC could bar him from being an officer. And the potential liability [from shareholder] lawsuits can be very large."

Huang's and Nvidia's legal exposure stems from three issues that led up to his shock resignation Nov. 12.

There's his alleged affair with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang, who worked for Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company under investigation for diverting advanced Nvidia semiconductor chips to China in violation of U.S. export rules. That, in turn, has raised questions about whether Huang and Nvidia were aware of any diversions.

There are Huang's two other alleged affairs with Nvidia employees.

And there is the sharp drop in the company's stock price in the wake of the scandal. Nvidia's share price has fallen 19% since Nov. 8, when Huang sent a company-wide apology acknowledging extramarital affairs.

Huang last week retained the law firm Paul, Weiss and its attorneys Melinda Haag and Walter Brown to represent him. Haag is a former U.S. attorney in San Francisco, and Brown is also a former federal prosecutor.

Huang's spokesman at Trident, a crisis communications firm, declined to comment when asked if Haag and Brown are representing him in any potential criminal case and other questions about his legal exposure.

Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment. Last week, Nvidia retained the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an independent investigation into Huang allegedly being targeted by a spy, as U.S. intelligence reportedly has concluded.

The civil liability Huang and Nvidia could face is underscored by a hearing Graziano, the securities attorney, attended Tuesday in U.S. District Court in San Francisco. A judge at the hearing approved a $175 million settlement from Seagate Technology Holdings to resolve a shareholder lawsuit alleging it concealed sales of hard-disk drives to Huawei in China in violation of export bans.

The Seagate settlement came three years after the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security — which is investigating Megaspeed's business with Nvidia — imposed a $300 million penalty on Seagate for its sales to Huawei.

Graziano said his law firm is "actively looking at securities law liability for Nvidia, Jensen Huang and other senior executives in the company given all the recent developments regarding their [potential] knowledge and facilitation of illegal chip sales to Chinese entities."

There is already a pending class-action shareholder lawsuit in San Francisco federal court against Nvidia and Huang by the Rosen Law Firm, for allegedly misleading and false statements related to Megaspeed and Alice Huang.

"Several hundreds of investors have contacted us and expressed an interest to join the case — investors of all walks of life, from mom and pops to investors with very large losses," Rosen attorney Phil Kim told CNBC in an email.

Katie Sweeten, a former federal prosecutor in the DOJ's National Security Division, said the question of "who knew what and when, and what was [Huang's] role" is potentially the biggest risk for Nvidia and him.

"Now DOJ can leverage their criminal authorities," Sweeten, a partner at Scale LLP, told CNBC's Kelly Evans on "The Exchange."

"They can bring grand jury subpoenas, search warrants for emails, bank accounts, personal devices, computers, things like that," Sweeten said.

While it is "not illegal to, you know, sleep with a spy ... it is illegal to pass certain types of information to a counterintelligence officer," she said.

Sweeten also pointed to potential export control violations, which "could be very serious."

She noted the DOJ can indict a company as well as its officials if there is evidence of criminality. Export control violations carry a maximum possible criminal sentence of 20 years in prison and "really large fines," she said.

"You can't send the company to prison, but they can face fines, civil penalties, debarment — where you can't export items down the line," she said.

One example of that came in July 2025, when the DOJ obtained a guilty plea and an agreement to pay more than $140 million from Cadence Design Systems for violating the Export Control Reform Act by unlawfully exporting semiconductor design tools to China's National University of Defense Technology, a school led by China's Central Military Commission.

Another potential legal risk for Huang comes from his planned appearances before Congress.

Huang is scheduled to give a closed-door interview Dec. 1 to three House committees. Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., wants Huang's testimony before that panel to be public, and told CNBC Tuesday he hopes to have that happen "before Christmas."

Sweeten said Huang "has to be very careful" about what he says there because of the risk of being criminally charged with lying to Congress, and of saying something "that absolutely can become part of a criminal or civil investigation."

"I expect Huang to take the Fifth on most questions" from Congress, Jonathan Kanter, a former assistant attorney general in the DOJ's Antitrust Division, told CNBC, meaning Huang will likely use his constitutional right against giving testimony that could be used against him in a criminal case.

"With a Justice Department criminal investigation into Megaspeed already underway and more investigations possible, anything he tells Congress could be used against him," Kanter said. "His lawyers are likely to advise him against taking that risk."

Ben Heineman Jr., a former senior vice president and general counsel of General Electric, and a senior fellow at Harvard University, told CNBC that Nvidia's board will be scrutinized over its actions before it pushed Huang to resign.

Heineman cited the board's apparent lack of succession planning and what looks like weak oversight of Huang, including relating to personal conduct such as the two alleged affairs with Nvidia employees and with an executive of an Nvidia customer.

"When there is a sort of reasonable suspicion, they need to investigate it, and they don't appear to have done that," Heineman said.

Nvidia and Huang could face investigation from state attorneys general, including in California, where the company is headquartered.

On Tuesday, California Attorney General Rob Bonta told Bloomberg Television that the situation at Nvidia with Huang is "something that we're interested in." Bonta's office later told CNBC, "We are monitoring the situation."

Huang's alleged affairs with Nvidia employees also open the possibility of workplace litigation.

Ari Wilkenfeld, a Washington-area employment lawyer, said a consensual relationship between a chief executive and a subordinate "is not in and of itself illegal."

"The liability never comes from the existence of the relationship alone. It comes from whether it was genuinely welcome, what job benefits flowed from it, and what it did to everyone else in the building," Wilkenfeld said. "California law recognizes that so-called sexual favoritism can create a hostile environment for an entire workforce.

"The affair is Huang's problem," Wilkenfeld said. "What, if anything, Nvidia did once it knew is the company's problem."

#2917. A trading strategy to ride out the Nvidia uncertainty and generate income in the process

Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has sent shockwaves through the tech sector, dragging Nvidia's (NVDA) stock down roughly 30% since Oct. 6. The market despises uncertainty, and losing a visionary founder, particularly one without a well-telegraphed succession plan, makes it worse.

However, for opportunistic investors, this panic has made the stock cheaper (obviously) while options have become significantly more expensive. Trading in the $160s, Nvidia's valuation has taken a big haircut, yet its underlying business fundamentals remain largely intact. While Huang was the architect of Nvidia's AI dominance, the company's moat — superior GPUs, the CUDA software ecosystem, and networking expertise — does not walk out the door with him. The company's structural advantage in the global artificial intelligence rollout persists.

Buying good companies at a discount is investing 101, but the current market dynamics may do something else for those who use options.  Huang's departure guarantees that Nvidia will be operating under a cloud of transition for the foreseeable future. Executing a permanent CEO search while navigating global regulatory scrutiny takes time. Consequently, Nvidia's implied volatility (IV)—the market's pricing of expected future price swings — has spiked to highs not seen since the tariff tantrum in the first half of 2025, and this elevated IV is highly likely to persist for several months as the leadership drama slowly unfolds.

This prolonged period of high implied volatility can be a goldmine for option sellers, specifically those executing options overlays such as covered call strategies. When you buy NVDA shares at these depressed levels and simultaneously sell out-of-the-money call options against your position, the premiums you collect are directly tied to IV. Because fear and transition-related uncertainty have dramatically inflated these option prices, the income generated from selling covered calls is now significantly higher than usual.

This lowers the risk profile of holding the stock considerably over time. Consistently collecting these inflated premiums systematically lowers your overall cost basis in the underlying shares. If the stock trades sideways or recovers slowly during the CEO search, you are generating an outsized cash yield on a stagnant asset. If the stock experiences further downside turbulence, the heavy premium income acts as a substantial downside buffer, meaningfully reducing the strategy's overall risk over time.

By deploying a persistent covered call strategy, investors can leverage the exact fear driving the stock down to generate robust, risk-reducing income while maintaining exposure to the undeniable future of AI.

#2916. NBA Trade Rumors: Jazz connected to superstar guard?

The Utah Jazz have given internal consideration to Kyri Irving, according to Ian Begley.

It's also no surprise that the Jazz "want to win."

When I hear rumors like this, I try to consider where the rumor is potentially coming from, and what the purpose of the rumor is.

My first bet is potentially the agent. Irving would make a lot of sense for Utah as a third guard/super sub who could play huge minutes come playoff time. Utah could have reached out to Irving's agent to see if he'd be up for that kind of role.

This could also be from the Mavericks' side. Maybe there was a phone call, and the Mavericks want to drive up any potential offer for Irving.

It's clear Utah expects to win more than they have, and they're talking about how to do it. We'll see if anything materializes because talk is just talk until someone gets desperate.
