#2915. Forget Anthropic: In Europe, the IPO hype is about a blue lagoon

While investors are fixated on Anthropic's blockbuster stock market debut, a very different IPO is making waves in Europe: Iceland's Blue Lagoon, the operator of one of the world's most famous geothermal spas.

Blue Lagoon Corp. raised roughly 14.3 billion Icelandic kronur ($110 million) through the offering, valuing the Icelandic geothermal spa operator at about $787 million, according to the company's investor presentation.

The Blue Lagoon traces its origins to 1992, when Blue Lagoon Ltd. was founded to study the water in the Blue Lagoon, an open-air pool of warm, milky-blue water set in a black lava field in southwestern Iceland. It grew into a business spanning a spa, hotels and skincare made with ingredients from the lagoon.

Shares will trade under the ticker "BLUE" on one of Europe's smallest stock exchanges, Nasdaq Iceland Main Market, part of the Nasdaq Nordic group, which also operates exchanges in Sweden, Denmark and Finland.

"Wellness is the new luxury, and we know that the wellness economy is growing faster than the economy as a whole, so we have tailwind from that," CEO Sigríður Margrét Oddsdóttir told CNBC on Thursday.

"Now is the right time for us to list," she added. "We are a company that thinks long-term, we have a clear vision for the next decade, and being publicly listed gives investors the opportunity to participate in our journey."

The company's operations are centered on Iceland's Reykjanes Peninsula, where, as well as the Blue Lagoon geothermal spa, it runs the Silica Hotel, the Retreat luxury hotel and spa, and the Michelin-starred Moss restaurant.

It also operates the Kerlingarfjöll Highland Base and Hrauneyjar properties in Iceland's highlands, and sells Blue Lagoon-branded skincare products internationally.

The 34-year-old company has averaged 11% annual revenue growth over the past decade, and next year is expected to be a record, with revenue growing by more than half, Oddsdóttir said.

The company plans to use the raised capital to fund expanding its existing properties, acquiring businesses, and developing new destinations.

In total, nearly 4,000 subscriptions were received in the initial public offering, worth about 15.3 billion kronur, about 7% more than the total size of the offering, the company said, citing strong demand from smaller investors, including retail investors.

Iceland's relatively small stock market had just 27 companies on its main exchange at the end of 2025, according to Nasdaq. The market is dominated by banks, seafood companies and other domestically focused firms.

The global wellness industry reached $7.5 trillion in 2025, up 8.9% from the previous year, according to the Global Wellness Institute. Spending on thermal and mineral springs grew 10.4% over the same period, with the institute forecasting annual growth of nearly 10% for the sector through 2030.

Tourism accounted for nearly 9% of Iceland's GDP in 2025, and is growing, according to Statistics Iceland. The country welcomed around 2.3 million international visitors that year, with the U.S. as its largest source market.

#2914. Value of Things: In the rearview mirror

We come to a very special Friday edition of Value of Things as the Texans won a boring 26-3 game on Thursday night football. Boring is good in this case. It was boring aesthetically and boring statistically. It was boring in every conceivable way. but it was the kind of boring that DeMeco Ryans imagined them being before the year started.

Obviously, people will want to big picture this thing and they will try to read into it what they will. We've seen this movie before. They did this to the Titans and Chargers. Those were two crappy teams that have only found one win on the season a piece. A part of you is thankful it wasn't against you and also thankful that you didn't allow them to stick around in the end. The other part of you realizes that there is virtually nothing that you can take from those games and transport it to any other game.

As we like to do in wins, we will look at the basic numbers from the game to see if we can see any trends building in those numbers. We will also look at the great, good, and bad from the game to see who gets game balls and what we can't ignore in victory what we would be screaming about in defeat. As per usual, we will also have our own C.J. Stroud section.

Total Yards: Texans 65/357, Colts 48/167Rushing Yards: Texans 37/167. Colts 17/38Passing Yards: Texans 28/190, Colts 31/129Third Downs: Texans 8/14, Colts 1/11Fourth Downs: Texans 0/1, Colts 1/2Sacks: Texans 2, Colts 1Turnovers: Texans 1, Colts 1Penalties: Texans 4/23, Colts 2/15Time of Possession: Texans 37:46, Colts 22:14

This was a thorough beatdown and I suppose we can take some solace in that. From a statistical standpoint, this is one of those get right games on both sides of the ball. It is one of those games that will getting you looking at the aggregate and saying, "see, it's not so bad." The defensive numbers will be elevated to average and the offensive numbers will end up looking better than we think. Sometimes the aggregate can fool you.

The Tennessee Titans game will probably go down as the best defensive effort of the season. There are so few shutouts in the NFL, so that one feels special even if the numbers might not be as good as they were here. I'm not sure what to make of Daniel Jones. He has moments where he looks more than competent. He uses his legs and you look up and he has turned in an impressive performance. Most of the time it looks like this. Granted, he doesn't have any receivers to speak of and if you bottle up Jonathan Taylor he gets really exposed. I suppose when you add it all up, he looks like a backup quarterback.

We've seen these performances from Davis Mills too. There are days when you think, "if I squint hard enough and let my imagination run wild then Mills looks like a starting quarterback." Then, something happens and you are reminded why Mills is a backup quarterback. Jones is effectively the same guy, but because of his draft pedigree he has managed to fool a couple of teams into believing he can be the guy. Be that as it may, the Texans did not give Jones or the Colts any hope in this one and that is what should have happened. Sometimes the great is simply doing what is expected. We have reached this portion of the season.

Maybe my eyes were playing tricks on me, but I thought I saw a Texans running back gain more than 100 yards in a football game. It was a Thursday night game, so maybe I dozed off and dreamt that. In all seriousness, this is what the Texans envisioned when they traded for David Montgomery. This was the game they had in mind. If you add in a healthy Woody Marks in the next game (hopefully) then you might actually have something. Of course, some of that might be a mirage given your opponent. The Colts did trade away a number of good players and some of them were on the defensive line.

The Texans again leave a football game surrendering only one sack. We have to reiterate that there is a difference between pressures and sacks. You can almost imagine Nick Caley as "well…actually" guy bringing up sack and turnover numbers to justify his existence. I said what I said last time and that opinion has not changed. Let's see what happens when the Texans face a team that is actually trying to win football games.

There was nothing truly ugly in this game because it was 26-3. When you thoroughly beat down an opponent you could argue that there is nothing really that bad. I would agree with that sentiment as well. I suppose this is a catch all for those few plays where the Texans seem to lose focus. We will get to Stroud in a minute, but defensively they are still giving up explosive plays. There is still the occasional blown assignment and you were just lucky to be facing a team that couldn't exploit those blown assignments. You might say that we are expecting perfection and that would be a fair reply, but when you are a 4-6 football team you put yourself in a position to need perfection.

This will go down as a statistically brilliant game for Stroud. He went 21 for 27 with 194 yards, three touchdowns, and the one pick. He did throw one other ball that should have been picked and almost was. The one interception he did throw seemed random and could be written off as bad luck, but it was a case of him trying to thread a needle and failing. So, this was not a great effort from Stroud in terms of how everything looked. The official count has him with a 118.2 rating. We will just say that this is one of those games that averages everything out. There are games where his rating is lower than what it probably should be for one reason or another.

The next step in the Stroud evolution is having a sixth sense for what the game calls for. There are games that call for him to be a gun slinger because he is all the Texans have. Then there are games where the defense does what it is supposed to do and the running game shows up. He started off taking too many chances, but settled in as the game went on. The sooner that Stroud can recognize the version he is supposed to be the better he is going to be. Granted, we are talking about the difference between being a top ten and top five quarterback. #2912. SpaceX’s subsidiary Cursor tells lawmakers it's considering phasing out Chinese AI models

SpaceX's artificial-intelligence coding platform, Cursor, is considering moving away from using of Chinese AI models due to "geopolitical risk," CNBC has learned.

Cursor, which SpaceX acquired at an implied $60 billion equity value in August, had built its coding model Composer 2 on top of Chinese lab Moonshot AI's Kimi K2.5.

It's among the U.S. firms that have adopted Chinese models, whose usage has spiked across the globe this year, worrying lawmakers in Washington. The battle for AI supremacy between the U.S. and China has reached new heights in 2026 as Chinese models have improved.

But now Cursor plans to "explore phasing out PRC [People's Republic of China]-developed open-weight models because of geopolitical risk," according to a report produced by the House Committee on Homeland Security and the House Select Committee on China, shared exclusively with CNBC ahead of its publication on Friday.

The report, which follows a months-long investigation into the adoption of Chinese AI models into the American tech stack, said Cursor "informed the Committees" of those plans. Airbnb and DoorDash also engaged with the investigation about their use of Chinese AI models.

SpaceX announced it entered into a formal agreement to buy Cursor in June; the deal was completed in August. SpaceX is developing the Grok family of models, which Cursor has been involved in training.

Cursor, SpaceX and DoorDash did not respond to a CNBC request for comment. Airbnb declined to comment. The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The report found that cost, customization and near-frontier performance of Chinese AI models were driving adoption, with the U.S. lacking a competitive open-weight alternative at "price and performance the market demands."

"Beijing is now seeking to turn those technological gains into global market share and long-term dependence," the report says. China's embassy in the U.K. did not respond to a request for comment. China's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond.

It also sets out recommendations to address the issues it has identified.

Those include launching a "national American open-weight initiative" that combines public computing power, shared evaluation infrastructure and "lawful access" to American frontier models for training.

The report also says an order, made public in October, that banned DeepSeek from federal civilian agency systems, should be built on, by prohibiting the use of "PRC-developed AI models" in federal information systems and in performance of federal contracts.

Separately, Washington is also concerned about Chinese companies accessing Nvidia chips remotely, via overseas data centers, and gaining ground by using "distillation," where new models use older, more established ones to help train them.

The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips.

#2911. Bitcoin suffered identical sell-off pattern ahead of Anthropic, SpaceX IPOs — what happens next?

Bitcoin has suffered nearly identical sell-offs ahead of two of the biggest public offerings this year, leaving investors wondering if competing demand for investor capital could be weighing on the cryptocurrency and perhaps delaying its recovery.

The price of the bitcoin dropped 22.7% in the 30 days before Anthropic's IPO and fell 22.3% in the month leading up to SpaceX's June 12 listing. Ether declined 25.3% in the 30 days preceding Anthropic's debut, and 28% in the same window ahead of SpaceX.

"Liquidity events can elevate correlations across asset classes quickly," Matthew Sheffield, chief investment officer at the ether treasury firm Sharplink, told CNBC. "The first 15 min of [Thursday's] Anthropic IPO put that on full display. Tech stocks, value stocks, oil, gold, crypto all sold off as traders sold assets to buy shares in the secondary market."

"Stores of value function as such over long horizons, but in the short term are still liquidity driven," Sheffield said. "We saw this in early Covid when the market fled to cash. Stock, bonds, commodities ... it didn't matter, you were being sold for cash."

While investors appear to be rotating capital out of crypto to make room for history-making IPO investments, that can't be said with precise certainty. Crypto has also been under pressure from ETF outflows, leverage, macro uncertainty and broader risk-off sentiment.

Still, the post-IPO price action may offer a data point in understanding where bitcoin's price goes next. With Anthropic now public, investors are watching to see whether bitcoin and ether find a floor, and if institutional demand returns.

"[After] the SpaceX IPO, bitcoin didn't truly find its final bottom until after the IPO was completed, and it didn't actually reverse the downtrend until 70 days later," said Matt Cole, CEO and chairman of Strive Asset Management, a bitcoin treasury firm. "My view is that [for] bitcoin, the most likely scenario is that it chops around here."

The expiration of IPO allocation restrictions can influence the timing of capital flows into digital assets, Sheffield said.

"Post SpaceX we saw the wealth effect in full force," Sheffield said. "Many brokers make traders wait 15-30 days before they are allowed to flip shares they received as allocations. … If you went long ETH versus SpaceX on the day of the IPO, on day 31 was when you would have become profitable."

Bitcoin's next critical test is between $60,000 and $62,000, according to Nicolai Sondergaard, a research analyst at Nansen. On Friday, it was sitting at about $62,000.

As of Friday, bitcoin was hovering at the upper end of a critical $60,000 to $62,000 support range. Its next move could determine whether it can stabilize or if it will face another leg lower and revisit its July low of $57,737.35.

Throughout November, bitcoin has been struggling from a combination of dollar strength, institutional selling, and ongoing leveraged bitcoin liquidations. The declines began in late October, as concerns over artificial intelligence valuations and spending fueled a broad tech sell-off. They were compounded by the $6.3 billion Binance hack and weakening institutional ETF demand.

Bitcoin is in the early stages of forming a bottom, according to Cole. Retail fear is elevated amid recent outages, quantum concerns and other short-term uncertainties, but bitcoin should continue to benefit from macro forces like rising debt and weakening fiat currencies, which should drive price higher, he said.

"Capital markets are open, … retail fears are high, and when you combine those things it's much more likely to be a dip-buying opportunity across the board, including bitcoin, than the start of a great financial crisis," said Cole. "It'll likely age as a volatile time to consider allocating to risk, not the opposite."

"The winter for bitcoin is basically at the end, but after winter does not come summer, it comes early spring," he added. "Anytime anyone's been around early spring, what you notice is it gets really cold still, it still rains – it's not necessarily great weather, and I think that's the environment we're in for bitcoin."

#2907. The bull market has a new problem. The 'smart money' is selling

Companies have shifted from buying back shares to issuing them, adding to the supply that the four-year-old bull market must absorb.

"No matter how you measure it, U.S. corporations have changed their behavior over the past two years, switching from repurchasing in 2024 to issuing today," Acadian Asset Management portfolio manager Owen Lamont wrote in a letter to investors this month. "The question you should be asking is: Why is the smart money selling?"

As of late last week, net new issuance of shares equaled 3.1% of total market capitalization, according to a recent Acadian analysis. While net issuance remains below the peaks during the tech bubble and the covid bubble, the analysis shows that the era of repurchases has ended and an era of equity issuance has begun.

And more supply came to the market this week with Anthropic's blockbuster IPO. The offering drew strong enthusiasm initially with the frontier AI laboratory selling shares in its IPO at $83 each, above the expected range and raising $81 billion. But the stock is falling on Friday and taking the broader stock market with it.

Some investors for years have cited the shrinking stock market as a reason why share prices can keep increasing. As companies repurchased stock, it shrunk the number of shares available for trading and so it helped boost prices. There was more money chasing fewer shares. Not to mention, it had the effect of boosting earnings per share by lowering the denominator in that ratio. Now that trend has reversed with increased supply acting as a potential headwind on the bull market.

A 2000 paper by Malcolm Baker and Jeffrey Wurgler found that when companies issued more equity over debt, low market returns followed, suggesting that managers timed the market when issuing securities. The Baker-Wurgler equity share, which measures equity issuance as a share of total stock and bond issuance, peaked at about 18% in 2021. It has risen in recent months but remains below that peak, Lamont wrote.

The Federal Reserve data show a similar trend in the year-over-year change in trailing 12-month gross stock and bond issuance. Debt gross issuance rose first in 2020, followed by equity issuance in 2021. More recently, debt issuance began climbing in 2024, followed by a surge in equity issuance in 2026.

Recent deals show companies tapping equity markets in different ways.

Oracle filed to sell $20 billion in stock through an at-the-market program and issued another $10 billion in common shares in November. In October, Meta priced a $25 billion common-stock offering and $12.5 billion in mandatory convertible preferred shares. Alphabet announced an $84.8 billion equity raise in June to help fund its AI infrastructure buildout. SpaceX raised $85.7 billion in its June IPO after underwriters exercised their overallotment.

"Before 2026, firms were net repurchasers of equity, consistent with the idea that they viewed their shares as undervalued. Today, for whatever reason, firms are issuing equity on net," Lamont wrote.

The investor said he cannot rule out that we are in an AI bubble now.

#2905. The Professional Women’s Hockey League is proving irresistible

The New York Sirens have proved quite the allure, drawing 18,006 fans to Madison Square Garden on April 4 for a sold-out women's hockey game against the Seattle Torrent and setting a U.S. arena attendance record for women's hockey

The Sirens defeated the Torrent 2–1 in a shootout and are set to return to Madison Square Garden on January 23to face the Detroit Clutch.

Women's sports are still too often discussed as though their audiences are hypothetical, waiting to be discovered. How many sold-out arenas will it take before the powers that be stop questioning whether fans are interested?

The Sirens' historic night was part of a much bigger trend. According to Field Level Media, more than 1.1 million spectators attended the Professional Women's Hockey League's 120 regular-season games in 2025–26, an average of 9,304 fans per game, a 28% increase from the previous season, playoffs included.

Those numbers don't mean every team will fill an 18,000-seat arena every night, but few teams in professional sports can guarantee full capacity every day, and men's sports aren't required to prove demand through perpetual sellouts before being considered worthy of investment.

The problem was never a lack of interest in women's hockey, but instead an industry unwilling to invest without guaranteed returns. Women's hockey shouldn't need to repeatedly shatter attendance records before the sports world acknowledges its potential.

The irony is difficult to ignore. Women's sports have historically received far less exposure, infrastructure, and investment than their male counterparts, yet are often expected to demonstrate their financial value before getting those opportunities.

The demand is there. The Sirens have made their case, and the broader attendance numbers reinforce it. Now the question is whether the powers controlling the resources are willing to listen.

What would listening look like? Accessible broadcasts. Consistent promotion. Venues with room for audiences to grow. Just as importantly, a willingness to build lasting relationships with fans instead of treating record-setting nights as pleasant surprises.

The PWHL's Takeover Tour offers a useful example. During the 2025–26 season, its 16 stops drew nearly 200,000 attendees, including games in markets experiencing the league for the first time. The potential audience isn't limited to established hockey markets. The opportunity to introduce the league to new fans is much bigger.

None of this guarantees financial stability. Arena rentals, travel, salaries, and expansion bring real costs, and investors have every reason to examine them. However, responsible caution shouldn't become an excuse for assuming women's hockey cannot succeed.

The league has already shown what happens when it gives fans something to follow. Its next challenge is making those opportunities routine rather than exceptional. The sports industry would be making a massive mistake in not making women's spots a priority.

#2904. Berkshire breaks out to record high with fourth-quarter rally reaching 19%

(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)

Berkshire Hathaway's red-hot shares are ending a strong week with four consecutive fresh record high closes.

Since the rally began with the start of the fourth quarter on October 1, the Class A shares have closed at record highs 11 times as they soared 19.1%.

The much more widely held B shares closed at new highs just 10 times but are also up 19.1% from their near-term low.

The gains are in sharp contrast to the S&P 500's 1.2% dip as investors appear to be seeing Berkshire as a relatively safe haven amid worries about AI stocks and spending.

Both Berkshire classes were up 3.9% on the week as the S&P advanced by 2.5%, its best week since early August.

Berkshire's B shares are now 7.5 percentage points ahead of the benchmark for the year so far.

After erasing their post-Buffett CEO announcement losses three weeks ago, Berkshire shares are now up almost 10% since last year's shareholders meeting.

They've gained around 29% since last August's lows and are up around 18% year-to-date.

Berkshire Hathaway is due to disclose its quarterly equity portfolio snapshot on Monday when it files its Q3 13F with the SEC.

We won't know for sure until then, but numbers in the company's third quarter 10-Q, released last Saturday, indicate Berkshire continued to reduce its Bank of America stake.

It would be the ninth consecutive quarter of selling.

As of June 30, Berkshire reported holding 483.4 million BAC shares valued now at $24.7 billion, it's fifth largest equity position.

On June 30, 2024, before the selling began, Berkshire owned just over 1 billion shares valued at $41.1 billion.

Since then, the number of shares in the portfolio has decreased by 53.2%, not including any Q3 sales, while the stock price has increased by 28.3%.

If there had been no reductions, the position would be worth $52.7 billion.

The belief Berkshire sold more BAC shares in the third quarter is based on a $372 million reduction in the cost basis for equities categorized by the company as "banks, insurance, and finance."

The 10-Q also reports $2.2 billion of pretax gains from equity sales.

Barron's notes Bank of America and American Express are the only financial stocks in the portfolio that have a cost basis low enough to generate a gain like that. Amex is one of the four stocks new CEO Greg Abel indicated would be held for "decades" to come in his February letter to shareholders.

In any case, Berkshire's almost 23% stake in Amex would have required it to quickly disclose any sales.

Based on the numbers in the 10-Q, the warrants Berkshire received as part of a 2011 $5 billion investment in the bank that it used in 2017 to buy 700 million shares at $7.14 each, and BAC's average stock price in the quarter, Barron's estimates 30 to 40 million shares may have been sold.

That would be roughly in line with the 30.2 million shares sold in the second quarter.

The case isn't as good, but Barron's thinks Berkshire may have bought more Alphabet shares in the period. That's based on a $2.3 billion increase in the cost basis for the category that includes Google's parent.

Overall, it looks like it will be a relatively quiet quarter with $2.4 billion in equity purchases and $2.8 billion in sales.

In the first quarter, Berkshire bought $15.9 billion and sold $24.1 billion of equities. In the second quarter, it purchased $23.5 billion and sold $3.7 billion.

All those numbers exclude the company's buybacks of its own stock.

In a term sheet filed early Friday, Berkshire Hathaway says it is selling more than 182 billion yen ($1.1 billion) worth of bonds with maturities between 2029 and 2056 and annual interest rates between 2.6% and 4.6%.

Bloomberg points out the rates, compared to benchmarks, are higher than its previous sale this year.

It quotes a fund manager as saying market sentiment "has become more sensitive," forcing issuers to make their offerings more attractive.

In April, Berkshire sold 272 billion yen ($1.7 billion) of bonds.

Berkshire uses the proceeds from the yen-denominated bonds to protect its ongoing investments in Japanese stocks from currency fluctuations.

Warren Buffett recommends Benjamin Graham's book, "The Intelligent Investor," and outlines what he considers Graham's three most important ideas.

WARREN BUFFETT: On investment books, if you're asking about that, I would recommend the first two books that Phil Fisher wrote back around 1960, "Common Sense [Stocks] and Uncommon Profits" and the second one ["Paths to Wealth Through Common Stocks"]. They're very good books.

You know, I obviously recommend, first and foremost, [Benjamin Graham's] "The Intelligent Investor," with chapters eight and 20 are the ones that you really should read.

Two of the — well, all of the important ideas in investing, really, are in that book, because there's only about three ideas. And those — two of them are emphasized in those two chapters...

One is that — to think of yourself — to think of investing as owning a business and not buying something that wiggles around in price.

And the second one is your attitude, which ties in with that, the attitude toward the market, that's covered in chapter eight. And if you have the proper attitude toward market movements, it's an enormous help in securities.

And the final chapter is on the margin of safety, which means, don't try and drive a 9,800-pound truck over a bridge that says it's, you know, "Capacity: 10,000 pounds." But go down the road a little bit and find one that says, "Capacity: 15,000 pounds."

#2903. U.S.-China trade, Taiwan and tech tensions remain unresolved as Trump returns from Asia

SHENZHEN, China — Even as Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders gathered for high-profile photos at the summit's close, key issues from Nvidia to Taiwan remained unaddressed.

"The intrigue is around not what was said, but what remains unresolved," said Gary Dvorchak, managing director at Blueshirt.

"Taiwan remains a major source of strategic uncertainty. North Korea was notably absent from the trilateral nuclear declaration," he said. "Southeast Asia, which is increasingly central to global manufacturing and investment, was overshadowed by major-power diplomacy."

President Donald Trump did not meet with North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un, despite speculation.

Taiwan, one of the 21 member economies of APEC, sent Acer Group founder and honorary chairman Stan Shih to Shenzhen. But the self-governed island, which Beijing claims is part of its territory, did not feature in any significant way during the event. Taiwan is set to hold key elections for Taipei mayor and other posts on Nov. 28.

Instead, the highlight of this week's APEC summit in Shenzhen was a trilateral meeting Thursday between Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. The three leaders, meeting together for the first time, reaffirmed interests in reducing nuclear risks and plans to increase oil production.

"The optics are impressive, but there's not much happening," Ian Bremmer, president and founder of Eurasia Group, said Friday of the trilateral on CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia."

Resolving the years-long Ukraine war would require involvement from President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European allies, Bremmer said.

Ahead of the trilateral, Trump and Xi also held their third bilateral summit of the year. Xi greeted Trump at the airport late Wednesday, reciprocating the hospitality shown in September when the Chinese leader visited Washington.

But little was shared publicly on whether the two countries agreed to reduce tariffs further, allow rare earths to keep flowing beyond a January deadline, or address tech competition.

Recent reports tying Jensen Huang to an alleged Chinese spy led to the executive's resignation as Nvidia CEO. It also raised questions in Congress about the effectiveness of U.S. efforts to restrict China's access to advanced chips used to train artificial intelligence.

Trump indicated to Fox News that Nvidia came up briefly in his talks with Xi. U.S. officials last week said Trump did not plan to raise the matter, while noting Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk would accompany the U.S. president.

No other executive was named. Other American business leaders, including Visa CEO Ryan McInerney, who also chairs the U.S.-China Business Council, joined the APEC CEO Summit and was seen at a welcome banquet Wednesday evening.

However, Musk did not appear with Trump at major APEC-related events. CNBC was present for the opening portions of a banquet Wednesday and the Economic Leaders' Meeting Thursday and did not see Musk.

In fact, Musk flew to Shanghai Thursday morning to visit Tesla's factory there, a company executive said on Chinese social media. Musk also showed up in a social media video with Ren Hongbin, chairman of the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade.

Musk addressed Wednesday's DealBook Summit in New York via video conference, having previously said on X that he would be joining from China.

Tesla and the White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment.

"We still don't have a durable resolution of the U.S.-China trade dispute," Dvorchak said, adding: "Business needs certainty, not just ceremony."

Trump visited Shenzhen after briefly traveling to the Philippines on Tuesday for a meeting with the leaders of Australia, India and Japan as part of the Quad grouping happening on the sidelines of the ASEAN Summit. Trump also met the prime minister of Thailand, Anutin Charnvirakul.

Topics of discussion included U.S. cooperation with the region, trade and critical minerals, U.S. Ambassador to ASEAN Kevin Kim told reporters Wednesday. He declined to comment on whether China's influence in the region was addressed.

Kim emphasized it was the second year in a row that Trump visited Southeast Asia, and noted the region "will be at the heart of SI [artificial intelligence] going forward," making it important that American technology is "getting into the right hands" through a regulatory framework the president is building.

Speaking to reporters a day later in Shenzhen, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi also highlighted the ASEAN and Quad events over APEC. "The major outcome of this diplomatic week was the Quad Summit," she said, noting via official English translation how the four leaders expressed "strong opposition to the unilateral approach to change the status quo by force or coercion ... [as well as] arbitrary export control."

Takaichi, the first Japanese leader in seven years to visit China, received a cool reception upon her arrival in Shenzhen for the APEC meeting.

Tensions between Japan and China have escalated since Takaichi drew Beijing's ire in Nov. 2025 when she said that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could draw a Japanese military response.

Takaichi said Thursday that Japan's position on Taiwan remained unchanged as stated in the 1972 Japan-China Communiqué.

The communique said Japan "understands and respects" the People's Republic of China's position on Taiwan, but does not explicitly acknowledge Taiwan as part of the PRC.

— CNBC's Anniek Bao and Lim Hui Jie contributed to this report.

#2902. What To Watch For: Pitt Panthers

PITT WILL BE EVEN MORE AGGRESSIVE THAN NORMAL ON DEFENSE

Pitt has the best run defense in the country, but I expect them to turn up the dial this weekend in how they defend the run. Pitt will come into this game fully aware that Louisville has struggled with allowing tackles for loss this year. They will also be aware of the fact that they have been much better in this area throughout their five-game winning streak. UofL is ranked 71st in tackles for loss allowed after being in the 130s a few weeks ago.

The thing about the Cards being so bad when it comes to negative plays is that they still lead the country in yards per play. However, the Cards haven't been overly explosive over the last few games. They've just been more consistent. Pitt will look to force those negative plays, because that's what has been the key to the wins for the Cards. The Panthers will be bringing linebackers more often to force those negative plays this weekend.

LOUISVILLE SHOULD LOOK TO LAYER ROUTES FOR RECEIVERS

Teams haven't had a ton of success passing the ball against Pitt this year, but the two teams that did worked hard to get their most dynamic receivers into space down the field. The game that really stood out to me was the Virginia Tech game where Que'Sean Brown went off for 147 yards. Tech did a good job of running off coverage on the outside, with Brown running underneath on shorter routes in the voided space.

I would love to see Brian and Jeff Brohm work in some of the deep crossing routes we've seen from this offense over the last few years. Pitt has diversified their defensive calls over the years, but when it comes down to it, they want to run quarters, which opens them up for a receiver leaking into open space when a receiver runs off that coverage. I think the Cards can take advantage of this on Saturday night.

LINCOLN KEINHOLZ'S LEGS WILL BE A BIG FACTOR

As I pointed out above, Pitt is going to really get after the Louisville running game in an effort to pile up negative plays. That will make it that much more important that Lincoln Keinholz makes plays with his legs. He has shown this year that he has a unique ability to extend plays outside of the pocket when he gets pressure. He has also been very good at finding receivers down the field in those situations. Those types of plays will be important in this game.

What will be more important, in my opinion, is his ability to get chunk gains on option runs. He has been contained, for the most part, this season on plays where he has to make a read and then get up the field. That has to improve in this game. I don't see Pitt giving up some of the longer runs he's had on QB Sweeps because of their team speed and discipline. But give me Linc on some inverted veer plays with Isaac Brown running towards the boundary. I think things could open up for him.

THE GAMEPLAN SHOULD BE THE SAME AS LAST WEEK FOR LOUISVILLE'S DEFENSE

Louisville held UNC to 293 yards, 5 yards per play, and one play of more than 18 yards. Just, like, do that again?

#2901. Anthropic raises $93.5 billion total as underwriters scoop up ‘greenshoe’ overallotment

Anthropic underwriters have officially exercised their overallotment of shares in the historic initial public offering, bringing the total raised to $93.5 billion, according to a release Friday.

The artificial intelligence company raised $81.3 billion on Wednesday and netted an additional $12.2 billion through the overallotment, surpassing SpaceX, which held a record IPO in June.

Anthropic said it sold an aggregate of 1,127,000,000 shares of its Class A common stock at $83 per share in the offering. It sold 980 million shares on Wednesday and its underwriters had the option to purchase up to an additional 147 million shares by Friday as part of the overallotment, which is commonly referred to as the "greenshoe."

Shares of the Claude maker opened trading at $111.50 on the Nasdaq on Thursday, but slid throughout the day and closed at $97.17. The stock sank 12% in premarket trading on Friday during a broad tech sell-off.

In addition to the sale of its Class A common stock, Anthropic closed a concurrent sale of its Class N common stock after a group of tech companies, including Advanced Micro Devices, Google, Microsoft, Nvidia and others, agreed to participate in a $26 billion private placement at the IPO price. Anthropic said Friday that aggregate gross proceeds from its IPO, including the private placement, totaled $119.5 billion, before deducting offering expenses.

Anthropic dodged an unforgiving series of obstacles on its road to the Nasdaq on Thursday, as investors brooded over Jensen Huang's shocking ouster at Nvidia, voters' stinging rebuke of the tech during the midterms and whether rising interest rates would stymie industry plans for a multitrillion-dollar AI infrastructure buildout.

CEO Dario Amodei co-founded the company in 2021 after he and a handful of other researchers, including his sister Daniela, quit their jobs at OpenAI, now Anthropic's chief rival. Anthropic is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude, which have captivated the corporate world and fueled the company's historic rise.

The siblings celebrated the IPO as a "milestone" in an interview with CNBC on Thursday, but said there's more work ahead for Anthropic.

"For us, it's like one stop on the journey," Daniela Amodei said. "We think about this as, 'Wow, this is an incredible moment for Anthropic for our mission, but we're going to wake up tomorrow and we're going to be the same company.'"

#2900. Man City coach Maresca plays down link between financial scandal and team's dip in form

Manchester City won its first seven competitive games of the season before being found guilty of large-scale financial rule-breaking, leaving the club's future shrouded in uncertainty.

Since that explosive verdict was passed down, just four victories in nine matches — including losses in each of its last three Premier League games.

"I don't think the players are focused on the noise," the City manager said Friday when asked if the huge legal case hanging over the club was affecting his players.

The word "noise" has typically been used by Maresca to describe anything surrounding a scandal that threatens to upturn the English soccer landscape, should City fail with the appeal it has lodged against an investigatory panel's ruling that the club's Abu Dhabi ownership artificially inflated revenue by more than $1 billion over nearly a decade to circumvent the Premier League's financial fair-play rules.

City has always denied wrongdoing and said it would be "relentless" in a fight to clear its name.

However, lose the appeal and among the possible sanctions facing City is a points deduction so large that it could lead to relegation, or even expulsion from the Premier League.

Sanctions might not come until after the appeal decision is reached — and that might not be until next year.

So, Maresca was asked, could this be weighing on the minds of the players out on the field? Some of them — like Norway striker Erling Haaland during the recent international break — get asked about the case during their media duties.

"I don't think they are worried about that," he replied.

Maresca pointed to City's three straight league defeats — to Aston Villa, Brighton and Nottingham Forest — and said there was an argument that his team could have won all three games, even if he also said City might not have deserved to win each of its first seven games.

Individual mistakes are certainly beginning to cost City dearly, while Maresca acknowledged the players are still getting used to his style of play after the departure of long-time manager Pep Guardiola.

The balance and make-up of City's expensively assembled, new-look midfield, containing summer signings Elliot Anderson and Enzo Fernandez, is coming under scrutiny, in particular, with the defense not appearing to be adequately protected.

"We are going to find more solutions for more balance in defensive line, midfield or up front," Maresca said

City will look to make it 21 straight wins over Fulham when the teams meet at Etihad Stadium in the league on Saturday to begin the 11th round of games.

City is third in the standings, six points behind first-place Arsenal.

#2898. Eintracht Frankfurt vs. Hoffenheim preview: Eagles look to carry pre-break momentum

Adi Hütter's return to Frankfurt has produced mixed results so far, but the Eagles are beginning to find some consistency.

As a result, they sit in tenth place with 12 points, having lost only once in their last five matches across all competitions.

Before the international break, Frankfurt rescued a dramatic 2-2 draw at Paderborn despite being reduced to ten men.

That day, Jonathan Burkardt's stoppage-time equaliser ensured they avoided defeat, while two recent 3-1 victories over Hamburger SV in the Bundesliga and DFB-Pokal provided encouragement ahead of the draw at the Home Deluxe Arena.

However, defensive performances remain a concern for Hütter, whose side have conceded 20 league goals already this season.

Saturday's encounter also brings an interesting reunion between the Austrian and compatriot Christian Ilzer, who spoke about the influence Frankfurt's head coach has had on his managerial career in his press conference on Friday.

Robin Koch has been declared fit for Saturday's encounter, although Can Uzun remains doubtful after suffering from a cold during the international break.

Elias Baum will serve a suspension following his dismissal against Paderborn, leaving Hütter to consider changes to his defensive setup. Jessic Ngankam also remains unavailable with an adductor injury.

Christian Ilzer's side have endured a similarly inconsistent campaign, but their recent improvement has lifted them into ninth place, level on points with Frankfurt.

After losing four of their opening five Bundesliga fixtures, Hoffenheim have taken nine points from their last four league outings, with an impressive 3-0 victory over Bayer Leverkusen in October followed by further encouraging performances, including a 2-1 triumph over Schalke immediately before the international break.

Fisnik Asllani opened the scoring against the Royal Blues before setting up Tim Lemperle for Hoffenheim's second goal, as Ilzer's squad begins to look more than the one seen last season after an injury-hit run at the start of the season.

While the attacking struggles are mainly over, Ilzer continues to contend with several defensive absences, with Robin Hranáč, Valentin Gendrey and Albian Hajdari all unavailable.

Summer signing Nathan De Cat also remains sidelined with a knee injury.

There is better news elsewhere, with Bambasé Conté and Patrick Wimmer making progress towards fitness, while compatriot Alexander Prass returned early from international duty with muscular problems, although Ilzer has not ruled out the Austrian featuring from the start.

#2894. Have the Chiefs finally fixed their pass rush?

Sometimes we make defense more complicated than it needs to be. In the modern game, much of an effective defensive unit depends on its ability to get after the quarterback. Look at the top of the leaderboard this year for proof: The (7-2) Minnesota Vikings and the defending champion Seattle Seahawks lead the league in pressure rate.

The top two defenses in points per drive allowed? You guessed it, the Vikings and the Seahawks.

Get after the quarterback, and you're more likely to get consistent stops. Fail to do so, and it could be a long day. That's the case for just about every defense in the league.

Except the 2026 Kansas City Chiefs, apparently.

The Chiefs have been a rare exception to this rule for much of the season. Kansas City currently ranks 26th in sacks, 27th in QB hits, and 29th in pressure rate, according to Pro Football Reference. But, somehow, they miraculously rank 5th in the league in points per drive allowed.

It doesn't really make sense. For much of the season, it's felt like smoke and mirrors. Some of it can surely be explained by the schedule. Let's be honest, the Chiefs haven't exactly faced a murderer's row of opposing offenses. The Chiefs have made do with a prototypical 'bend-don't-break' defensive approach for much of the season.

But the tide seems to be turning over the past couple of weeks. The Chiefs are bending less. The pass rush is getting home more.

It's incredibly rare to win as often as the Chiefs did early this season with the kind of pass rush they were producing. In fact, only seven other teams in the past 15 years won at least 5 of their first 7 games while allowing 9 or fewer sacks in those seven games. The others were the 2025 49ers, the 2020 Titans, the 2018 Patriots, the 2016 Raiders, the 2015 Falcons, the 2014 Cardinals and the 2014 Cowboys. Those teams finished the season ranked 32nd, 30th, 30th, 32nd, 32nd, 24th and 28th in the league, respectively, for sacks in those individual seasons.

That's not exactly a great omen for the 2026 Chiefs. They've been trying their darndest the past couple of weeks to buck the trend.

Kansas City produced just nine sacks over their first seven games, but they've followed that up with an eight-sack outburst over the past two weeks. In fact, if you look at sack yardage lost by the opposition, the Chiefs have pushed their opponents back more (58 yards) over the past two weeks than they did in their first seven weeks combined (39 yards).

What's changed? Well, a combination of everything.

For one, edge rusher George Karlaftis has taken his game to an entirely different level. He's been earning pressures the entire season, but he's finally converting those pressures into sacks. Karlaftis had 18 pressures and two sacks in his first seven games of the regular season, and he's 8 pressures and 3.5 sacks over the past two.

Part of what's helped Karlaftis take that step is those around him winning one-on-one battles. Second-year defensive lineman Ashton Gillotte is probably the first name worth mentioning. He produced just two pressures and one sack in his first seven games, according to Pro Football Reference. He has doubled those numbers over the past two games with 2 sacks and 4 pressures.

Chris Jones also finally looks like himself again. The future Hall of Famer tallied just three hurries and 0.5 sacks in his first 7 games of the regular season. He's added 2.5 sacks and 3 pressures over the past couple of weeks.

The results are hard to ignore. The Chiefs produced 8 sacks in a 2-game stretch for the first time since December of 2024. It's worth noting this is a feat the Chiefs accomplished at some point in the 2019, 2022, 2023 and 2024 seasons. They reached the Super Bowl in each of those four years.

Time will tell. This pass rush has been underwhelming far more often than it's been great this season. But the past two weeks were legitimate signs of life. The Jets and Falcons aren't great teams, but their offensive lines aren't awful.

Brandon Thorn of Establish the Run is as respected as any offensive line analyst covering the game, and he currently has the Jets ranked as his 12th-best offensive line in the league. He has the Falcons at 19th. Not world beaters, but this wasn't the Chiefs taking advantage of the early-season Packers MASH unit offensive line.

This weekend should set up well for another dominant performance by the Chiefs' D-Line. The Cardinals' quarterbacks have been sacked 8 times over the past two weeks. Thorn ranks their offensive line as the third worst in the league. This could be yet another get-right game for the defensive side of the ball before things start to get real.

What lies ahead will dictate the Chiefs' postseason seeding. The Bills (4th), Rams (14th), Bengals (5th), and 49ers (3rd) all have top-half-of-the-league offensive lines, according to Thorn. The Chiefs' defensive line will have its work cut out for them. The past two weeks have been encouraging. There's still work to be done.

Pressure has been building on this defense to get after the quarterback. It's nice to see them finally applying some of that pressure to the opposition.

#2892. Why extending Riley Moss was a smart decision for the Denver Broncos

The Denver Broncos continued their tradition of rewarding their homegrown talent. Yesterday, news broke that the Broncos had agreed to terms with fourth-year cornerback Riley Moss on a four-year contract worth $67 million. As of now, the guarantees have not been made available. However, the average annual value makes him the NFL's 23rd highest paid corner. In my opinion, that's quite the bargain.

This summer, I asked Broncos Country who they felt deserved extension priority—Moss or Ja'Quan McMillian. I was under the impression that Denver would have to just choose one. It was a close battle, but Moss came ahead with 56-percent of the votes.

Flash forward to recent memory and fans seemed to have changed their tune. A little over a month ago, Scotty Payne wrote an article and put a poll up on Mile High Report's X account asking the same question. The result? McMillian in a landslide with 94-percent of the votes.

Would I love for McMillian to come back too? Absolutely. He has been an underrated playmaker in their secondary and has a penchant for big plays in crunch time. It appears Denver will revisit negotiations after the season, but I have a feeling the Broncos' standout nickelback may test the open market. Though I'd like to offer some thoughts on why extending Moss was a good decision.

The Broncos' defense under Vance Joseph is known for their aggressive man-to-man coverage assignments. This season due to injuries in the secondary, they have utilized more zone coverage than prior years. However, their man numbers are still higher compared to many teams in the NFL.

In fact, I'd argue that Joseph would like to be running more man than he has this season. Every team uses a mixture of both, but the difference compared to past season is notable. With a healthy Moss and Surtain, I expect Denver's man coverage numbers to go up quite significantly in the second half of the season.

The main critique on Moss has been those pesky pass interference penalties. That's fair. However, I'd just say it's also a part of the process considering how often he is targeted and tasked with man-to-man assignments. Last year, Moss was targeted an astounding 118 times. However, he allowed just a 58-percent completion rate and had the most pass breakups of any corner in the league.

This season, the targets have been significantly less. The former Iowa prospect has been thrown at only 35 times. Through eight games, Moss has allowed 18 receptions for 223 yards. That's only a 51.4 completion percentage allowed—certainly one of the best marks in the NFL for any defensive back. Even with those penalties, he has proven to be a great player for Denver.

Only time will tell if the Broncos can come to terms with McMillian too. As I wrote in my article this summer, I felt that they would likely only choose one for cap purposes. Truth be told, they have the cap flexibility to accommodate a deal. Additionally, there are also various contracts that may be moved on to bolster their salary cap space.

However, I question whether or not General Manager George Paton and the rest of the Broncos' brass would want to invest such a monumental number of guarantees at the cornerback position. McMillian will likely get a lucrative deal in free agency and have no shortage of suitors. In the event he embarks on greener pastures, the Broncos do have his replacement already in house.

That's second-year cornerback Jahdae Barron. The former Jim Thorpe Award winner was a versatile defender for the Texas Longhorns. Barron played just about every spot imaginable in their secondary. His cross-training across the backend of the defense has continued into the pros in Joseph's scheme.

While many fans have already written him off as a potential bust due to lack of playing time, I still remain confident he has the ability to contribute at a high level. He seems like a more natural fit on the inside anyway. I'm not sure Barron had the length or athleticism to routinely hold his own in press and go head-to-head against bigger wide receivers in man coverage.

It's also important to note that Kris Abrams-Draine will be a free agent at the end of the 2027 season. Abrams-Draine has primarily been a boundary backup for Denver in his first three seasons. He has played well when the opportunity presented itself.

Quite frankly, I think he is a starting caliber player and there is a chance he could wind up receiving a nice free agent deal a few years down the line. With Moss extended, that's a little bit less of a worry at the boundary position moving forward, though they will still have to find depth at some point in time beyond the '27 season.

#2889. Research moves closer to identifying CTE in living patients

The ability to detect CTE only through autopsies prevents football players from knowing whether they have it during their careers. Work continues to change that.

Via ESPN, a pair of studies published by The Journal of the American Medical Association show that a new blood test could detect advanced stages of CTE in a living patient.

A study from Boston University and Banner Health was based on blood drawn from a small sample of former players during their lifetimes. Autopsies performed after they died showed that they had CTE. The researchers then found a marker for CTE based on the levels of a specific type of protein in their blood.

“I’m cautiously optimistic that we can really understand this finding and move it forward in the next five years or so,” Dr. Michael Alosco, one of the authors of the study, told ESPN. Alosco described the test as a “game changer.”

The study applies only to advanced stages of CTE.

“We are still in the discovery phase and it’s a small sample size,” Alosco said in a statement released regarding the study. “But if future studies validate these findings, this blood test will allow us to detect CTE with a high level of accuracy and open the doors to clinical trials and treatment.”

The ultimate goal remains developing a test that would show any degree of CTE in a living patient. It would allow football players to know whether they already have CTE, and possibly the extent of the disease.

Football players would first have to decide whether they want to know if they have CTE and, if they do, whether they will keep playing.

More broadly, football leagues at every level would have to decide whether players would be prevented from participating if they have CTE.

The development of a test to diagnose CTE could also lead to research aimed at identifying potential treatments for it.

Where the work leads will be determined over time. And the knowledge acquired by football players will allow for informed — if not complicated — decisions as to whether they will choose to keep playing, and whether they will be medically cleared to do so.

#2882. Nvidia has lost $2 trillion in value. Here's what options traders expect from earnings

Jensen Huang's forced exit from Nvidia shocked Wall Street and Washington, wiped $2 trillion off its market value, and raised serious questions about national security and regulation of the AI complex. Traders, for the moment, must content themselves with the comparatively mundane business of Tuesday's earnings, and options traders are expecting big moves.

With volatility in the stock near the highest since April 2025, options traders are now pricing a 7% reaction in the stock after its report, the biggest implied move going into an Nvidia report since February 2025, and well above the median move of 3.2% over the last eight quarters.

Implied volatility reached 68 Monday, compared to under 40 in early October, according to ThinkOrSwim data. Nvidia vol reached a multi-year high above 92 in the aftermath of President Trump's tariff Liberation day in April '25. In other words, the company that for much of the AI boom was the most reliable winner in the market, is now more volatile than all but 35 companies in the S&P 500.

"Longer term, I see significant downside risk unless Nvidia can attract an exceptional leader, someone like Tim Cook or AMD's Lisa Su," Nigam Arora, founder of the Arora report, said in a text ahead of the company's after-market report on Tuesday.

Since hitting all-time highs in October, Nvidia shares have fallen 35%, shedding $2 trillion in market capitalization along the way. Including Nvidia, there are only five companies in the S&P 500 worth more than $2 trillion. However, there is evidence that bulls have been holding out hope while bears snatch up profits: the ratio of open puts to call contracts has actually widened towards calls, according to Barchart data. The ratio is currently 0.87, down from a one-year high of 1.02 two weeks ago and the lowest since the first week of October.

The most popular contract by volume on Monday was the 155-strike put expiring at the bell Monday, but the most popular trade for later expiry was the 160-strike call expiring Thursday, and the second-most-common purchase was the 190-strike call expiring Friday, SpotGamma data show.

One catch is that most call contracts traded Monday looked like neutral to bearish positions opened by traders selling calls. Of the 5 million options traded on Monday, 3 million were calls, but more were likely opened by sellers than buyers. Of the $2.3 billion in options premium traded on Nvidia Monday, $1.2 billion was tied to puts, SpotGamma data show.

With bears taking profits in puts the past month, there's another potential snag on open interest. There are very few open put contracts at or below the $157 level at which the stock closed Monday. That suggests any bad surprise would find many traders with little downside protection.

By the same token, there's notable open interest in call contracts from the 175-strike and above, suggesting profit-taking on a bounce could limit Nvidia's recovery past levels it breached over the past week.

Either way, Tuesday's earnings could provide fireworks.

#2881. Kirk Cousins on possibly playing 18 games: "Just part of the deal"

Because Vikings quarterback Kirk Cousins was traded after the Vikings’ bye but before the Raiders’ bye, Cousins won’t have a bye in 2026.

Which means he’ll potentially play 18 regular-season games.

During a Thursday press conference, Cousins was asked whether he has considered the possibility of playing a game on each and every weekend of the 2026 regular season.

“I thought about it,” Cousins told reporters. “I thought about it, but added to the altitude, added to the new system, added to not knowing people’s names. Just part of the deal. And, again, kind of one minute at a time, one day at a time, one practice at a time, and kind of keep blinders on, and we’ll look up, and it’ll be March.

“But until then, I think I’m just kind of, keeping it, you know, the short game, if you will, short view in front of me, just trying to stay focused there.”

It’s the right attitude. It’s the only attitude. He has gone from a situation in which he was destined to be replaced with rookie Fernando Mendoza to a team with a 7-2 record and a realistic shot not only at making it to the postseason but also of advancing through multiple rounds when it gets there.

And he’s right about the imminent arrival of March. Given the speed with which the season unfolds, it’ll be over before anyone knows it. It’s a finite window of time and, as Cousins said after Sunday’s win over the Packers, “There’s more to the story being written.”

#2880. Lakers vs. Kings Preview: Time to start another winning streak

After witnessing their nine-game losing streak come to an end, the Lakers (13-3) have the opportunity to get back in the win column on Friday against the Sacramento Kings (1-13). This is considered an NBA Cup Game for both teams under Group C.

Who: Los Angeles Lakers vs. Sacramento Kings

Nobody is more disappointed in the Lakers' losing streak ending than the team themselves. After Wednesday's loss to the Utah Jazz — where they put up their worst offensive game of the season — head coach JJ Redick and Luka Dončić were pretty bullish on not bringing up the fatigue card despite this being their third game in four nights.

That alone says a lot about this team's character and their determination to be the best they can be, night in and night out. It's what makes the upcoming match against the Kings quite interesting because we're going to see how the Lakers bounce back, especially with the added stakes of an NBA Cup Game.

On Friday, Los Angeles will see a Sacramento team that has lost seven games in a row. That means the Kings could come into this matchup either very hungry for a win, struggling to find their footing or perhaps a little bit of both. Maybe playing on the road will help these Kings because they just finished a disastrous 0-7 homestand.

Ideally, the Lakers shouldn't need Dončić to score 40 points again in this one because it would nice to see a collective team effort win. In their last meeting against the Kings, when the Lakers came away with a 13-point win, we saw arguably their best defensive effort of the season. Hopefully, we see that same level of intensity again because the Lakers could use as convincing a win as possible to keep their NBA Cup hopes alive.

If the Lakers regain their offense and play like the team that had just won nine straight games, then they should be able to take care of this one. Let's see if they can start another winning streak by defeating the Kings on Friday.

The Kings have struggled to close out games, which could work in the Lakers' favor. Ideally, L.A. won't need a clutch-time performance but if it comes down to that, they should be able to capitalize.

The Kings also don't guard the 3-point line very well. In their previous game against the Phoenix Suns, the latter shot 44% from deep.

On to the injury report, only Austin Reaves (left heel contusion) is out.

As for the Kings, Ben Simmons (right Achilles tendon repair) and Maxime Raynaud (right patella subluxation) are out. Precious Achiuwa (left lower leg contusion) is doubtful, while De'Andre Hunter (left hip soreness) is questionable.

#2877. San Antonio vs. Los Angeles, Final Score: Spurs outlast Clippers in 124-112 win

It didn't take long for the Spurs to get back on the winning track. The Silver and Black didn't amaze, but they took care of business at home against a shorthanded Clippers team. The 124-112 score might suggest that it was a comfortable victory, but it was mostly a close game in which the more talented squad simply stepped on the gas late to close it out.

The Spurs, facing an inferior opponent after the loss to the Pistons but missing Dylan Harper, didn't look as dominant as it would have been ideal to start the game. The pace wasn't great, and neither was the decision-making for most of the first half. Defensively, they had good stretches but also moments in which they allowed dribble penetration without much resistance or left shooters open. It wasn't the strong bounceback many were hoping for, but because of their tremendous talent, they managed to lead by 14 points at one point in the second quarter.

Unfortunately, the lead disappeared as the bench had one of its all-too-familiar poor runs. In all fairness, however, the second unit wasn't the only reason why the home team only led by three at the break, as the starters didn't return with the energy required to pull away. Some good moments showed the high ceiling the Silver and Black have, but it wasn't a particularly inspiring first half. The Clippers deserve credit for capitalizing on the at times lackadaisical and downright sloppy play from the Spurs, but a lot of San Antonio's wounds in the opening two frames were self-inflicted.

In the second half, the visitors went from simply being opportunistic to actively hurting the Spurs on the offensive end. The threes were falling, and they were not afraid to hunt mismatches, using Brook Lopez in the post, especially in the third quarter. Ty Lue's guys were confident after coming back to make it close earlier and put themselves ahead on the scoreboard with more consistent play, while San Antonio relied on individual stretches of greatness from different players. Castle had it going as a scorer, Devin Vassell made some defensive plays, and even some of the bench guys got in on the action.

A legitimate blowout was out of the question after three quarters, but the Spurs have been good at elevating their play when they need to throughout this season. It's been enough for them to beat lesser teams, and it happened again against the Clippers. It wasn't the prettiest of games, something that has also been a trend this year, but San Antonio did what it needed to. As the minutes passed, the Silver and Black got a double-digit lead, and they didn't squander it late. Hopefully, it will be the beginning of another long win streak.

As expected, Mitch Johnson started Julian Champagnie in place of Dylan Harper, out with a hip injury. The Fox-Castle-Vassell-Champagnie-Wembanyama unit started most of last season and outscored opponents by over 17 points per 100 possessions, so it should be fine. Still, there were some moments early when the lack of a third ball handler seemed to bother San Antonio. The turnovers piled up as some players, especially Stephon Castle, often forced the issue. The Spurs will miss Harper, which was expected.

Devin Vassell continues to be cold in the outside shooting department (3-for-16 in the last four games), but as usual nowadays, he made an impact elsewhere. Hopefully the shooting touch returns soon.

Carter Bryant was the first guy off the bench for the Harper-less Spurs. In the second half, Jordan McLaughlin got the call. Mitch Johnson is experimenting with his rotations and trying to find guys that can replace Harper's athleticism and ball-handling. We might see different players get minutes depending on what the team needs on any given night.

The second unit has been getting a lot of flak, mostly deserved, for their play early in the season, but they were huge for the Spurs on Thursday. They brought a lot of energy to a game that sometimes lacked it, at least from San Antonio's side.

Brandon Ingram, the big piece going back to the Clippers in the Kawhi Leonard trade, was out with an injury. The other player Los Angeles received in the transaction, Gradey Dick, wasn't all that effective in limited minutes. The Clippers' major summer move had little effect on the result of this one.

The release of Grand Theft Auto VI provided the Spurs' broadcast with the perfect excuse to show one of the best photos ever: the 99 team playing StarCraft together after winning the title. Look at those magnificent nerds.

The Spurs will host the Pelicans on Saturday. New Orleans will be in the second game of a back-to-back after playing the Thunder on Friday.

#2875. Miami Dolphins vs. Buffalo Bills: Three reasons why Miami will win, lose

This week has not been kind to the making of content for this post. The flow of hope for getting win from here on out is down to a trickle. Let's see if we can salvage any for this contest.

The Bills pass defense has been the weaker part of their defense this season. They had games against Joey Fagnano and Carson Wentz where they held them to under 200 combined yards. But they have allowed 250+ passing yards to just about everyone else. Last week, Kyle McCord made his debut against a weak Colts defense and played alright. He threw for 209 yards and got the RBs involved in the passing game. I don't expect McCord to light it up, but he has the opportunity for some success against a middle of the pack pass defense.

Despite being one of two 8-1 teams in the league, they have a turnover differential of zero. They have 14 takeaways and 14 giveaways. QB Josh Allen is playing well, particularly as a rusher, leading the team with 11 rushing TDs. He is in the middle of the pack for passing TDs. But he has 7 INTS and 4 fumbles on the season. James Cook has 4 fumbles this season. Turnovers are the great equalizer, and Miami is getting better at generating them. The Dolphins have generated at least one turnover in each of the last 5 games. All it takes is for one errant throw or fumbled ball to swing momentum and turn the tide.

I generally don't think divisional games can be trap games, but the odds for that are never zero. The Bills face the 7-2 Chiefs the following week. Then go on the road to face New England, Green Bay, before facing Chicago and Denver. Part of me thinks Buffalo will look at this game as a must win – the final "gimme game" before a slate of playoff bound opponents. Another part of me thinks they can be looking ahead to the Chiefs and might slip up. The 1-8 Dolphins led by Kyle McCord will be easy to overlook. But if the defense steps up just enough, they can make this a tougher out than expected.

Miami lost 3 of their top interior defensive linemen in the span of a week. Sieler, Phillips, and Biggers are out for the season. The Dolphins are stuck relying on Kenneth Grant and some guys. The current IDL on the roster are Grant, Keith Cooper Jr., and Jordan Jefferson. They have some bigger edge players like Eric Watts (6'5" 277) and Rodney McGraw (6'4", 273) that can perhaps move inside on some passing downs. They can also big the bigger edge players in run defense. Miami also signed Matthew Butler to the practice squad. Butler was with the Dolphins in 2025 and in camp this offseason before being cut. He adds some depth and scheme familiarity. But the Bills have one of the better offensive lines, ranked 3rd in pass block win rate and 1st in run block win rate. The Bills are the 3rd in rushing attempts, 2nd in rushing yards, 6th in yards per attempt, and 1st in rushing TDs. The Dolphins run defense had a solid game against Jahmyr Gibbs and the Lions, but had their worst outing against the Colts, allowing 172 yards, the most in any game this season. Some good news is that Grant and Cooper both had solid games against the Colts. But even if they play out of their minds this week, it is still a horrible matchup for the Dolphins.

The Bills are at the top in terms of winning pass and run blocks. On the defensive side, they are less so. They are currently 29th in pass rush win rate and 23rd in run stop win rate. That said, the Dolphins' run offense is stagnating. They haven't rushed for more than 78 yards in any of the last 3 games. Having an injured Malik Willis contributed to that. However, after an early breakout for Ollie Gordon II, he has been limited to under 4 YPC in the last 3 games. Part of that for last week could be having a backup QB as the starter – defenses will worry more about the run. But part of that is the offensive line. The Lions and Pats were better run defenses. The Colts were not – one of the worst in the league and the Dolphins still couldn't get going on the ground The offensive line has to take their share of that blame. Starting center Aaron Brewer missed last week in concussion protocol and did not practice Wednesday. He returned Thursday, but hasn't cleared protocol just yet. His backup, Andrew Meyer, was bad against a good-not-great Colts front. Meyer was also a problem with the batted balls for McCord that cost Miami some big plays, including a potential TD. RG Jonah Savaiinaea looked like an improved player early on but has been moving in the opposite direction.

In the passing game, the Bills aren't high at the win rate, but they are 4th in the league in pressure percentage at 28%. They are tied with 4 other teams at 17th for sacks with 21. They only have 2 players with more than 1.5 sacks on the season. BUT… they have one of the league's top rushers in Gregory Rousseau, who is tied for 4th with 8 sacks on the season. He leads the league in pressures with 37. He is NOT in the top 22 in pass rush win rate, which would lead me to believe he is getting pressures and sacks due to volume – only 4 other teams have as many or more pass attempts against them than the Bills. This leads back to Miami's OL and Austin Jackson. He has been a liability against every top edge rusher he has faced; Aidan Hutchinson took his lunch money 2 weeks ago. Now he has to face Rousseau, who may not win as early and as often as Hutchinson but still gets to the QB. If the Dolphins can't keep the Bills defense honest by running the ball and/or get too far behind, the Bills pass rush is very likely to heat up McCord.

Do you remember the last time Miami won in Buffalo? I certainly do. It was the 2016 season where the Dolphins snuck out an overtime win thanks to Jay Ajayi rushing for 206 yards on 32 carries and some heroic kicks made by Andrew Franks. Outside of that game, the Dolphins haven't had much success on the road against Buffalo. Since 2000, the Dolphins have played in Buffalo 27 times including the playoffs and have gotten 7 wins. They haven't beaten Josh Allen in Buffalo, but this isn't just about the Allen-led Bills. From 2000 until 2019, when Allen took over as the full-time starter, the Bills had 3 winning seasons and they were 9-7 seasons. They had three 8-8 seasons. Their record was 127-177 and the average season was 6.7 wins and 9.3 losses. Allen has started 9 games against the Dolphins in Buffalo, so that's still 7 wins in the other 18 attempts. When they DID win, the average record for Buffalo was 6-10. The average margin of victory in those games was 10.7, and it's been 7 or less in the last 3 times.

So even when Buffalo was mid, the Dolphins still couldn't win there. They absolutely haven't won there any time Buffalo has finished with a winning record. The last time the Dolphins won in Buffalo in the same season Buffalo finished with a winning record was 1996. This week, the Dolphins take a talent deficient team that is now weaker due to injuries and starting a backup QB in his second ever NFL game on the road to a place they don't win at, even when the opponent is bad. Now… the last 2 times Miami has marched into Buffalo with a backup QB starting the game, they have a record of 1-1. They got their last win with Matt Moore starting for Ryan Tannehill. Skylar Thompson went into Buffalo in the playoffs and fell just short, losing 34-31. If there is ANY hope in this regard, it's that recent history shows Miami backups making the game a tougher out than Buffalo expected.

The injuries, the roster, the season outlook… this game is more likely to look like the week 2 bloodbath against the 49ers than the recent close games. Buffalo is churning along with the top seed in the AFC in mind. The Dolphins are in the middle of a rebuild. Perhaps Miami can catch lightning in a bottle and pull out a big upset. But I have a feeling most fans will be tuned out before halftime.
