#2874. Warriors finish winless road trip with lopsided loss to Grizzlies

It turns out that Steph Curry is pretty important to the Golden State Warriors success. When the Dubs head out on a five-game road trip just over a week ago, they did it with an eight-game winning streak and all the momentum in the world. And then, just a few minutes into the five-city trip, Curry suffered an oblique injury, and a few hours later, the Warriors lost to the Houston Rockets. What followed was brutal: a 38-point loss to the San Antonio Spurs, a 21-point defeat at the hands of the New Orleans Pelicans, a 22-point loss to the upstart Dallas Mavericks, and finally, on Thursday night, a 28-point loss to the surprisingly great Memphis Grizzlies.

The silver lining, if you're into that sort of thing, is that the Warriors looked the best that they have since Curry was injured, despite losing 126-98. The execution was the best it had been in a while, but ultimately, an astounding lack of shooting did the Dubs in.

As had been the case in all of the other Curry-less games, the Warriors got off to a comically slow start. They trailed 5-0, and then 8-2, and Steve Kerr's first timeout came when the Warriors trailed 13-4 just a few minutes in, as the team was racking up the turnovers. Even the good news was bittersweet: Charles Bassey scored the first seven points for Golden State, but also collected three quick fouls.

Still, the Warriors were executing well … mostly. They couldn't resist turning the ball over, with eight giveaways in the first quarter alone, but they were creating things on offense and getting good looks. Unfortunately, the good looks weren't falling, and they weren't able to do much on defense. Even with a nice run to end the opening frame, the Warriors trailed 31-24 after the first.

The Grizzlies came out firing in the second quarter, and quickly led 43-29 with an astonishing 21 points off of turnovers. That, combined with the Warriors' inability to make seemingly any jump shot, made it clear that unless there was a serious reversal of fortunes, the Warriors would not be winning. And there was, unfortunately, no reversal of fortune.

Memphis was turning Golden State's turnovers and missed shots into offens of their own, and used a 14-1 run to turn the game into a blowout at 47-30. But Golden State's response was impressive. The defense really stepped up late, and put the clamps on the Grizzlies with some of their best possessions in the past week (low bar, I know). That led to some much better offensive possessions, with the team getting significantly more aggressive to make up for the unsuccessful shooting. After trailing at one point by 18, the Warriors ran off a 10-0 run, and thanks to a strong defensive stand to end the half, only trailed 55-47 at the break. They had only made three shots from beyond the arc, they had no players in double figures, and Yaxel Lendeborg had yet to make a field goal, yet somehow they were in the game.

It wouldn't last long. For the third quarter in a row, the Grizzlies started the third hot, and quickly pushed the lead comfortably into the double digits. It felt like the Warriors were so close to playing well, but just couldn't quite get over the hump. They would execute well but miss shots, and then they would follow it up with some impressive individual plays supplemented by poor execution. The third quarter was ultimately defined by a distinct lack of easy shots … even when they scored, they simply couldn't get anything easy, and labored over every possession, good or bad. They still couldn't make any threes, and they still had too many turnovers, though credit where it's due: the energy and effort level didn't fade a bit, from opening tip until final buzzer. But energy and effort were no match for talent and execution, and the Grizzlies took a 92-73 lead into the final frame.

From there, it was just window dressing. The Grizzlies again were on fire to start the quarter, and quickly pushed the lead well into the 20s, making it clear that there would be no miraculous comeback for the Dubs. Both teams emptied their benches fairly early, as Memphis rolled to a 126-98 victory, their second win of the season against Golden State.

The Warriors had a serious talent deficit, playing without not just Curry, but also Draymond Green, Jimmy Butler III, Moses Moody, and Brandon Williams. Charles Bassey led the way with 16 points, and also grabbed 13 rebounds for a double-double, while Will Richard had another strong game off the bench, scoring 15 points and playing excellent defense. But Yaxel Lendeborg and Brandin Podziemski once again struggled to carry the offense with Curry out, with the former scoring 11 points on 3-for-11 shooting, and the latter 15 points on 5-for-12 shooting. While Lendeborg struggled on offense, he played a good defensive game, and finished with eight rebounds, seven assists, one steal, and two blocks.

For Memphis, Jaylen Wells (22 points and seven rebounds on 8-for-10 shooting) and rookie Cameron Boozer (16 points, six rebounds, and five assists on 6-for-6 shooting) starred in a total team effort. But the biggest discrepancy, as it has been for much of the road trip, was the shooting. Golden State shot a miserable 5-for-29 (17.2%) from deep, while the Grizzlies went an excellent 15-for-35 (42.9%). That, along with 22 turnovers, is how you lose by 28 points.

#2873. Anthropic was supposed to save the AI trade. What went wrong?

Anthropic's historic IPO — the largest in U.S. history — delivered a big win for the company and its investors. But it failed at another task: reviving animal spirits in the AI trade.

The Nasdaq Composite closed down 2.25% amid a broader market pullback with the S&P 500 declining 2% to 7,175.

Investors had been looking forward to the Anthropic IPO as a "clearing event" — reviving the tech sector after months of choppy trading, the Nvidia espionage scandal, and growing concerns that AI chip sales to Asia are likely to slump as Washington cracks down on potential violations of export controls.

Some of those worries resurfaced Thursday as a short seller, Hunterbrook Media, alleged in a report that firmware sold by chipmaker AMD had turned up in U.S.-blacklisted companies. AMD stock closed down more than 7%. The chipmaker told CNBC it complies with U.S. law.

Adding to the worries, the House Foreign Affairs Committee released documents showing that a subagency of the Commerce Department approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies. That also raised the prospect of an Asia sales slowdown under stricter export controls.

Many investors and analysts continue to express confidence in the AI trade, noting that Anthropic's successful market debut — the stock closed up 17% from its IPO price and raised more than $81 billion — bodes well for capital spending across tech.

But investors acknowledged that this is a high-tension moment and said it's time to be more strategic about the trade.

Dan Niles, founder of Niles Investment Management, described himself as a "circumspect bull," making the comparison to market conditions in 2022 when the big indices tanked in the back half of the year.

"You could have still made money that year. You just needed to have the right combination of longs and shorts," he said.

Part of the challenge, Niles said, has been a price war between the two cutting-edge frontier labs, Anthropic and OpenAI. That has posed a threat to the overall revenue and profit potential of AI and the capex going into it. Fierce competition on price is producing collective losses between the two top companies, he notes.

"The combined revenue growth for OpenAI plus Anthropic went from growing 75% sequentially in Q2 to 48% in Q3," he told CNBC. "The combined losses went from $7.9 billion to about $8.4 billion from Q2 to Q3."

While uncertainty is high now, some resolution may be on the horizon if a greater degree of commercial and regulatory clarity emerges over the next few months.

Trading experts also told CNBC that the tech sector's troubles Thursday were a more serious matter than Anthropic simply siphoning capital from other parts of the market.

"There's a reset of AI in general," said JJ Kinahan, senior vice president at Cboe Global Markets.

Investors for years have profited in tech by buying the dip, he said, but "there's been an attitude change that [you] can't buy things blindly and they'll all go up." Nvidia's ongoing declines have shaken confidence in the buy-the-dip strategy, he said.

Anthropic's next few trading days will be a key gauge of the market's strength. Friday will be a "wild card," Kinahan said. It could be a "final flush out" for the market, or a bounce that leaves the market in "no man's land" while volatility remains elevated.

A better gauge may be Monday, when options on Anthropic start trading, providing insight into whether retail investors will back the company in force — providing more of a vote of confidence in the AI trade.

"If people think we're going up [on Anthropic] they'll buy stock, but retail particularly will just buy calls," he said. "There's a bigger test coming Monday."

For now, investors continue to sell AI-related stocks.

Neoclouds, the generally highly indebted AI-dedicated computing providers at the outer edges of the AI trade, were down substantially Thursday, with CoreWeave closing down more than 6%.

Hyperscalers such as Alphabet and Amazon.com, viewed as relatively defensive AI bets, also finished lower.

One bright spot: Cybersecurity stocks continued to rally, with Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike both closing up. AI is finding security holes across software infrastructure, creating a scramble to patch the vulnerabilities before hackers can exploit them.

— CNBC's Daren Fonda contributed reporting.

#2871. Knicks eke out lucky win in Minnesota after fourth-quarter collapse

"For 'Dancing with the Stars,' " Karl-Anthony Towns said. "For us, at the end of the day, as long as we win, this team is just trying to stack the number on the left side."

The Knicks did stack another win in that left standings column. Perhaps they didn't deserve to.

They did just about everything they could to throw away that win amid a brutal collapse.

Karl-Anthony Towns goes up for a shot over Rudy Gobert during the Knicks' 102-99 win over the Timberwolves on Nov. 19, 2026, in Minneapolis. NBAE via Getty Images

Somehow, they escaped with a 102-99 win over the Timberwolves on Thursday night.

The Knicks led by 12 entering the fourth quarter and then quickly went up by 16 after Tyler Kolek's 4-point play to start the quarter. They had led since early in the first quarter and were in complete command.

But they proceeded to miss their next 13 shots and saw their lead dwindle to four. Target Center finally had life.

It appeared they had stabilized a bit when Towns' driving layup and Mikal Bridges' subsequent 3-pointer put the Knicks back up by nine.

But Towns, after a Timberwolves challenge, was handed a flopping technical for trying to draw a foul called on Rudy Gobert. A free throw, a Gobert alley-oop and an Ayo Dosunmu 3-pointer later, and the Knicks led by just three. Towns then was called for an offensive foul, and Bridges badly missed a jumper on the Knicks' next offensive possession.

The Timberwolves couldn't find a quality shot, though, with Dosunmu and Gobert both missing shots. Minnesota never got closer than three.

LaMelo Ball badly missed a potential game-tying 3-pointer with under 10 seconds left. Jonathan Kuminga got the rebound but threw it away to Landry Shamet, and the Timberwolves weren't able to foul as the Knicks tossed the ball up the court.

Miles McBride (left) and Jaden McDaniels battle for the ball during the Knicks' win over the Timberwolves on Nov. 19, 2026, in Minneapolis. AP Photo/Ellen Schmidt

"It was hectic," Josh Hart said. "We gotta get better at finishing a game like that. But it's a win, 3-1 on the road trip. We'll take it."

Despite the ugly finish, the Knicks closed their four-game road trip with a win over a strong opponent. The Timberwolves have not missed much of a beat this season without injured superstar Anthony Edwards and possessed the league's best defense entering the game.

"Great to finish off a road trip, getting a win in a pretty tough environment by a well-coached team," head coach Mike Brown said. "It'll make the plane ride a little bit better going home."

Nobody has shot over 50 percent from the field against them this year. The Knicks could not change that, though they shot 57.1 percent by halftime as Towns — returning to Minnesota as an opponent for the third time since the Knicks' blockbuster trade to acquire him two years ago — was dominating his old team. He scored 17 points in the first half, and Jalen Brunson then erupted for 14 points in the third quarter. The Knicks' offense as a whole was humming.

It appeared the Knicks would cruise the rest of the way before the Timberwolves defense came alive.

"Our execution the first three quarters was at a pretty high level against this team," Brown said. "And then you give them credit. Fourth quarter, they did a phenomenal job defensively, kind of bogged us down. The ball and the pace offensively in the frontcourt wasn't popping like it was the first three quarters."

Towns shot 1-for-5 in the fourth. Brunson went scoreless in the period. As a team, the Knicks went 3-for-18 from the field and scored just 12 points over the final 12 minutes.

Brunson finished with 21 points. OG Anunoby added 15.

Kuminga led the Timberwolves with 23 points. The Knicks held Dosunmu, who has broken out in Edwards' absence, to just six points. Ball had 15 points on rough 6-for-21 shooting. The Timberwolves' 99 points were their fewest this season.

For three quarters, it was vintage Knicks — getting a little bit from everyone. Until it unraveled in the fourth quarter, where the Knicks had been so good in recent games.

"If you wanna win a championship, you gotta be ready to win in any way possible," Towns said, "because you never know what the game will be."

#2869. J.J. McCarthy has won at every level; will that continue in Giants’ playoff run?

When the New York Giants traded for quarterback J.J. McCarthy following Jaxson Dart's season-ending injury, nobody really knew what to expect. McCarthy's 2+ years with the Minnesota Vikings did not go well, and the quarterback-needy Vikings shipped him out of town.

Then, a couple of weeks into his time with the Giants, a Week 6 cameo in what looked like a blowout loss to the New Orleans Saints turned into nine minutes of mayhem that changed the Giants' season. McCarthy went 11 of 21 for 243 yards in slightly more than 11 minutes as the Giants nearly climbed out of a 34-10 hole in a 34-27 loss.

That convinced head coach John Harbaugh to name him the starting quarterback, and McCarthy went 20 of 28 for 252 yards in an overtime victory over the Houston Texans.

Now, three weeks later, the quarterback scorned by a Minnesota team that was forced to make a desperation trade for Kirk Cousins to fix its own issue at the position is being asked to guide the Giants on an eight-week run that will — hopefully — end with the Giants winning their first NFC East title since 2011.

The 23-year-old has been impressive to date, and the Giants are 2-1 in his three starts. With the pressure and quality of competition about to ratchet up, will that continue.

Questions have been asked about how much head coach John Harbaugh trusts McCarthy after the Washington loss, in which the Giants called a quarterback run that failed on a key third-and-3 at the two-minute mark, forcing a punt and leading to the Commanders' game-winning drive. McCarthy has been questioned for, with receivers open underneath and only a field goal being needed to tie the game, throwing a deep shot to Malik Nabers that was intercepted near the end of the Washington game when he had receivers open underneath.

"I think he's proven that he's capable of winning games and making the plays, and I probably feel more strongly about that now than ever," Harbaugh said. "We're definitely in the process of growing that confidence for sure. I mean, I understand what you're saying, for sure. But he's earned that right. I'm excited about where he's going."

Harbaugh said McCarthy has been "playing winning football."

"I want him to play as good as he can possibly play. I want him to be confident. I want him to be aggressive. I want him to be smart. I want him to complete passes. I want him to handle all the blitz checks. I just want him to continue to play the best football he can play," Harbaugh said. "I'm not sitting there like a scout saying he can work on his plant foot or his follow-through. We look at that stuff, the coaches will. All you really focus on is, let's go play the best game we can possibly play. Let's play a winning football game.

"He's been playing winning football. I'm really happy with the way he's playing. Okay, let's play winning football and go win the game. There's going to be some plays that he'll have a chance to make. He'll make most of them. He won't make them all. But I hope he makes the ones that make a difference in the game. That's probably the biggest thing for any quarterback."

McCarthy explained this week what "winning football" means to him.

"Winning the game is the number one thing, and there's a bunch of stats, traits, how a quarterback would play that would contribute to winning the game, and that's all about decision making, timing, accuracy, and just being smart, and knowing that you have the program in your hands every single play when you touch that ball and making the best decisions possible," he said. "That's the number one thing I think makes winning football, and I try to do that to the best of my ability every single week."

The numbers show a McCarthy who has clearly been better in three starts and one real relief appearance as a Giant than he was in 10 starts with Minnesota last season.

Offensive coordinator Matt Nagy said McCarthy's growth since coming to the Giants is "real."

"We need to make sure that we continue to just keep supporting him like we do every week with the play calls, the play designs, the players in the right spot. Let him play fast. He's done that," Nagy said. "Winning helps, and learning through experiences, too. The more we can get wins, the more experiences we get. He's a positive kid. He likes to stay positive. When he's out here at practice, he's juiced up all the time, which I love. He's got great energy. And then on game day, he turns that energy into a calm. So, just continue to get stuff on tape so that he can kind of see where we all grow as coaches with him and him with us."

McCarthy certainly shouldn't be afraid of the big moments to come. He is no stranger to big games. McCarthy won state and national championships in high school. He won a national championship in college at Michigan.

"When it comes to games in late November, when you're getting closer and closer to playoffs, the attention to detail, the urgency to really make sure you're doing your one-eleventh on every single play means the most, and especially against great teams like Jacksonville," McCarthy said.

Backup quarterback Jameis Winston, in his 12th NFL season, said it will be important for McCarthy to not try and do too much on his own.

"The most important thing about big moments is keeping it simple and doing what's required," Winston said. "It's not having an unreal game, but it's being consistent and giving the best chance to win.

"We're going to make sure we do everything possible to support him. That's a collective team thing … we view it as togetherness and how we're going to rally together to win football games."

NFL teams using their third starting quarterback by midseason — earlier in the Giants' case — don't typically make playoff runs. Just three years removed from being the 10th overall pick in the 2025 NFL Draft, and with those high school and collegiate national titles on his resume, McCarthy doesn't come with the typical "who the heck is that guy?" third quarterback pedigree.

#2863. Carlos Alcaraz matches one of Roger Federer’s records at the ATP Finals after latest win vs Flavio Cobolli

Carlos Alcaraz cruised to another straightforward victory on Friday at the ATP Finals to round off a flawless group stage run.

After comfortably beating Frances Tiafoe and Daniil Medvedev in Turin, Alcaraz made it three wins from three by defeating home hope Flavio Cobolli 6-4, 6-1. Doubts had been cast over the Spaniard's availability for the match with Cobolli after he underwent an MRI scan to examine pain in his hamstring and knee.

But Alcaraz showed few, if any signs of discomfort in the bout with the Italian, and will now face Ben Shelton for a place in the championship match at the ATP Finals.

Photo by Benjamin Vodant / Hans Lucas / AFP via Getty Images

Alcaraz is now through to the final four stage of the year-end competition for the third time in his career. The 23-year-old has just matched Roger Federer's all-time tally for ATP Finals semifinals made before turning 24.

Boris Becker holds the record, having made the penultimate stage of the ATP Finals five times before his 24th birthday, doing so in 1985, 1986, 1988, 1989 and 1990. Stefan Edberg, Ivan Lendl, John McEnroe, Pete Sampras and Mats Wilander all managed it four times.

Alcaraz first reached the semifinals of the ATP Finals in his debut at the tournament in 2023, when he was beaten by eventual champion Novak Djokovic. Alcaraz crashed out in the round-robin stage in 2024, but reached the final in 2025 and lost to his rival, Jannik Sinner.

With Sinner absent from the tournament this year due to a knee injury, Alcaraz has a golden opportunity to hoist the title for the first time in his career. He will face Shelton in the semifinals and will likely take on Alexander Zverev in the final should he get there.

Since his group stage exit at the 2024 ATP Finals, Alcaraz has not lost a round-robin match at the event. He went 3-0 at last year's edition and has done the same this season, overcoming Tiafoe, Medvedev and Cobolli without conceding a set.

In doing so, Alcaraz has become the fifth player to go flawless in the group stage of the ATP Finals two seasons in a row. He joins Federer, Djokovic, Medvedev and Sinner on the list of players who have achieved the feat.

Alcaraz is bidding to become the first Spaniard since Alex Corretja to win the ATP Finals. Rafael Nadal reached the title-bout of the ATP Finals twice but never won the tournament.

#2862. As Anthropic shares tank, investors scramble to hedge. It could be very expensive

As Anthropic shares tumble toward their IPO price of $83, investors are looking for ways to hedge. Unfortunately, they may have to wait until Monday, when options on the AI giant are expected to list.

If Anthropic breaks its IPO price, it will represent a 27% decline from Thursday's intraday high of $113. The wild price swings offer clues on how expensive it might be to buy protection on the new tech giant once options begin trading.A 20% intraday move points to an implied volatility somewhere between 100 and 150 for Anthropic options, according to estimates from single-stock market-makers on the Cboe trading floor in Chicago.

Options traders are also looking at how SpaceX traded in the days following its offering for clues on how options might price.

Implied volatility in SpaceX started at 116, but that didn't deter options traders big and small from piling into the contracts tracking the stock, with about 1.7 million contracts traded on the first day for a total options premium of about $2.5 billion. Far out-of-the-money call contracts were some of the most popular trades as the stock soared 40% in its first three sessions.One key difference between now and then? Anthropic is trading against the backdrop of S&P 500 volatility close to 30, compared to 17.3 when SpaceX debuted. "I expect ANT options to be super active," said Tom Sosnoff, co-founder of the trading platforms ThinkOrSwim and TastyTrade. "I expect heavy options volume."One thing Anthropic and SpaceX have in common is heavy retail involvement in both IPOs, with retail brokerages receiving a 20% allocation from SpaceX and reports pointing to between a 15-20% allocation from Anthropic on Thursday. "Round one of the Anthropic IPO easily goes to the individual investor," Sosnoff added. "Retail participants bailed early at the best prices of the day while institutional investors paid up to top off their underwhelming allocations. I believe retail was aggressively reloading in the mid-90s."Further signs of retail demand will become evident when options likely begin trading on Monday. One thing to watch: the spread between out-of-the-money call and put contracts, which was heavily skewed toward calls in the case of SpaceX. "I would be careful comparing Anthropic to SpaceX," said Dennis Davitt, CIO and Co-Founder of Millbank Dartmoor Portsmouth. "From a market-structure perspective, the two are dramatically different. The availability and cost of borrowing will be different, the companies are at very different stages of maturity, and SpaceX has allowed employees to monetize portions of their holdings over time. All of those factors matter when pricing options."

It was more of the same bad Bucks basketball to open the second: more turnovers, missed free throws, and bad fouls as the Blazers quickly upped their lead to double digits, 32-22. Thank goodness for Nate Ament, though, who poured in a quick five points—paired with triples from Tyler Herro and Kel'el Ware—to reduce Milwaukee's deficit to just one at the six-minute mark as they went on a 12-4 run, down 40-39. Of course, Scoot Henderson, who was shooting 20.0% from three coming into the game, went 4/4 in the first half as Portland closed on a 15-3 run to take a 60-58 lead into halftime.

The Bucks started the third with great energy on both ends. They opened with a perfectly run post-entry play where Herro got the ball off a screen for a three; then, a few plays later, Burries stole the ball, and Herro drained another three—this time from the corner—Bucks up 68-63 after two minutes. Portland brought Jrue Holiday in to stem the tide, and, like clockwork, the Blazers responded with a 15-2 extended run. Yep. HOWEVER, the Bucks didn't go quietly as the second unit came in and offered a real spark, cutting the deficit back to three with a few minutes remaining. Crucial late plays from Jakucionis and Rollins put the Blazers up 96-92 after three.

After playing his first minutes of the season last night and making a great impression, Caris LeVert opened the fourth with an elite defensive play, stealing the ball from Dame and converting on the and-one. A few plays later came the sequence of the night: Rollins flipped it to Ware for the baseline poster, then Rollins ripped Dame in the backcourt for the lefty finish, then Burries stonewalled Henderson in the backcourt to force the eight-second violation—Fiserv was rocking! The Blazers would fight back to extend their lead to six, but the Bucks answered with an 8-0 spurt made entirely off of buckets from Ware and Burries to take a 108-106 lead with six minutes to play! But of course, Jrue Holiday—who had made big shots all night—dropped consecutive buckets to give Portland back the edge, leading 112-108. At the three-minute mark, after buckets from Ament and Herro, it was a one-point game, but poor backcourt composure allowed Portland extend their lead to seven, which was enough in the end. Damn.

The Bucks won the possession game by a huge margin (91-77), but they just couldn't convert enough open shots. They were particularly horrid in the first quarter, shooting 8/21.

Trade Kel'el Ware. Trade Myles Turner. Trade Jericho Sims. Pete Nance is the only big you will ever need. Team-high +8 and one of just two Bucks with a positive rating.

#2858. Cowboys offensive line versus the Titans defensive line

The Dallas Cowboys will be back in action on Sunday against the Tennessee Titans. They need to win in the trenches on offense to carry the day, as they can't rely on the struggling defense. Here's how it looks.

Here are the Cowboys offensive line metrics for the 2026 season so far.

Last three-week trend: Steady protection, not elite

Every opponent will look at the Cowboys offensive line and ask, where can we break it? Here's what to watch for.

PRESSURE POINT: Jacob Martin has become Tennessee's main problem off the edge

The Titans no longer have Jeffery Simmons after they traded the four-time Pro Bowl defensive tackle to Chicago at the end of October. The player Dallas now has to locate is Jacob Martin.

Martin leads Tennessee with 7.5 sacks and has 31 total pressures, 17th among qualifying edge defenders. He added another sack and three quarterback pressures against Jacksonville last week. That is impressive production for a Titans defense that has only 21 sacks as a team.

Martin wins largely with speed. At 242 pounds, he wants to get an offensive tackle moving backwards and then attack the quarterback before the blocker can establish his position.

Dallas handled a much more intimidating group of individual pass rushers against San Francisco, so there is no reason to panic. But Martin cannot be the player who turns a favorable matchup into a difficult afternoon.

PRESSURE POINT: How quickly does T.J. Bass settle in?

This is probably Tennessee's first place to attack. Tyler Booker had become one of the Cowboys' most reliable offensive linemen. Before the 49ers game, his pressure rate allowed was just 4.6%, fifth-lowest among NFL right guards, now due to a high ankle sprain, T.J. Bass steps into his position.

Bass has already started this season when Tyler Smith was injured, so Dallas is not putting an inexperienced player onto the field. Schottenheimer specifically praised his versatility after Booker went down, but Tennessee should test him immediately.

John Franklin-Myers is the Titans' best remaining interior defensive lineman and led their defensive front with three pressures against Jacksonville. Expect Tennessee to move Franklin-Myers around and see whether it can create confusion between Bass, Cooper Beebe and Steele.

Every defensive line has a weakness, here are the Titans soft spots and where the Cowboys offensive line should attack.

GREEN LIGHT: Run directly at Jacob Martin

Martin is Tennessee's best pass-rush threat, so make him do something else and take him out the game. PFF gives Martin a 47.1 run-defense grade, ranking 105th among 111 qualifying edge defenders.That creates an obvious opportunity.

Whenever Martin is on the field, Dallas should make him defend Javonte Williams rather than allowing him to simply chase Dak Prescott.

If Martin has spent two quarters fighting through run blocks, he cannot attack every passing snap with the same freedom. The best way of slowing down Tennessee's leading pass rusher might be making him tackle Williams.

The Titans do not rely heavily on blitzing. As it stands, Tennessee's blitz rate sits at 26%, that places them among the least aggressive blitzing teams in football and that means Dallas should see plenty of four-man rushes.

The offense should therefore trust the offensive line and not leave an extra blocker beside the tackles unless Martin begins consistently winning. If Guyton, Smith, Beebe, Bass and Steele can handle Tennessee's four rushers, Dallas can put more receivers into routes. That should be particularly valuable against a Titans defense allowing 267 passing yards per game, worst in the NFL.

Here's the Tennessee Titans defensive trends for this season at the defensive line.

Last three-week trend: Front is struggling

Tyler Booker's injury makes this the matchup to watch. Bass enters the starting lineup at right guard and immediately faces Tennessee's most dependable interior defensive lineman.

Franklin-Myers can line up in several positions across the front, but expect Robert Saleh to find opportunities to place him across from Bass.

The Titans run defense has allowed 137 yards per game over the last four weeks, their most productive pass rusher is one of PFF's lowest-graded edge defenders against the run. Dallas should know exactly what to do, run Javonte Williams like a madman.

Use play-action after the linebackers start creeping toward the line, then trust the offensive line when Tennessee rushes four.

San Francisco presented Dallas with one of the most talented defensive fronts in football and Prescott still went down only once on more than 50 pass attempts. Tennessee should be a much easier challenge.

Tyler Booker suffered a high ankle sprain against San Francisco and is expected to miss time.

John Franklin-Myers played last week after dealing with a back issue and had been a full participant in practice before the Jacksonville game. Other than that their defensive line has no new injuries, their issues, however, show up a lot in their linebacker corps. So keep watch on that this week in practice reports.

#2856. Why the Celtics Aren't Allowed to Trade Mitchell Robinson Right Now

Why the Celtics Aren't Allowed to Trade Mitchell Robinson Right Now originally appeared on NESN. Add NESN as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Mitchell Robinson's slow start has some Celtics fans wondering if he'll be traded.

There's just one problem: Boston can't trade Robinson right now.

If the Celtics are interested in moving the 28-year-old center, they'll have to wait until Dec. 15. That's not because trades aren't allowed right now. It's because Robinson is part of a group of players who aren't currently trade-eligible.

Here's everything you need to know about Robinson's situation.

MORE: Ex-NBA Player Expects Jaylen Brown to Get Booed by Celtics Fans For One Reason

The Celtics signed Robinson to a three-year, $47.4 million contract in the offseason. ESPN's Shams Charania broke the news on July 1, and the Celtics officially announced his signing on July 7.

Under the NBA's Collective Bargaining Agreement, a free agent who signs a standard contract cannot be traded until three months after signing or Dec. 15, whichever comes later.

In Robinson's case, Dec. 15 is the date he becomes trade-eligible.

Dec. 15 is an important date on the NBA calendar because it makes a large group of offseason free-agent signings eligible to be traded. While teams can make trades throughout the season, their options expand considerably in mid-December.

There's been no indication that the Celtics are considering trading Robinson. For now, the idea is purely speculation.

The reason it's become a topic is that Robinson is off to an underwhelming start this season.

Robinson's per-minute numbers aren't all that different from when he was with the New York Knicks, but he's not making nearly the same impact. His Player Efficiency Rating has never been lower, his offensive rebounding rate is at its lowest mark since his third season and he's averaging a career-low 0.8 blocks per game.

Neemias Queta has taken over as Boston's starting center, and Robinson's role has become less secure. Luka Garza has started at center when Queta has been unavailable, while rookie Chris Cenac Jr. has seen an uptick in minutes.

#2855. Puka Nacua's suspension arises from diversion program

The NFL’s statement announcing the three-game suspension for Rams receiver Puka Nacua didn’t specify the reason for it. Further information provided by the league makes the basis for the ban clear.

It comes from Nacua’s entry into a “diversion program,” related to the incident that triggered a civil lawsuit alleging (among other things) that he bit a woman on New Year’s Eve.

In September, we explained that Nacua had begun the steps required to complete a diversion program, which happened without Nacua entering into a formal agreement to do so. It’s one of the unique facets of California law; namely, California gives some defendants the ability to embark on the steps to comply with a diversion program without the kind of express deal that would have automatically triggered review under the Personal Conduct Policy.

The approach ultimately didn’t avoid the NFL scrutiny.

The suspension of Nacua for three games, with the acknowledgment from the league that failure “to satisfy the conditions of his diversion program” will result in “additional and more substantial discipline,” means that the mere commencement of the process of compliance, even without an express agreement with prosecutors, was enough to get the process rolling.

It also led to a negotiated conclusion that entails Nacua being suspended for games he otherwise would have missed, due to his status on injured reserve. While it all looks convenient at best and fishy at worst, it represents the outcome of a bargain aimed at resolving the situation without full-blown activation of a process that would have entailed a formal hearing before Judge Sue L. Robinson, the person jointly appointed by the NFL and the NFL Players Association to hear the evidence and to issue a preliminary decision.

Fiserv Forum aired a video tribute to Lillard amid that November 2025 meeting, and the nine-time All-Star received a standing ovation after it played that night.

Thursday marked the 36-year-old guard's first time taking the court against Milwaukee since his injury and his two-season stint with the Bucks. Lillard was subdued talking about the matchup in the lead-up to tip-off, but he came away with his best performance in 624 days.

March 5, 2025, was the last time Lillard had a 30-point game. He scored a season-high 33 points on Thursday in a 124-114 victory over a reeling and rebuilding Milwaukee (1-15).

Portland (10-5) bounced back after dropping consecutive games to the Minnesota Timberwolves.

Lillard once again received a warm welcome from Bucks fans. Milwaukee ultimately waived him to sign center Myles Turner in the summer of 2025. The Bucks are still paying Lillard after they decided to stretch the remaining $113 million on his contract.

So, on Thursday, Milwaukee fans watched their team lose its 12th straight game and Lillard shoot 10 of 18 from the field, including 5 of 12 from the beyond the arc.

Plus, another former Bucks player, Jrue Holiday — part of Milwaukee's NBA championship team in 2020-21 — put on a show of his own. He logged 22 points, 7 assists and 4 steals.

Holiday stepped back to hit a crucial jumper with about 5 ½ minutes to go. Another 36-year-old guard, Holiday went on to help the Trail Blazers create separation late, even coupling a steal with a layup.

The lead changed hands incessantly on Thursday. Herro drew the Bucks within one at the 3:18 mark in the fourth quarter. The Trail Blazers, though, scored the final nine points, with Lillard netting the last two at the free-throw line.

#2852. Lions' Aidan Hutchinson says he'll make big change after season-ending injury

Aidan Hutchinson is keeping his feet on the ground going forward.

The Detroit Lions star edge rusher saw his season come to an end during the team's 35-10 victory over the New England Patriots in Germany on Nov. 15 – and it had nothing to do with a hit he took. Hutchinson sacked Drake Maye in the first quarter, jumped in the air to celebrate and suffered a torn ACL when he came back down.

It was unbelievable in the moment and the shocking nature of the injury remains that way for Hutchinson in the aftermath, which he spoke about in an Instagram post on Nov. 19:

"I honestly can't believe it," Hutchinson said. "I've jumped hundreds of times on a football field and never in a million years did I think this would happen to me. But even something like this won't hold me back.

"I can ask why over and over again, but it'll never make sense. All I can do is surrender to the path. Only God knows why and I trust in Him.

"Very grateful for all of your prayers and well wishes."

Hutchinson then explained that he knows two things for sure, writing that he "always" comes back stronger and "that's the last time I go airborne," before leaving a parting message for his teammates.

#2851. FSU vs NC State: Score predictions, analysis from FSU Wire

For the first time since firing Mike Norvell, the Florida State Seminoles (5-5) are set to play in Doak Campbell Stadium this weekend. The Seminoles are set to host the NC State Wolfpack on Saturday afternoon in their final ACC game of the season.

A win would make them 4-4 in ACC play, their first time finishing .500 or better since winning the conference in 2023. While they are heavily favored over the Wolfpack, it won't be easy as the Seminoles will be without numerous starters. FSU will be without its top four running backs, top wide receiver, starting center, starting cornerback, top defensive tackle, and several key rotational players.

That has put more pressure on younger or unproven players, especially at running back. Interim head coach Rick Stockstill addressed it earlier in the week, admitting that former walk-on Zay Parks will have a big role and that they are considering moving players to help him out.

We've taken a pretty good hit right there. But Zay Parks, who played a little bit throughout the year, not a whole lot, played more snaps against Pitt than he had and has been on special teams. He's in the mix there, and we're looking at possibly moving some guys that were running backs in high school that we're looking at trying to fill those holes right now because we don't have a lot of options, to be honest with you.

NC State (4-6, 2-5) is also playing under an interim head coach, with Todd Goebbel taking over after they fired Dave Doeren. They are 1-2 under him, with them losing their last two games to the Duke Blue Devils and Syracuse Orange. They have already hired Philip Rivers as their next permanent head coach, with him set to take over after the end of the season.

Here are our predictions for FSU's game against NC State.

The Noles are riding a wave of momentum, but CJ Bailey will put up a fight. Ashton Daniels will ultimately win the game on the ground for FSU.

The Wolfpack's defense allows close to 30 points per game on the season, and I think the Seminoles' offense will take advantage of that. Their defense will get timely stops against a capable offense, and the momentum that Florida State is on will carry them to a win.

I think Florida State gets it done Saturday, although I wouldn't be surprised if this one is closer than people expect. The Seminoles have looked like a completely different team under Rick Stockstill, especially defensively after holding Pitt to just 10 points last week. Still, this is an FSU offense that hasn't been particularly consistent, and NC State has enough firepower with quarterback CJ Bailey to make things interesting.

Rick Stockstill has FSU on the verge of making a bowl game, and they will clinch it in his first game coaching inside Doak Campbell Stadium. The injuries at running back can not be ignored, but Ashton Daniels and the offense will have enough success to get it done against a bad NC State team.

#2847. Preview: Jazz look to build scorching hot win streak in the desert

For the Utah Jazz, winning two games in a row might as well feel like 2o. With an outstanding A+ road trip in Los Angeles, things could not be brighter despite a 3-13 record. The young core is finally showing its fruition. Keyonte is evolving as a facilitator; Darryn Peterson is a do-it-all guard; Brice Sensabaugh can apparently score from anywhere.

Back at the Delta Center, fans will have their first look this year at the inaugural Jazz NBA Cup court, in all of its purple glory. I don't think the bright painted floors will ever grow on me, but you have to admit its better than most.

They'll be taking on the Phoenix Suns, equally trapped in the whirlwind of the Western Conference with a 7-7 record. The Jazz have likely already been eliminated from the NBA Cup — taking two hits in both of the Cup Road games. Phoenix, on the other hand, still has a chance to claim a wildcard spot since they've only played one Group A match thus far.

I'll give the Suns their kudos; compared to the Jazz, they recovered from an abysmal 1-5 start to the season and have climbed all the way back to .500. There are still questions related to team chemistry and players' roles, but Phoenix still goes out there and shows effort every single night.

Spearheaded by Devin Booker in his 12th season, the Suns' biggest strength is their high-efficiency shooting. Their team shoots 47.5% from the field, placing them inside the top 10 in overall shooting efficiency. Young big men Khaman Maluach (60.9% FG) and Oso Ighodaro (58.0% FG) anchor most of the finishing, alongside Booker (48.0% FG). The Jazz likely won't have much of a footing against their bench unit either — Phoenix boasts one of the league's top benches, with players like Jordan Goodwin (9.8 PPG), Luke Kennard (9.4 PPG) and Collin Gillespie (9.3 PPG) regularly putting up double-digit nights. A victory over the red-hot Suns (victors of 6 of their last 8) would give Utah solid footing to build on, hopefully towards the NBA Playoff picture.

It should come as a given, knowing our Jazz, but Utah's two-game winning streak could have easily been a 14-game losing skid with a couple of swing possessions. The stat sheet may show a double-digit victory in the Jazz's triumph over the Lakers, but these teams were neck and neck all night. Utah could have easily blown the game open earlier, had it not been for their 20 turnovers through the first three quarters. That was shown in Inglewood too, where the same Jazz team coughed up 14 turnovers in three quarters against the Clippers.

Phoenix rarely beats itself — 5th lowest turnover rate in the NBA — and thrives off unforced errors led by Gillespie and Goodwin. With Lauri, JJJ and Nurkic still sidelined, the game will continue to be run exclusively by Utah's young backcourt. Keyonte George averaged 3.5 turnovers a game, while backup Isaiah Collier (2.0 turnovers) and Darryn Peterson (1.9 turnovers) also carry heavy ball-handling roles.

Utah can't count on miracle fourth quarters forever. Soon enough, they'll have to learn how to push through full-court coverage and slow down the pace on the scoring end. If Keyonte and DP can't take care of the rock, Phoenix's transition game will bury them early on.

While Dončić dominates through size and slow-paced pick-and-roll manipulation, Devin Booker (24.8 PPG, 5.4 APG, 48.0% FG) attacks defenses with constant off-ball movement and a lethal mid-range game. The Joshs will have to fight through pin-downs and flare screens all night to prevent Booker from settling into his sweet spots. Booker enters Friday shooting a lethal 94.5% from the charity stripe on 6.1 attempts per game. If Green and Okogie get too aggressive, Booker will turn those whistles into free points.

Because Utah is missing its top frontcourt defenders, the Jazz saviour Mo Bamba plays a critical role behind Green and Okogie. With Bamba on the floor, Utah's defense improves by 3.8 points per 100 possessions thanks to his 4.5% block rate, giving Utah's wings confidence to crowd Booker's jumper without worrying about giving up uncontested layups if he drives past them.

Coming into this season as a third-string emergency big, Bamba has transformed into a starting-caliber NBA player. Bamba's biggest hurdle is staying on the floor. He fouled out in 20 minutes against Houston earlier this month and picked up four fouls against San Antonio. #2846. Vikings explored all options before deciding to stay in Minnesota this week

As Sunday’s Mexico City game between the Vikings and 49ers approaches, one of the big issues is the decision of the 49ers to spend the week at altitude in Colorado Springs while the Vikings opted to stay in Minnesota.

On that point, multiple 49ers players have claimed that the Vikings tried to secure the Air Force Academy facility at Colorado Springs, but the 49ers had beaten them to the punch.

The Vikings, we’re told, explored all options — including going to Air Force Acadamey facility and going to Mexico City early. They ultimately decided to implement a plan premised on staying in Minnesota as long as possible.

Obviously, the Vikings could have figured out something that would have allowed them to spend the week somewhere that would have allowed for full acclimation. There are other practice facilities in Colorado. And, again, early arrival in Mexico was always a possibility.

The issue has likely become a focal point of the days preceding the game because of the dramatically different approaches used by the 49ers and Rams before their Week 1 game in Australia. San Francisco went early; the Rams arrived late. And the 49ers stunned the Rams, 27-7.

In that case, it was about time and distance traveled. Here, it’s the same time zone, and the flight is roughly four hours — not much farther for the Vikings than a trip to Seattle, San Francisco, or L.A.

Teams that play in Denver don’t spend the week in Colorado. And while the altitude results in more sideline shots of players with oxygen masks during games, no one ever says, “Well, that team lost to the Broncos because they weren’t acclimated to the altitude.”

The Vikings-49ers game won’t turn on that. If the 49ers win, it will be because they were the better team during those 60 minutes of clock time. And, if the Vikings win, it won’t be because they someone cracked the code on playing at altitude.

#2841. Knicks 102, Timberwolves 99: Knicks Cut Down Wolves

After couple great resume wins that included the first time in Minnesota Timberwolves franchise history where they defeated the same team, twice in a row, on back-to-back nights, the home stand continued with a familiar face back in town. Karl-Anthony Towns and the defending champion New York Knicks arrived at Target Center with hopes of toppling his old squad. KAT returning to Minnesota is always a big game and an emotional matchup for the fanbase and, as per usual, he was welcomed back with open arms.

The Timberwolves have been on a hot streak as of late, winners of seven of eight games with a single lapse in play against the Chicago Bulls. They looked to continue a successful home stand and take advantage of the early season uneasiness the Knicks have been experiencing.

While the Timberwolves still are dealing with a handful of injuries so far this season, they did get Jonathan Kuminga back to give a much needed boost to a team that had to grind out a win against the Blazers on Tuesday night.

The first quarter started at a breakneck pace as both teams kept finding the bottom of the net. Towns started the game well at his former home, while LaMelo Ball's aggression showed up early on as he was launching shots.

It was a game of runs early on, as each team had their stretch of dominance – Knicks had a 10-0 run early, and the Timberwolves matched pace with a 13-2 run of their own. The Knicks continued to be red hot as they shot over 70% from both the floor and from three in the first quarter. KAT led the way with 10 points while LaMelo held serve from the other side with nine of his own. New York took the advantage into the second by a score of 33-26.

Chris Finch started the quarter with a technical foul as he'd been in the referees ear for much of the start of the game. KAT and the Knicks continued their bucket-getting at an absurd clip as Josh Hart woke up from his season long slumber, draining a few threes.

During the middling minutes, the Timberwolves fell into too much isolation offense and struggled to generate good looks on the offensive end of the floor. New York went on a 9-0 run down the stretch and shot 10/16 from three in the first half which gave them a healthy 15-point lead heading into halftime. Jaden McDaniels was perfect from the floor in the first half and led the way with 11 points for Minnesota.

Jonathan Kuminga came out of halftime swinging, taking it strong to the basket and mixing in outside shots as he scored 14 points in the frame. Minnesota kept trying to claw back into the game, but the turnovers they committed made it hard for them to mount a run. They cut the lead a few times, but Jalen Brunson did a great job staving off runs with his shotmaking.

The Wolves continued to struggle to spur a fourth quarter run to start the final period. A Jaden three brought some wind into the sails as they went on to tighten up the defense as the Knicks had zero field goals over a seven minute span in the fourth.

Still, it wasn't enough. The Wolves had trouble getting over the hump, but a reviewed KAT flopping technical gave them life again.

Minnesota had their chances, but missed their final five shots of the game including a LaMelo Ball three that could've tied the game with seconds left. New York played keep away and took the close win, 102-99.

New York got greedy tonight even though Thanksgiving isn't until next week.

Second chance points are always backbreakers, and the Knicks took advantage in winning that battle 12 to four.

New York had hit their shots throughout much of the first half, which is already tough to deal with, and when that is compounded with multiple opportunities on the same possession it makes it feel that much worse.

Throughout the game, the score always seemed much closer than it felt. With Jalen Brunson denying any run in the third quarter, it started to feel like one of those games where the Timberwolves wouldn't be able to get the boulder rolling down the hill. It felt that way for much of the game, but then the Timberwolves started to gain some traction in the fourth.

This run was defined with their top ranked defense putting the Knicks in jail. Minnesota held New York to 12 points in the fourth quarter, including that aforementioned seven minute stretch where they did not score a field goal. The Timberwolves made it extremely hard on Jalen Brunson and navigated screens adeptly on defense to avoid the matchup hunting the Knicks were searching for.

Unfortunately, the Wolves wasted the great defense with tough turnovers that plagued them during the earlier quarters as well. They played extremely hard to get back into the game and rode the momentum that they created, but came up short in the closing minutes.

While they didn't deserve to win today, their best chance to tie the game was unfairly taken by an inadvertent whistle that Chris Finch was livid about in his postgame press conference.

Finch said, "The one that everybody in the arena saw hit the rim? … I mean it was clear that it hit the rim, it hit the rim and it went straight down to the floor… I mean were continually told that these are the best in the world and you know you can't miss that one". I’ve spent a lot of Saturdays in Beaver Stadium, first on the field and then up in the booth,” Ham, 77, said in his statement. “I’ll be back alongside Steve [Jones] this weekend, and there’s nowhere else I’d rather be.”

Jones treated Ham at the scene, saving his life, according to Penn State coach Matt Campbell. Ham remained in the hospital several days before returning to Pennsylvania on Saturday.

“I’m feeling good, and I owe a great deal to the people who took care of me and stood by me through all of it,” Ham said.

Ham was a six-time All-Pro with the Steelers, with whom he won four Super Bowl championships. He also made eight Pro Bowl appearances. He earned All-America honors at Penn State in 1970.

He entered the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1988 and the College Football Hall of Fame two years later.

#2839. What do you think of Rams’ Puka Nacua’s suspension?

The speculation surrounding Puka Nacua and his suspension has raised questions such as when did the Los Angeles Rams know the suspension was coming? Did Nacua's potential suspension influence L.A.'s decision to place him on IR?

One question I have, did Sean McVay know the suspension was coming, and if so, was that why Nacua was accounting for 100% (slight exaggeration) of the passing game while Nacua was available? Then again, Matthew Stafford has had a habit of feeding his top targets, so perhaps the two situations are unrelated.

Field Yates of ESPN says that some people do find the timing of the suspension "fishy". Maybe it is, but the rules are the rules and reportedly the NFL Players' Association was able to help arrange this deal for Nacua, and Nacua will take it and serve his suspension.

There has been precedent for this type of situation with players serving their suspension on IR, which indicates nothing truly new is happening for Nacua with regard to how his suspension is being handled. What's done is done.

Will Nacua learn from his alleged negative past behavior? That's a big question for the young receiver. Either Nacua avoids negative headlines or he doesn't. For now, Nacua will serve his suspension, try to get healthy and go from there. 32 teams around the league will be watching how Nacua bounces back or doesn't.

Whether he likes it or not, all eyes on Nacua.

"Timing of Puka Nacua suspension is "awfully convenient"

"The NFL will say that this punishment was handed down because they finally completed the process," Yates said of the league's investigation of Nacua. "We were wondering at the beginning of training camp whether he was going to be suspended to begin the season. …I've had people around the NFL reach out to me and say, 'Funny how that works out, right? Guy gets to miss three games that he would have missed anyway.' So this one smells fishy to a lot of people around the NFL. I find it awfully convenient. I find it awfully convenient."

Whispers about a potential Nacua suspension had hovered over the Rams ever since it was learned this past March that a woman had filed a civil lawsuit accusing him of biting her and of making an antisemitic comment on Dec. 31, 2025. While he checked himself into a rehab facility in the spring to reportedly focus on his "personal growth," it was assumed he'd eventually have to serve a ban."

"There is precedent for players serving suspensions while on injured reserve or otherwise unavailable because of injury. It is not a new rule or an exception created for Nacua.

Most recently, in 2025 the Steelers' Daniel Ekuale was suspended five games for a violation of the performance-enhancing substances policy following a season-ending injury.

In 2024, the Cowboys' Sam Williams was suspended three games for violating the personal conduct policy while already out for the season. The Browns' Mike Woods was suspended six games in 2023 for violating the personal conduct policy while he was out on NFI.

In 2018, the Saints' David Parry, was suspended four games for violations of the personal conduct and substances of abuse policies while on injured reserve."

"The NFL's statement announcing the three-game suspension for Rams receiver Puka Nacua didn't specify the reason for it. Further information provided by the league makes the basis for the ban clear.

It comes from Nacua's entry into a "diversion program," related to the incident that triggered a civil lawsuit alleging (among other things) that he bit a woman on New Year's Eve.

In September, we explained that Nacua had begun the steps required to complete a diversion program, which happened without Nacua entering into a formal agreement to do so. It's one of the unique facets of California law; namely, California gives some defendants the ability to embark on the steps to comply with a diversion program without the kind of express deal that would have automatically triggered review under the Personal Conduct Policy.

The approach ultimately didn't avoid the NFL scrutiny."

"The suspension is effective immediately, and Nacua will be eligible for reinstatement on Dec. 14.

Nacua is currently on injured reserve after suffering MCL and PCL sprains in his right knee, along with turf toe. According to Schefter, players can serve suspensions while on injured reserve.

His remaining three games on IR will count toward the three-game suspension. Nacua missed Sunday's game against the Arizona Cardinals, the first of the mandatory four games he must sit out while on injured reserve."

""Our defense is sitting somewhere in the 20s for turnover ratio," McDuffie told The California Post in an exclusive interview. "So it's a big mindset this week: turnovers, turnovers."

But that message of needing to force turnovers carries even more weight heading into a nationally televised Thanksgiving Eve showdown between two teams tied for the NFC's seventh and final playoff spot."

"It won't be easy. The defending champion Seattle Seahawks are still in the mix, and the San Francisco 49ers have the NFC's best record. #2832. Aidan Hutchinson: That's the last time I go airborne

Lions head coach Dan Campbell said he isn't going to tell players to stop celebrating big plays because of defensive end Aidan Hutchinson's torn ACL, but Hutchinson is going to be making some changes on his own.

In a post to his Instagram account, Hutchinson made his first public comments since suffering his injury last Sunday. Hutchinson leaped in the air after sacking Patriots quarterback Drake Maye and his knee went out upon landing.

Hutchinson wrote that he has "jumped hundreds of times on a football field and never in a million years did I think this would happen to me" and that it will "never make sense" why things played out the way that they did. He added that he does know he will come back stronger from the injury and "that's the last time I go airborne."

Hutchinson closed the post with a message asking his Lions teammates to "hold down the fort til I'm back." That won't be until 2027, but Hutchinson has shown once already that he can make a full recovery from this kind of injury so there is some light at the end of the tunnel in Detroit.

Note: True-shooting percentage (TS) is a scoring efficiency metric that accounts for threes and free throws. Entering Thursday's games, league-average TS was 57.5%.

#2830. 2. Bundesliga preview: Wolfsburg vs. Holstein Kiel

VfL Wolfsburg will be looking to strengthen their promotion push when they host bottom-placed Holstein Kiel on Saturday, with the visitors beginning a new chapter under recently appointed head coach Mitch Kniat.

The Wolves currently occupy fifth place in the 2. Bundesliga table with 19 points from their opening 11 matches, while Kiel find themselves at the opposite end of the standings, having collected just eight points during a difficult start to the campaign.

With the hosts hoping to remain within touching distance of the automatic promotion places and Kiel desperate to climb out of the relegation zone, both sides have plenty riding on this weekend's encounter.

VfL Wolfsburg head into Saturday's fixture looking to get their promotion challenge back on track after suffering a 2-1 defeat against Hertha BSC in their previous league outing.

Tobias Strobl's side had enjoyed a five-match unbeaten run in the league before travelling to Berlin, where they ultimately came away empty-handed despite Kento Shiogai reducing the deficit shortly after half-time.

The result saw Wolfsburg slip to fifth in the standings, although they remain firmly in contention for promotion, sitting on 19 points after five victories, four draws and two defeats.

One of the positives for Strobl has been his side's attacking output, with the likes of Fabian Reese, Alexander Bernhardsson and Robert Glatzel providing considerable quality in the final third.

Reese has been particularly influential since arriving from Hertha during the summer, registering five goals and six assists in his opening 11 league appearances. His experience and attacking versatility have made him an important figure in Wolfsburg's promotion ambitions.

However, consistency remains an issue. Strobl acknowledged ahead of the weekend that his team have yet to win consecutive league matches this season, insisting that they still need to find the final few percentages in their performances.

Saturday's encounter therefore represents an important opportunity to respond, particularly against a Kiel side struggling for confidence.

Wolfsburg will also be motivated by their previous meetings with the visitors, having avoided defeat in both Bundesliga encounters during the 2024/25 campaign.

Holstein Kiel travel to Lower Saxony hoping that a change in the dugout can provide the spark needed to turn their season around.

Following their disappointing 2-1 home defeat against Arminia Bielefeld before the international break, Kiel decided to part company with head coach Tim Walter, subsequently appointing Mitch Kniat as his replacement.

Kniat arrives at the Holstein-Stadion after three seasons in charge of Bielefeld, where he guided the club to promotion from the 3. Liga and the DFB-Pokal final in 2025.

Kniat's immediate task is to improve a side that have managed just one league victory in their opening 11 matches, leaving them bottom of the table with eight points.

Defensive shortcomings have been a recurring problem, while their inability to turn promising performances into positive results has also contributed to their difficult position.

Nevertheless, there were encouraging signs during Kniat's first days in charge. Kiel recorded an impressive 4-0 friendly victory over Danish side Odense BK during the international break, providing the new coach with an early opportunity to implement his ideas.

Kniat has spoken about wanting his team to play with greater intensity, passion and a clearer tactical identity. His first competitive test, however, is a particularly challenging one against a Wolfsburg side with genuine promotion ambitions.

Phil Harres will be an important figure for the visitors, with the striker expected to lead the attacking line and provide the goals needed to improve their fortunes.

A positive result on Saturday would represent an important early statement under their new manager, although Kiel will need to produce a considerably more convincing defensive performance than they managed against Bielefeld.

Although Saturday's encounter will be the first-ever meeting between the clubs in the 2. Bundesliga, Wolfsburg and Kiel have a lengthy history of competitive encounters.

The two sides have crossed paths more than 60 times across various competitions, including the Oberliga Nord, Regionalliga Nord and Bundesliga.

Their most recent league meetings came during the 2024/25 Bundesliga campaign. Wolfsburg secured a 2-0 victory away from home in August 2024, before the return fixture at the Volkswagen Arena ended in a 2-2 draw.

However, Kiel claimed a memorable victory in their most recent competitive encounter, knocking Wolfsburg out of the DFB-Pokal with a 1-0 win at the Volkswagen Arena in October 2025. Alexander Bernhardsson scored the decisive goal against his former club.

Wolfsburg will therefore be keen to avoid another frustrating afternoon against the Storks, particularly with three points carrying considerable importance in their promotion pursuit.

Wolfsburg will be without Cleiton, who is suspended following his dismissal against Hertha BSC.

Rogério and Mattias Svanberg are also among the players expected to miss out through injury, while Trevor Benedict has previously been listed as unavailable.

Strobl is expected to make some adjustments to his defensive line, with Mathys Angely potentially coming into the starting XI in place of Cleiton.

For Holstein Kiel, Adrian Kapralik is a significant absentee after suffering a broken metatarsal during the international break, an injury that is expected to keep the Slovakian winger sidelined for an extended period.

Lasse Rosenboom and Sebastian Schonlau are also potential absentees, while Kniat will otherwise be hoping to work with the majority of his available squad for his first competitive fixture in charge.

VfL Wolfsburg (4-2-3-1): Wellenreuther; Kumbedi, Wahl, Angely, Mæhle; Vini Souza, Arnold; Damar, Bernhardsson, Reese; Glatzel

Holstein Kiel (4-3-2-1): Weiner; Sekine, Madsen, Zec, Tolkin; Meffert, Davidsen, Balzi; Therkelsen, de Regt; Harres

The Colts were outgained by the Texans, 354 yards to 167. They converted one of 11 third-down tries. Jones completed 12 of 27 passes, for 144 yards, no touchdowns, and an interception.

There’s a business reason that points to the Colts eventually getting Jones off the field. His contract has a $10.51 million injury guarantee for 2027. It vests in March. They’ll inevitably bench Jones to keep him from getting an injury that would keep the Colts from releasing him before the injury guarantee converts to a full guarantee.

That’s what the Giants did to Jones two years ago. He then requested, and received, his release.

The same thing could be happening, sooner rather than later, for Jones in Indianapolis. Which means that he could be available to another team.

That possibility highlights the Colts’ decision to not trade him for whatever they could get. And maybe they tried.

Maybe, in the end, his availability in trade is what helped the Vikings keep the Raiders’ asking price for Kirk Cousins to a third-round pick.

And maybe, in the end, the Vikings will have a chance to add Jones to the depth chart while showing Carson Wentz the door.

#2824. Clippers vs. Spurs takeaways: Victor Wembanyama adds to highlight reel

Victor Wembanyama and the San Antonio Spurs remain the standard in the Western Conference and will continue to get everyone's best shot this season.

The Spurs served as a tough test for the Los Angeles Clippers. They gave the Spurs their best shot in a 124-112 loss in San Antonio on Thursday, Nov. 19. Wembanyama led the game with 32 points and 11 rebounds for the Spurs.

It was a bounce-back win for San Antonio, which had a 12-game win streak snapped against the Detroit Pistons earlier in the week.

The Spurs were missing Dylan Harper, who was out with a hip rotator strain, on Thursday. He avoided serious injury but is expected to miss at least a week.

Here's some takeaways from Thursday's game:

Wembanyama can simply do things that others can't.

His latest example came with 3:36 left in the fourth quarter against the Clippers on Thursday. Rui Hachimura's missed shot was rebounded by Stephon Castle, who threw the ball right down the court to a wide-open Wembanyama.

While Wembanyama could've dunked the ball, he seemed to settle for a jump shot inches from the rim.

Wembanyama laughed when asked about the play and stated that dunking has led to a blister on his hand.

"I'm not going to lie, I've had this blister forever and it's killing me," Wembanyama told reporters after the game. "Every time I dunk, it kills me. … It's actually so painful."

While the Clippers still have a lot of work to do if they want to be in a position to compete for a play-in spot later this season, coach Tyronn Lue's team showed some promise and potential against the West's best on Thursday.

L.A. shot the ball well for most of the game and kept the game close behind the effort of veterans Darius Garland and Brook Lopez. Both scored 23 points each.

Garland's had high-scoring performances early this season, but turnovers have been a problem for the guard. He managed to limit his mistakes Thursday, having just one turnover on a big stage against the Spurs.

Max Strus went 5-for-10 from the field, including 5-of-9 from the 3-point line for 18 points.

Clippers center Yanic Konan Niederhauser made his season debut. The second-year player was dealing with a right foot Lisfranc injury and was limited to 11 minutes against the Spurs due to a minutes restriction. He went 1-for-4 shooting and finished the game with two points, three rebounds and a steal. He did find himself in foul trouble with a team-high five personal fouls.

While the Clippers will have to figure out the center rotation following Niederhauser's return, Lue has encouraged Isaiah Jackson to stay ready.

"Nothing (Jackson) has done wrong," Lue said before the game. "You want to try to reward him for what he has done since Yanic has been out. We will see how the flow of the game goes."

Jackson shot 3-for-5 from the field, finishing with six points, four rebounds and three steals in nine minutes of play. He also recorded two blocks against Wembanyama, once at the rim and the second at the 3-point line at the end of the third quarter.

San Antonio managed to get the best of one of Los Angeles' NBA teams, but a meeting with the other still looms.

The Lakers will head to San Antonio next week for an NBA Cup showdown. The Spurs sit at the top of the NBA Cup Group C standings with a 2-0 record. The Lakers are third after splitting their first two games.

A win for the Lakers would not only place them in a tie for the top spot in the group but also provide a glimpse at where things stand in the conference.

The Lakers are tied with the Spurs and LeBron James and the Philadelphia 76ers for the best record in the league at 13-3. Los Angeles has played well throughout November but had its nine-game winning streak snapped against the Utah Jazz on Wednesday, Nov. 18.

The upcoming Spurs-Lakers matchup will provide a glimpse at two of the league's early MVP front-runners on the court together. Luka Doncic is averaging a league-leading 38.1 points per game along with 7.6 assists and 7.0 rebounds. Wembanyama is averaging 28.4 points, 12.0 rebounds and a league-best 4.1 blocks per game.

#2822. Alabama Football 2026 vs. Chattanooga Preview

Hey, it's cupcake week! It's an annual tradition where the SEC front loads their schedule while the Big 10 plays their FCS opponents in September, then come November, they complain about the SEC getting an off week. Anyway, it's neither here nor there – Alabama gets an FCS opponent for Senior Day, and something of a breather week before taking on Auburn.

And, look, Nick Saban spent the better part of 20 years getting mad in press conferences this week because he wanted his team on edge and not comfortable going into these low-level matchups. We've long been conditioned to say to never take an opponent lightly – And for Kalen DeBoer and the Alabama football team, that should absolutely be the case.

But for the rest of us fans and bloggers, there's not much reason for us to pretend like this is going to be a game and go super deep into analyzing it. The Mocs are an FCS team, and that's that. They are a solid one, though. Head coach Rusty Wright has been at the helm since 2019, and has only once finished worse than 3rd in the Southern Conference. This year, they're 7-4 and are playing a brand of old-school football that is leading to some crazy low scoring games. They're scoring all of 21 points per game, and holding their opponents to 13 per game. And they're doing it pretty much without a passing game.

QB Battle Alberson has completed 66 of his 133 passes (49%…oof) for 881 yards and three touchdowns. Senior wide receiver Ashton Schumann has 27 catches for 388 yards, and nobody else on the team has double digit catches. The Mocs just don't pass very much.

The corollary to that is that they have been an excellent rushing team with a whole lot of volume. Thankfully, they're not a triple-option flexbone team that will annoy everyone and cut block all over the place. They're generally a shotgun or pistol team that, while the do run plenty of read option with the QB, mostly play straight up.

Kevin Lalin has 208 attempts for 1082 yards, while his backup, Journey Wyche, has 142 carries for 759 yards. The duo both have over 5 yards per carry. Meanwhile, the QB, Alberson, has 343 rushing yards and 6 TDs of his own, mostly on those backside keepers.

The Chattanooga defense has been one of the best in the FCS this year, only giving up 13 points per game. Their pass defense in particular has been excellent, holding opponents to 154 yards per game on 5.6 yards per pass attempt. On the other hand, their run defense has faced a lot of volume, giving up 119 yards per game. But with only a 3.4 yards per carry average, it's not like that unit has been bad either.

For Alabama, this game is such a talent mismatch that it's hard to compare schemes or matchups. The Tide will win, and as long as they don't sleepwalk into the game, they'll win easily. So instead of a prediction, here are a few specific thigs that I'd like to see in the game:

With a game not in doubt, I'd really like to see Russell try to go for a whole football game throwing quickly and in rhythm, rather than scrambling to buy time and make plays down field. For all the talk about his sky high talent, in my opinion, I think his ceiling is limited until he can run an offense on time and on schedule to minimize the effectiveness of opponent blitzes.

If there were ever a time to give EJ Crowell an actual significant number of carries, this is it. To this point, he's shown more ability to force missed tackles than any running back we've had since Najee Harris, but it's hard to showcase much when you get two carries per game. I'd like to see Ryan Grubb just go run-heavy all day long, and I'd like to see Crowell get the bulk of them to really get him into some sort of rhythm and gain some confidence in game.

Next year, Bray Hubbard, Keon Sabb, and Zabien Brown will all be gone, and, honestly, I wouldn't even count out Red Morgan being a surprise NFL entrant with the way he's playing lately. I'd like to see some defense backs from the second team really stand out. Ivan Taylor is there, and we're getting pretty confident in him. Can Jireh Edwards play an entire half (or maybe three quarters) and flash the impact we'd like to see? And more importantly, can someone step up at outside corner? Maybe Chuck McDonald plays some outside. Or maybe Jordan Edmonds finally gets on the field. Zyan Gibson, anyone?

I don't think relying on Dijon Lee and Carmelo O'Neal rolling into 2027 is something any of us want to be doing this offseason.

At 4-6 the Texans still have an uphill battle to make the playoffs. But they traded for Montgomery in the hopes that he could have big games late in the season while they’re fighting for a playoff berth, and on Thursday night, Montgomery and the Texans’ offensive line did that.
