#2817. Spurs use strong fourth quarter to put away Clippers at home

The San Antonio Spurs overcame a season-high 21 turnovers, using a strong fourth quarter to defeat the Los Angeles Clippers 124-112 at the Frost Bank Center on Thursday night in the penultimate game of their three-game home stand.

The victory is the 13th in the last 14 games for San Antonio, who bounced back from a loss on Tuesday against the Detroit Pistons. The game was the first of several without guard Dylan Harper, who was officially diagnosed with a left hip rotator strain that he suffered at the end of Tuesday's game. He is expected to miss between two to four weeks.

As a result, Julian Champagnie replaced Harper in the starting lineup, and the transition was smooth, considering his starting position last season. Carter Bryant was the first one off the bench for Spurs coach Mitch Johnson, replacing De'Aaron Fox at the 8:54 mark of the period. Johnson said pregame that Harper's injury would cause the Spurs to play around with the rotations a bit more, so that is something to keep an eye on as the week go by.

"We still made some mistakes here and there, but the main thing is we were all connected," Spurs forward Victor Wembanyama said after the game. "And we were mostly on the same page tonight, so that compensated for some of the mistakes."

A low-scoring first quarter saw the Spurs take the 24-21 lead into the second. The Clippers tried to pull Victor Wembanyama away from the paint and it led to a few easy Clippers points at the rim. Wembanyama and Stephon Castle finished the period combining for 14 of San Antonio's 24 points.

The Spurs took a three-point lead into the second half. San Antonio led by as many as 14 points in the second quarter and went on a 21-7 run, but turnovers and poor coverage on the perimeter allowed Los Angeles to stay in the game going into the third quarter.

Los Angeles took that momentum into the second half and opened the quarter on a 11-4 run as San Antonio's defense struggled to get back as the Clippers hit back-to-back three-pointers. That led Johnson to call timeout and talk things over with his team. Johnson's message finally sunk in the fourth quarter as the Spurs outscored the Clippers 34-22 in the final period to pull away for the win.

San Antonio won the game despite a season-high 21 turnovers, something Johnson said has also contributed to the team's shooting woes.

"I actually don't think our passing has been very sharp this year," he said after the game. "I think we've had a lot of passes that have not been on target and I think it's affected our shooting at times."

Of those 21 turnovers, Stephon Castle committed seven of them. Per ESPN, Castle became the first Spur with 7+ turnovers in a single half since Tim Duncan in 2003.

"I don't think it was anything they were doing," Castle said of his turnovers. "I think for me, I was getting probably just one dribble too deep into the paint… So, being able to make the adjustment at halftime, I think, kind of opened it up for me."

Wembanyama led the Spurs with 32 points and 11 rebounds, while Castle and Champagnie combined for 41 points to pace the San Antonio starting unit.

Jordan McLaughlin had a solid outing with five assists and three steals in 11 minutes. He also did not turn the ball over once, which prompted praise from Coach Johnson and McLaughlin's teammates after the game.

De'Aaron Fox had just one shot going into the fourth quarter and took five on the night. He finished with 10 points, but he will need to be more aggressive in the coming games with Harper out.

Keldon Johnson turned back the clock to last season's Sixth Man of the Year run as he had 10 points, 5 rebounds, and 3 assists off the bench. San Antonio will need that contribution from him more consistently to take the load off the starting unit as Harper and Tobias Harris get set to return next month.

The Spurs are now 13-3 on the season and will wrap up their three-game homestand on Saturday night at the Frost Bank Center against the New Orleans Pelicans at 7 p.m.

#2816. 3 keys to a Cincinnati Bengals victory against the Washington Commanders

The Cincinnati Bengals will take their version of the greatest show on Earth to Washington in Week 11 against the Commanders in primetime, playing them on Monday Night Football. Washington is 3-5-1 this season, but coming off a crucial win against the AFC East division-leading New York Giants on Thursday Night Football last week.

The Bengals are coming off a primetime victory of their own, defeating the Pittsburgh Steelers 38-18 at Paycor Stadium on Sunday Night Football. The win improved the Bengals to 7-2 on the season, and they currently have a one-game lead over those Steelers for first place in the AFC North.

Let's take a look at 3 keys to the Cincinnati Bengals continuing their winning streak this week.

Jayden Daniels is completing a respectable 64.8% of his passes so far during the 2026 season. He has 10 passing touchdowns to 2 interceptions in the 7 games he has played this year. Daniels has an additional 280 rushing yards on the season.

Even more so than those numbers, the Bengals likely remember what Jayden was able to do against them in primetime football back in 2024. Daniels completed 21 of 23 passes for over 250 passing yards, 2 passing touchdowns, and an additional 39 rushing yards with a touchdown on the ground. He helped Washington pull off the victory 38-33 that night in Cincinnati.

While Daniels is a dangerous player, it is important to note that this is a completely different defense than the one he faced back in 2024. While this defense hasn't been dominant, they certainly have shown a lot more than what we saw in 2024 and 2025. They are also coming off two really good performances against Atlanta and Pittsburgh.

This won't be an easy game for Cincinnati, but they do have a defense that we should have much more faith in than we did back in 2024. The talent is substantially different, and they have started to play some really complementary football at all three levels of the defense.

There is no reason to change up what is working. Let Joe Burrow do what Joe Burrow does best, and that is throwing the football all over the field with surgical precision. Coming off of a 400-yard and 4-touchdown passing performance, the Bengals should just keep on throwing the football.

There will be times to take deeper shots down the field, but the most impressive part of what Burrow is doing is just how patient he has become. He isn't putting the ball in harm's way; he is settling for the check-down passes when necessary, and is allowing the running backs to catch passes as an extension of the run game.

When you have a quarterback that is playing at an MVP level, you have to let him cook. That is fully what I expect to see again this week in a primetime matchup against the Commanders' defense. The Commanders have the 31st-ranked passing defense this year. They are allowing 244.8 passing yards per game.

Joe Burrow. Ja'Marr Chase, Tee Higgins, and the rest of the Bengals offense should be in for a big night.

About the only way teams currently have a chance to beat the Bengals is if they decide to beat themselves. When they lose the turnover battle, they will have a chance to lose the game. We saw that against Pittsburgh and Jacksonville early in the season this year.

We also saw them get pushed to overtime when they had 4 turnovers against the Tennessee Titans. If they take care of the football, they should win this game in Washington this week. If not, they will be in for a closer contest than they hope for, and potentially an upset loss on the road. Sometimes, it really is that simple.

#2814. Ashton Jeanty's bad season running the ball overshadows his receiving production

In the time of hot takes, nuanced opinions rarely get much attention, and so in the case of Raiders running back Ashton Jeanty, little has been said about him this season other than that he’s a bust. Last year the Raiders took Jeanty with the sixth overall pick in the NFL draft, and this year he’s averaging 3.09 yards per carry, worst in the NFL among the 34 running backs with at least 70 carries this season.

First running back drafted to last running back in the yards-per-carry rankings? Bust. Case closed.

Except it’s not that simple. There’s no excusing the Raiders’ awful rushing offense and Jeanty’s role in it, but it’s also unfair to talk about Jeanty without acknowledging that he’s one of the best receivers out of the backfield in the NFL.

Jeanty has 46 catches this season, second only to Cincinnati’s Chase Brown among NFL running backs. And Jeanty has 417 receiving yards, second only to San Francisco’s Christian McCaffrey. There are a lot of running backs who get praised for what they can contribute in the passing game -- Detroit’s Jahmyr Gibbs, Atlanta’s Bijan Robinson, Pittsburgh’s Jaylen Warren -- and Jeanty has produced more in the passing game than all of them.

Jeanty’s 17 receiving first downs are tied with McCaffrey for the most of any running back in the NFL this season. Although Jeanty has only one rushing touchdown this season, he has three receiving touchdowns, tied for the second-most among NFL running backs. (Kansas City’s Kenneth Walker has four.)

On Sunday against the Seahawks, when Raiders rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza struggled in his first NFL start, Jeanty was his leading receiver, with four catches for 46 yards. With the Raiders trying to mount a comeback in the fourth quarter, it was Jeanty turning a short pass into a 38-yard gain that got the Raiders into range for the field goal that made it a one-possession game. The Raiders lost, and Jeanty deserves his share of the blame for their inability to do anything on the ground, but the loss would have been worse if not for Jeanty being available as an outlet receiver for Mendoza.

Jeanty hasn’t been the player the Raiders thought they were getting after he was college football’s leading rusher at Boise State. But his contributions to the Raiders’ offense are real, even if they’re not spectacular.

Mao Shimada topped the Grand Prix Finland women's short program by nearly 10 points, extending Japan's dominance of figure skating's premier international circuit this season.

Shimada, the four-time world junior champion who is also undefeated in her senior debut season, tallied 79.06 points with a triple Axel, triple flip and a triple Lutz-triple toe loop combination, with the Lutz under-rotated.

It was enough to take a sizable 9.98-point lead over Niina Petrokina of Estonia going into Saturday's free skate (live on Peacock at 7 a.m. ET).

Grand Prix Finland continues later Friday with the men's short program and rhythm dance, live on Peacock.

GP FINLAND: Full Results | Broadcast Schedule

Shimada bids to give Japanese women a fifth win in the first five of six Grand Prix regular season events.

She previously won Skate Canada. Olympic bronze medalist Ami Nakai won Grand Prix France and Saatva Skate America. Two-time world medalist Mone Chiba won Cup of China and is the favorite at next week's regular season finale, NHK Trophy in Japan.

The only nation to sweep Grand Prix titles in one season in a single discipline was Russia in the women's event in 2019.

Also in Friday's women's short, U.S. Olympian Isabeau Levito placed sixth of 12 skaters, erring on both jumps of her triple flip-triple loop combination and then under-rotating a triple Lutz.

Levito, who was third at Skate Canada, needs to finish on the podium this week for a realistic chance to qualify for December's Grand Prix Final, which takes the top six skaters from the Grand Prix regular season.

Earlier Friday, Canadians Lia Pereira and Trennt Michaud topped the pairs' short program as they eye a sweep of their Grand Prix regular season starts.

American pairs were third (Katie McBeath and Balazs Nagy), fourth (Audrey Shin and Spencer Howe) and fifth (Valentina Plazas and Maximiliano Fernandez). McBeath and Nagy and Shin and Howe were added to the field on Wednesday, replacing pairs from Russia who were unable to travel to the event due to Finland's entry restrictions on Russian citizens.

If the standings hold through Saturday's free skate, McBeath and Nagy will have a chance at qualifying for the Grand Prix Final depending on the results of the last Grand Prix regular season event in Japan.

McBeath and Nagy were third at Skate America last week in their Grand Prix debut as a team after pairing up this past spring.

Two-time U.S. champions Alisa Efimova and Misha Mitrofanov already qualified for the Final.

#2808. Chicago Bears-New Orleans Saints: Keys to a Chicago victory

After all those primetime games, not having the Bears in action made the bye week feel longer than usual.

Now the Bears kickoff a very tough, but important stretch of football. The Saints and Dolphins stand as the only two losing teams on their remaining slate. And they still have to face the gauntlet of the NFC North four more times.

It starts with the Saints, though. And while their record is not good, it's the NFL. Chicago is in no position to overlook an opponent.

The Saints have talent. They've been in most of their games this season. In fact, all but two of their games have been decided by one score or less.

Our crew breaks down what it will take for Chicago to get the win on Sunday.

Sam: This is the worst defense the Bears have faced in a month. However, they have a formidable pass-rushing duo in Chase Young and Chad Granderson. If the Bears slow them down, they will be able to get back to the run game we saw earlier this season. That will set up play action.

#2807. Puka Nacua serving suspension while on IR raises an important question

The news that Rams receiver Puka Nacua will serve a three-game suspension while on injured reserve raised plenty of eyebrows, because on the surface it seems very convenient.

It seems convenient because it is convenient. More accurately, it's strategic.

The suspension is the result of a negotiation between the league and Nacua. In lieu of taking the process to a full-blown hearing before Judge Sue L. Robinson, whose findings of fact (e.g., "no violation was committed") cannot be appealed by the NFL to the Commissioner, the two sides reached a compromise. They made a deal.

It happens every day in civil and criminal courts throughout the country. Controversies get resolved by negotiation. The mutual uncertainty — one side will win, one side will lose — becomes an outcome that, ideally, both sides don't like but they'll accept.

So the league, which may have been concerned that Nacua wouldn't be suspended at all, agreed to a three-game suspension. Given the timing of the deal, the league necessarily agreed to let Nacua serve the suspension while otherwise unable to play.

The NFL didn't have to do that. It could have dragged its feet. It could have rolled the dice on the decision to be made by Judge Sue L. Robinson. The league ultimately negotiated, and accepted, a situation that allows Nacua to engineer the process in a way that suspends him at a time when he otherwise wouldn't be playing.

The league realizes that many will disagree with the outcome. That's why the initial statement regarding the suspension was followed by an email that said this:

"A player's injury designation does not delay discipline or prevent a suspension from being served.

"Consistent with prior cases, the suspension begins when it is imposed.

"There is precedent for players serving suspensions while on Reserve/Injured or otherwise unavailable because of injury. This is not a new rule or an exception created for Nacua.

"• Daniel Ekuale, Pittsburgh, 2025 season, was suspended five games for a violation of the performance-enhancing substances policy following a season-ending injury.

"• Sam Williams, Dallas, 2024 season, was suspended three games for violating the personal conduct policy while already out for the season.

"• Mike Woods, Cleveland, 2023, was suspended six games for violating the personal conduct policy while he was out on NFI.

"• David Parry, New Orleans, 2018, was suspended four games for violations of the personal conduct and substances of abuse policies while on injured reserve."

Indeed, Chiefs receiver Rashee Rice had hoped to serve his Personal Conduct Policy suspension for a street-racing incident during the 2024 season, while he was on injured reserve due to a serious knee injury suffered in Week 4. (That didn't happen, because Rice's lawyers were unable to get the prosecutors to finalize the plea deal until after the 2024 season ended.) Similarly, kicker Justin Tucker served his full 10-game suspension in 2025 while not employed by any NFL team.

Here's the philosophical question that the NFL could in theory revisit: Should certain suspensions only be served by a player who is healthy enough to play?

The current system allows players to navigate the process in a way that allows suspensions to be served while the player is injured. And, again, the league chose to resolve the Nacua case at a time when he was injured. The league could have insisted on a suspension that begins once he's healthy, as part of the negotiation. Ultimately, the league exercised the discretion that is inherent to the negotiations that ended the case in a way that allowed to be suspended while injured.

The league could have refused to settle the case in a way that allowed Nacua to serve a suspension while injured. Some will say the league was doing Nacua (and, in turn, the Rams) a favor. The truth may be that the league had real concerns about losing the case before Judge Sue L. Robinson, and that taking a harder line may have resulted in no suspension at all.

Either way, the current system permits it. Moving forward, the league should consider whether — when it comes specifically to the Personal Conduct Policy — it will allow a player to serve a suspension that (while expensive as it relates to the forfeiture of pay) costs the player no playing time.

#2804. Old connections, new roles: The coaching history behind Bills vs. Dolphins

The Buffalo Bills and Miami Dolphins have been seeing each other twice a year since 1966, and over those 60 years, both teams have had their turn making life miserable for the other.

In the early years, Miami dominated the rivalry, winning championships and making trips to the Super Bowl. Then came the Jim Kelly-Dan Marino era, when two future Hall of Fame quarterbacks battled for AFC supremacy. Kelly and the Bills made four consecutive Super Bowl appearances while Marino never returned after his lone trip following the 1984 season.

These days, the rivalry belongs mostly to Buffalo. Since Josh Allen arrived in Western New York in 2018, he's gone 14–3 against Miami, including a playoff victory. The Dolphins have managed to sneak in three wins — just enough to make Allen and the rest of Bills Mafia angry before the next meeting.

But the Dolphins coming to Buffalo this week look very different from the team that challenged the Bills' hold on the AFC East just a couple of seasons ago. Tua Tagovailoa, Tyreek Hill, and Jaylen Waddle are gone. So are Minkah Fitzpatrick and Bradley Chubb, who now wears a Bills uniform. De'Von Achane is still in Miami but sidelined with an injury. And with starting quarterback Malik Willis also on injured reserve, Kyle McCord is preparing for just his second NFL start.

Miami may have a new look, but that doesn't mean everyone on its sideline is unfamiliar with Buffalo. Several members of Jeff Hafley's coaching staff have faced the Bills in previous stops around the league, while others have crossed paths with the coaches now leading Buffalo.

For this week's Time Capsule, we're looking beyond the players to revisit some of those coaching connections, the games they've been part of, and the history they're bringing into Sunday's matchup.

_____________________________________________________________________________

Buffalo defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard and Miami passing game coordinator Kevin Patullo have already been on opposite sidelines, and their last meeting didn't end particularly well for Patullo. In October 2025, Leonhard was Denver's assistant head coach and defensive passing game coordinator, while Patullo was running Philadelphia's offense.

The Eagles entered the game undefeated and looked ready to stay that way, building a 17–3 lead early in the third quarter. But Denver's defense kept Philadelphia off the scoreboard for the remainder of the afternoon, giving the Broncos' offense time to mount a comeback.

Philadelphia quarterback Jalen Hurts completed 23 of 38 passes for 280 yards and two touchdowns, but Denver sacked him six times. The Eagles managed just 45 rushing yards and converted only two of 11 third-down attempts. After scoring on their opening possession of the second half, they never reached the end zone again.

Denver scored 18 unanswered points in the fourth quarter to win 21–17, handing Philadelphia its first loss of the season.

Patullo has some history with Buffalo, too. He spent three seasons with the Bills from 2010–12 before eventually landing in Philadelphia, where he was part of two victories over Josh Allen. The first came in November 2023, when Allen accounted for 420 yards and four touchdowns, only to watch Jalen Hurts score the winning touchdown in overtime. Philadelphia also edged Buffalo 13–12 in December 2025, despite struggling offensively throughout the afternoon. Now Patullo will be helping Miami offensive coordinator Bobby Slowik prepare for Leonhard's defense.

_____________________________________________________________________________

Buffalo head coach Joe Brady and Miami offensive coordinator Bobby Slowik were on opposite sidelines in October 2024, when Brady was running the Bills' offense and Slowik was calling plays for the Houston Texans. It was an afternoon Allen and the Bills would probably prefer to forget.

Houston jumped out to a 20–3 lead behind quarterback C.J. Stroud, who finished with 331 passing yards and a touchdown. Meanwhile, Allen struggled through one of the least productive passing performances of his career, completing just nine of 30 attempts for 131 yards.

Buffalo eventually fought its way back, tying the game at 20 in the fourth quarter. But with the score still tied and less than a minute remaining, the Bills took possession deep in their own territory and threw three consecutive incompletions. Houston got the ball back with enough time to set up Ka'imi Fairbairn's 59-yard field goal as time expired, giving the Texans a 23–20 victory.

Now Brady is Buffalo's head coach, and Slowik is running Miami's offense. Will Brady's experience against Slowik in Houston give him something useful to share with defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard as the Bills prepare for Sunday's matchup?

_____________________________________________________________________________

Buffalo offensive coordinator Pete Carmichael Jr. and Miami senior defensive assistant and run game coordinator Joe Barry have faced each other twice as coordinators, with each coming away with a win. Both meetings came when Carmichael was running the New Orleans Saints' offense and Barry was Green Bay's defensive coordinator.

The first was in September 2021, when New Orleans handed Green Bay a 38–3 loss. Jameis Winston threw five touchdown passes, despite finishing with just 148 passing yards. The Saints scored on five of their first seven possessions, while Barry's defense struggled to find an answer for Carmichael's offense.

The second meeting, in September 2023, went much differently. New Orleans led 17–0 at halftime, but quarterback Derek Carr left the game with a shoulder injury in the third quarter. That put Winston back under center against Barry's defense, but there would be no repeat of his five-touchdown performance. This time Barry had an answer for Winston, and the Saints failed to score again. Green Bay put up 18 points in the fourth quarter to win 18–17.

Barry figured out how to stop Winston the second time around, but he'll have a different challenge Sunday. Carmichael now has Josh Allen running his offense, while Barry is working with a young Miami defense that has been surprisingly effective despite its inexperience. Whether that group can slow down Allen is another question — one we will get an answer to on Sunday.

_____________________________________________________________________________

There may be plenty of familiar names and shared history between these coaching staffs, but none of that will matter much once the ball is kicked off Sunday. By the end of the afternoon, they'll have another game to add to their résumés — the only question is how that entry will read.

Timberwolves head coach Chris Finch speaks on the sideline as guard Bones Hyland looks on during a Nov. 16, 2026, in Minneapolis. AP Photo/Ellen Schmidt

"It was fun to see him at the heart of it, too," Finch said. "Especially as they were kind of tweaking their offense going along and all of his skills came to the surface through that."

Towns called it "bittersweet" returning as a champion, having wanted to deliver a title to the organization with which he spent his first nine years.

#2802. As he did with the Giants, Colts QB Daniel Jones is struggling, right after getting paid

Daniel Jones’ career has had some ups, but also plenty of downs, both with the Giants and with the Colts. He has a knack for having his “ups” in contract years, and his “downs” after getting paid.

Jones was awful in Thursday night’s loss to the Texans, continuing the worst season of his career — which comes after the Colts signed him to a two-year, $88 million contract in the offseason.

It’s not the first time Jones has performed poorly after getting a big deal. In fact, that’s all Jones has done throughout his NFL career.

Jones’ career started when the Giants made the surprising decision to select him with the sixth overall pick in the 2019 NFL draft. That earned him a four-year, $25.7 million contract, with the Giants having a fifth-year option. Jones didn’t live up to expectations on that rookie contract, and was playing some of the worst football of his career when his third season ended early with a neck injury, so the Giants declined his fifth-year option.

But Jones then played very well in his fourth year, leading the Giants to a surprise playoff berth and a win in the wild card round. That led the Giants to sign him to a four-year, $160 million contract in 2023, committing more money to him than his fifth-year option would have cost. Jones responded to that with a fifth season in which he played poorly, suffered another neck injury and then suffered a season-ending torn ACL.

Jones returned in 2024 but was so bad the Giants first benched him, then cut him. Jones spent the rest of that season on the Vikings’ practice squad.

In 2025 the Colts signed him to a one-year contract, and he responded by winning a quarterback competition with Anthony Richardson and then playing the best football of his career early in 2025 as the Colts jumped out to an 8-2 start. He started to struggle down the stretch in that season, and then his season was cut short by a torn Achilles tendon, but the Colts were so impressed by his start that they signed him to a two-year, $88 million contract in March.

And now, in the first year of that contract, Jones is worse than ever. His 13 interceptions are the most of any quarterback in the NFL this season and already a career-high, with six more games to play. He’s paired that with just seven touchdown passes. He still hasn’t had a single game this season with more touchdowns than interceptions. His 65.4 passer rating is a career low. His 30.3 QBR is a career low. His 58.4 percent completion rate is a career low. His 5.6 yards per pass average is a career low. Jones was once an effective runner, but his 2.9 yards per carry average is also a career low. Any way you slice it, Jones is worse than ever.

He’s also more expensive than ever. Whether the Colts keep him or cut him, he’s going to have a massive salary cap hit in 2027, the kind of cap hit that will make it that much harder for the Colts to rebuild their roster.

If the Colts cut Jones, he may sign another one-year contract with another team. No matter how well he plays, that team would be wise not to give him a lucrative extension.

#2792. 2026 NASCAR Season: The Biggest Names Who Went Winless

Not everyone will look back fondly on the 2026 NASCAR Cup Series season.

While Kyle Larson celebrated his third championship and Tyler Reddick racked up six victories, some of the sport's most recognizable names went the entire season without visiting Victory Lane.

Three of the 16 drivers who qualified for the Chase failed to win a race, while several established veterans experienced a rather forgettable year behind the wheel.

Here's a look at some of the most notable NASCAR Cup Series drivers who went winless in 2026.

One year removed from his career-defining Brickyard 400 victory, Bubba Wallace went winless in his fifth full-time season in the Next Gen era.

It wasn't an entirely unproductive year for the 23XI Racing driver, though. Wallace recorded 17 top-10 finishes, five top-fives and led 317 laps en route to an 11th-place finish in the championship standings.

Perhaps what made Wallace's winless campaign particularly frustrating was the success elsewhere within his own organization. Reddick won six races, while Corey Heim collected a pair of Cup Series victories on a part-time schedule.

Wallace will enter 2027 with a new crew chief in Davin Restivo.

The 2026 season marked the second consecutive winless campaign for Brad Keselowski.

The 2012 Cup Series champion finished 19th in the standings, recording just two top-five and six top-10 finishes across 36 starts.

His most recent Cup Series victory remains his May 2024 triumph at Darlington Raceway.

Few would have predicted a winless season for Ross Chastain after his Coca-Cola 600 victory in 2025.

The Trackhouse Racing driver missed the Chase altogether, finishing 18th in the standings with three top-fives, eight top-10s and 141 laps led.

Meanwhile, teammate Shane van Gisbergen collected two victories of his own.

It was a difficult year for Alex Bowman, who made just 32 starts and finished 26th in the championship standings.

The Hendrick Motorsports driver recorded four top-five and eight top-10 finishes but remarkably failed to lead a single lap all season.

Bowman was the only one of Hendrick's four full-time drivers who failed to win a race in 2026.

Austin Cindric finished 10th in the championship standings despite failing to win a race.

The 2022 Daytona 500 champion was the lone Team Penske driver to go winless in 2026, with teammates Ryan Blaney and Joey Logano combining for seven victories.

Among the other full-time drivers who failed to reach Victory Lane this season:

Of the drivers who went winless in 2026, only Cindric, Wallace and Buescher qualified for NASCAR's 10-race Chase.

#2790. Puka Nacua serving suspension while on IR raises an important question

The news that Rams receiver Puka Nacua will serve a three-game suspension while on injured reserve raised plenty of eyebrows, because on the surface it seems very convenient.

It seems convenient because it is convenient. More accurately, it’s strategic.

The suspension is the result of a negotiation between the league and Nacua. In lieu of taking the process to a full-blown hearing before Judge Sue L. Robinson, whose findings of fact (e.g., “no violation was committed”) cannot be appealed by the NFL to the Commissioner, the two sides reached a compromise. They made a deal.

It happens every day in civil and criminal courts throughout the country. Controversies get resolved by negotiation. The mutual uncertainty — one side will win, one side will lose — becomes an outcome that, ideally, both sides don’t like but they’ll accept.

So the league, which may have been concerned that Nacua wouldn’t be suspended at all, agreed to a three-game suspension. Given the timing of the deal, the league necessarily agreed to let Nacua serve the suspension while otherwise unable to play.

The NFL didn’t have to do that. It could have dragged its feet. It could have rolled the dice on the decision to be made by Judge Sue L. Robinson. The league ultimately negotiated, and accepted, a situation that allows Nacua to engineer the process in a way that suspends him at a time when he otherwise wouldn’t be playing.

The league realizes that many will disagree with the outcome. That’s why the initial statement regarding the suspension was followed by an email that said this:

“A player’s injury designation does not delay discipline or prevent a suspension from being served.

“Consistent with prior cases, the suspension begins when it is imposed.

“There is precedent for players serving suspensions while on Reserve/Injured or otherwise unavailable because of injury. This is not a new rule or an exception created for Nacua.

"• Daniel Ekuale, Pittsburgh, 2025 season, was suspended five games for a violation of the performance-enhancing substances policy following a season-ending injury.

"• Sam Williams, Dallas, 2024 season, was suspended three games for violating the personal conduct policy while already out for the season.

"• Mike Woods, Cleveland, 2023, was suspended six games for violating the personal conduct policy while he was out on NFI.

"• David Parry, New Orleans, 2018, was suspended four games for violations of the personal conduct and substances of abuse policies while on injured reserve.”

Indeed, Chiefs receiver Rashee Rice had hoped to serve his Personal Conduct Policy suspension for a street-racing incident during the 2024 season, while he was on injured reserve due to a serious knee injury suffered in Week 4. (That didn’t happen, because Rice’s lawyers were unable to get the prosecutors to finalize the plea deal until after the 2024 season ended.) Similarly, kicker Justin Tucker served his full 10-game suspension in 2025 while not employed by any NFL team.

Here’s the philosophical question that the NFL could in theory revisit: Should certain suspensions only be served by a player who is healthy enough to play?

The current system allows players to navigate the process in a way that allows suspensions to be served while the player is injured. And, again, the league chose to resolve the Nacua case at a time when he was injured. The league could have insisted on a suspension that begins once he’s healthy, as part of the negotiation. Ultimately, the league exercised the discretion that is inherent to the negotiations that ended the case in a way that allowed to be suspended while injured.

The league could have refused to settle the case in a way that allowed Nacua to serve a suspension while injured. Some will say the league was doing Nacua (and, in turn, the Rams) a favor. The truth may be that the league had real concerns about losing the case before Judge Sue L. Robinson, and that taking a harder line may have resulted in no suspension at all.

Either way, the current system permits it. Moving forward, the league should consider whether — when it comes specifically to the Personal Conduct Policy — it will allow a player to serve a suspension that (while expensive as it relates to the forfeiture of pay) costs the player no playing time.

#2789. What the Falcons need in 2027, based on 10 games in 2026

You can make the reasonable case that the Falcons need a bit of everything and I wouldn't argue with you, given the state of the team. There's nine straight losing seasons underway, the team is 3-7 with three straight losses and five losses in their last six games, and the clear limitations were showing up long before the Falcons traded away Jessie Bates and Ryan Neuzil. You'll likely see this roster entering 2027 with a third of the roster turned over and five-to-seven new starters, if I was to throw a dart in the here and now.

But where is that help most needed, and what are the Falcons likely to invest in the spring? Based on what we've seen to this point and what we know about this team's priorities, here's my best guess.

Yeeting Ryan Neuzil to Baltimore was a sign that the Falcons were sellers, yes, but also a clear signal that Neuzil was not in their plans for 2027 as the starting center. Given that Jake Matthews is older and Jawaan Taylor is both on a one-year deal and has struggled with penalties and run blocking, the overhaul is likely to involve at least two and possibly three positions.

Ideally the Falcons would not have to change out both tackles in one year, though they have Mike Jerrell, Ethan Onianwa, and Cameron Williams as potential in-house options with youth; the options at center are nonexistent. Levin may be fine the rest of the way and would likely be back in 2027 as a backup to the new center, but Atlanta's not going to settle for a 30-plus year old journeyman at the position.

Tackle is a bit less straightforward, but Taylor is out. His pass protection has been better than his run blocking by a mile, but Taylor has not been a standout and is up to a team-high seven penalties, a fair number of which have been concentrated in the red zone. This team will almost certainly want to replace him with a young, long-term option, with a new draft pick likely to go up against the likes of Onianwa for 2027.

Matthews is where things get interesting. Ideally, you're not turning over the majority of your line in a single offseason, but while Matthews has been better than Taylor across the board, his run blocking has been uninspiring and he's got six penalties of his own. The team would be on the hook for a $20.5 million cap hit in 2027 and another $12 million in 2028 if they cut him without a post-June 1 designation, at which point they'd instead be on the hook for $8.5 million in 2027 and 2028; either way they'll also have $3.5 million on the books in 2029. This team needs to decide if Matthews' slow decline is slow enough that they can keep their ironman left tackle for another season, or if they need to make a major change after well over a decade.

Regardless of their choice there, you'll have at least two new starters sandwiched around the team's two highly-paid, largely excellent guards. One era of Falcons football defined by Dwayne Ledford's coaching and preferences is drawing to a close.

Xavier Watts is going to be one of the team's starters a year from now, even if his second season has been decidedly lackluster compared to his first. The other spot is very much up for grabs, however.

With Jessie Bates traded, DeMarcco Hellams has currently stepped in and played well in his initial game, but he's not the caliber of playmaker and lacks the range Bates brought to the position. The Falcons are more likely to view him as a very good backup heading into 2027 than a potential starter, which means they'll want to invest in another player.

The compelling veteran options in free agency are all older, with Bates, Kevin Byard, and Jeremy Chinn among the best options clocking in at 29 or older; Jaquan Brisker is probably the guy I'm most interested in and he'll be 28. Brian Branch is beyond intriguing but is not likely because of his injury history and the level of investment the Lions have in him.

The likelier move? A draft pick invested in the position, with Hellams and Sydney Brown as insurance. The Falcons have made a concerted effort over the past three drafts to get younger on defense at every level, and there are some legitimately interesting players in this class from Georgia's KJ Bolden to Watts' former teammate Brauntae Johnson.

Cameron Thomas, James Pearce Jr., and Jalon Walker is a good starting point for this group. It is definitely not enough, however.

The Falcons like to rotate and have had to be unusually reliant on Thomas for major snaps, mostly because he's their lone consistently healthy and effective player in the group. Pearce is off to a slow start two games off of his eight game suspension, and the team has to have in the back of their mind that after his suspension, arrest, and negotiated diversion program for stalking and attacking Rickea Jackson, any further legal issues may jeopardize his future in the league. Walker, meanwhile, should be great but will be returning from a major injury that has cost him the entire 2026 season.

They need depth and insurance, which they can find affordably as they did with Za'Darius Smith, Samson Ebukam, Charles Snowden, and even Thomas, but I'd argue there's a need for another high-upside or well-proven starter here given how John Timu and Jeff Ulbrich like to rotate this group. They'll have the money to do something audacious like chase Andrew Van Ginkel—they're not going to do that, but they'll have the money—but K'Lavon Chaisson, Uchenna Nowsu, and Tuli Tuipulotu would all raise the floor and ceiling of this group. A team that likes fresh legs could also invest a draft pick or two in service of making this group even younger.

Jahan Dotson would be an incredible third receiver in this offense as a vertical threat who can shake defenders with his speed over the middle; he's done a good enough job without major target volume as the team's outside threat opposite Drake London that I have zero complaints about that signing. Perhaps a healthy Zachariah Branch in year two takes enough of a step forward that he takes on a major role, giving Atlanta real speed and better bang for their buck in 11 personnel.

Would be, perhaps, if, etc. Atlanta needs another high-end receiver in this group pretty badly to allow them to use Dotson and Branch more creatively and take more pressure off London, who has been carrying this group since he got here. London's consistent excellence has masked the fact that the Falcons have been relying on guys who would not be starting for many teams and/or are one year wonders in Atlanta, i.e. Darnell Mooney and Ray-Ray McCloud. Without a huge step forward from Branch, there is just not enough here for the Falcons to enjoy a high-level passing game without elite quarterback play they're unlikely to get in 2027.

This is a little more speculative, but it fits with the team's needs and what we know about their coaching staff. Kyle Pitts has had a disappointing season against expectations, and this team could be looking for a second pass-catching tight end to pair with him. Last year's Browns led the NFL in 12 personnel usage under Kevin Stefanski and Tommy Rees, but this year's Falcons team is 9th with a much lower usage rate. That's primarily because Charlie Woerner and Nick Muse are not huge receiving threats, to say the least, and Kyle Pitts and Austin Hooper are merely adequate blocking options; last year's Browns could bring Harold Fannin Jr. and David Njoku to bear as legitimate pass catching weapons.

It would not surprise me at all to see the Falcons prioritize a late day two or early day three tight end who can address that need and open up more two tight end formation usage for Atlanta. Texas Tech tight end Terrance Carter Jr., who reminds me a bit of Fannin, is one player I'd keep an eye on in April.

This is one of the central questions of the months ahead. Do the Falcons jettison Michael Penix Jr. or invest in him? Do they go into next year treating as a do-or-die season and decline his fifth year option? Or are they bought in, warts and all, and ready to invest in him with the expectation that a better supporting cast and another year in the system will draw more out of him?

Penix, frustratingly, has made that question difficult to answer with a roller coaster style of play this season. I'd still lean toward the Falcons making a move to replace him, because of Penix's inability to work effectively under pressure, still spotty accuracy at times, and struggles to work the middle of the field, as well as his unwillingness or inability to hit layups. He's seemingly getting worse when the heat is on as the season continues and is sailing basic throws that would keep the offense functional, both of which are making a creaky offense creakier. There are still plenty of skills to recommend him—Penix is learning to tuck and run and proving effective at doing so, he's more willing to throw the ball away when he needs to, the big time throws are still very much a part of his game—but it's marred by the areas where progress has proven fleeting or regression has crept in.

The talent is there for more than this, and at his best Penix can get hot and dice up a defense for an entire afternoon. The problem is that we've really only seen that in three out of the eight games he's appeared in thus far, with stretches in a couple of others, and the offense has been dead in the water with him under center and the team trying to pass early over the past three weeks. Your franchise quarterback should not be a "yeah, but" or "well, if" sort of player, but that's what Penix is right now.

There's enough organizational investment in Penix and seeming faith in his ability that no one should be stunned if the Falcons decide not to pivot, especially with so many resources to surround him with upgraded talent if they do believe in him. But I think there just isn't enough progress three years into this—and eight games into this season—to believe the Falcons will tether themselves to Penix over the long haul if there's a really good young quarterback they like available when they select in this draft.

The Falcons made a flurry of roster moves this offseason designed to raise their floor, but injuries and lackluster returns from some of those signings have left this team feeling shallower than we'd hoped. For every Corey Levin who has been solid enough to step in when injuries mount, there's a Samson Ebukam or Brian Robinson Jr. dealing with injuries or Christian Harris who simply hasn't panned out. The lack of depth has been most noticeable at wide receiver, where Chris Blair blocks his ass off but hasn't been an asset as a receiving option and Olamide Zaccheaus has had a disappointing year, and at outside linebacker where Za'Darius Smith has been offering limited snaps, Ebukam has been hurt, and the team has had to cycle through options like Snowden, Drake Jackson, and Bralen Trice.

There are enough obvious success stories here that I think I trust Ian Cunningham to overhaul the positions that have been weakest; Brian Robinson Jr. and Khalil Herbert at running back, Austin Hooper and Nick Muse at tight end, Gervon Dexter and Maason Smith on the defensive line, and Kendal Daniels and Harold Perkins Jr. at linebacker suggest he's capable of acquiring talent and depth where he needs to. But nobody bats 1.000 and receiver in particular has been a trouble spot for multiple years now, so the team must do more than wave their hands at some of these position groups with a couple of veteran minimum signings and hope for the best.

#2788. Neemias Queta is flourishing

"I feel like his growth and his role has gone kind of under the radar," Joe Mazzulla said of Neemias Queta after the Celtics' 131-94 win over the Mavericks on Sunday night.

Coming into last season, we did not know what to expect from Neemias Queta as he entered his first season as the Celtics starting center. He had some good moments in his first two years as a Celtic, but nothing to show he was going to be the long-term center.

There were growing pains at the start. The Celtics lost games early on due to their lack off rebounding but since that point, Queta has surpassed even his biggest fans' expectations.

With Queta as the closest defender this year, teams are shooing 41.3% on shots less than 6 feet away from the rim. That is the best mark in the NBA among players who have faced 4 or more shots around the rim per game. The average mark is 63%.

According to databallr, teams shoot 20% worse in general when Queta is on the court.

Databallr has a stat called DDPM which "estimates how much a player improves expected team defense per 100 possessions. It rolls together rim deterrence, contests, rebounding, disruption, foul discipline, and context-adjusted defensive information." Neemias Queta's DDPM is +2.3, which ranks in the 98th percentile of the NBA.

That shows in Queta's on/off numbers as well. With Queta on the floor this year, the Celtics are giving up 102.5 points per 100 possessions (compared to 112.1 with him on the bench) and have a net rating of +23.8 when he is on the floor (compared to +0.2 with him off of it).

Perhaps there is no better example of Neemy's impact than at the end of the Raptors game when he blocked 2 shots at the rim late in the game to seal a Celtics win. One of them came up one with 17 seconds left and the other with the Celtics up 5 with 4 seconds left.

One more block for Neemias Queta to end the game. Celtics pull out the win on the 2nd night of a back to back after being down as many as 22 points! https://t.co/YS3DB6PeDQ

— Celtics Clips (@celticsclipss) November 12, 2026

In what was a five-point win for the Celtics — Queta was a +27. His impact on both ends of the court cannot be overstated.

Queta is not a good defensive center; he is one of the best defenders in the NBA. The way he impacts the rim allows for the Celtics to play more aggressive on defense, which is something they wanted to do this season.

He is anchoring the 2nd best defense in the NBA right now. The Celtics defensive rating is 106.0, just 2nd in the NBA behind the Minnesota Timberwolves, at 104.0.

He has started to take and make corner threes this year. He doesn't shoot them a lot; he has only shot 6 to start the season but he has made 4 of them. He isn't taking contested threes or any threes above the break so we can't call him a three-point threat or a stretch big, but he has made the ones he takes so I can't complain about them.

The advanced numbers say his offense has been average. Databallr's ODPM has Queta at 0.0, in the 67th percentile and the Celtics only score 1.00 points per possession with Queta as the roll man in the pick and roll.

However, the on/off numbers say Boston is significantly better on offense with Queta on the court. The Celtics score 126.4 points with Queta on the floor and 112.1 with Queta off the floor. If we take Jayson Tatum off the court, the Celtics are scoring 131.4 points per 100 possessions with Queta on the court. Granted that is just 74 minutes, but it shows that these numbers are not skewed thanks to most of Queta's minutes happening with Tatum on the floor.

One reason for this is that he has the most screen assist points in the NBA per 36 minutes, with 15 points per 36 minutes. He has also been setting a ton of flare screens, which are off ball screens set and a player moves away from the ball. His screening creates a ton of opportunities for Boston in the half court.

The Celtics have gotten a lot of praise for their player development. They might not have a bigger win than Queta. Turning him into one of the best defensive centers in the NBA is not something many (including the Sacramento Kings who waived him) saw coming. Having Queta as a security blanket at the rim has been a big deal for the Celtics this year as their defense has become one of the best units in the NBA.

#2786. One Confirmed Name for Manchester City Starting Line-Up Against Fulham Revealed by Enzo Maresca

MATCH PREVIEW: Manchester City vs Fulham (Premier League)

It has not been a great start to the brand new season for Gianluigi Donnarumma - who is now Manchester City's undisputed number one choice between the sticks after the departure of James Trafford to Leeds United in the summer.

Now into his second year at the Etihad Stadium, the Italian remains one of the most decorated goalkeepers in world football, but a series of costly errors has placed his form under the microscope and left supporters wondering whether a change is needed.

With each mistake, calls have grown louder for current understudy Gerónimo Rulli to be handed an opportunity, and ahead of Saturday lunch-time's home game against Fulham, the question of who would start in goal was unsurprisingly asked to the manager

Speaking to the media on Friday, Enzo Maresca confirmed that Gianluigi Donnarumma would keep his place for the fixture at the Etihad Stadium, although the head coach did not ignore his goalkeeper's recent lapses, while insisting that his faith has not wavered.

"I think with Italy he made a mistake in the build-up and then was Man of the Match - he made many good saves," said Maresca.

"Again, we made some mistakes in the last games, Gigio was part of that, he is aware, and hopefully he's not going to make any more mistakes."

The vote of confidence means it will be Donnarumma, rather than Geronimo Rulli, charged with keeping Fulham at bay as Manchester City look to halt a run of three successive defeats and steady a season that has badly wobbled after a record-breaking start.

Last week, Gianluigi Donnarumma endured another mixed evening as the Azzurri met France in the UEFA Nations League, and a misplaced pass in the early stages was pounced upon by Michael Olise, who darted into the area to put France ahead in the 10th minute.

To his credit, the Manchester City goalkeeper responded with a performance up there with his very best, denying France from close range and keeping out a fierce long-range effort that cannoned back off the post - a string of saves that helped Italy roar back to win 3-1.

It summed up the inconsistency of his current form: an avoidable error one moment and a reminder of his shot-stopping class the next.

Back in club colours, the picture has been similarly shaky, with Gianluigi Donnarumma culpable for RB Leipzig's first goal in Manchester City's recent 2-3 UEFA Champions League win, allowing a tame Ridle Baku effort to beat him at his near post.

He failed to keep out a Nicolas Jackson shot straight at him against Aston Villa, and made a real mess of a Maghnes Akliouche shot against Paris Saint-Germain to effectively end City's chances of a memorable comeback.

Such moments have understandably fuelled the debate over his place, but still only 27-years-old, Donnarumma remains a European champion with Italy, a Yashin Trophy winner once rated as the finest goalkeeper on the planet, and a multi-UEFA Champions League winner from his time at PSG.

There is plenty of the season left for the Italian international captain to rediscover his best form, but the mistakes must stop for the good of the team and Manchester City's Premier League title chances.

#2783. Open Thread: How the 24-second clock became the standard for the NBA.

As I've stated on many an occasion, I am a math geek. So you can imagine my pleasure in fiding this post:

The 24-second clock that is used in the NBA came about through a mathematical means.

Apparently before the adoption of the 24-second clock, teams simply dribbled out games for much longer than what qualifies as garbage time these days. One of the team owners came up with the equations that the game, which was forty-eight minutes, or 2280 seconds, divided by the average number of shots teams took in a game, or 120 shots, was equal to 24 seconds per shot. Thus eliciting a more timely and interesting game.

I have not personally verified the validity, but now I have plans during the holiday break.

#2782. Ravens want more from their return game heading into Panthers game

Baltimore's special teams unit hasn't consistently delivered the production the team needs, and special teams coordinator Anthony Levine Sr. isn't satisfied with what he's seen from the return game. Asked about the unit's overall performance and some of the decisions involving punts near the goal line, Levine didn't hesitate to acknowledge that improvements are necessary.

"Overall with our return game, we're not happy with where our return game is at right now," Levine said. "No, we have to be better on both sides. We have to be better blocking. We have to be better with our decision making. We just overall have to be better."

LaJohntay Wester returned one punt for 20 yards and made three fair catches in Monday night's 23-20 loss to the Los Angeles Chargers. Chris Moore handled all four Baltimore kickoff returns, totaling 82 yards with a long of 24. Wester's 20-yard return showed what one clean opportunity can produce. Levine's review also covered the less visible decisions that determine where Baltimore starts its next drive.

Levine also accepted responsibility for the problems, making it clear that the coaching staff and players all have a role in correcting them.

"So, I have to be better. They have to be better, and everybody has to be better overall," Levine said.

One area receiving attention is the decision-making of punt returner LaJohntay Wester. Levine explained that allowing a punt to bounce near the goal line can create an unpredictable situation, particularly when the ball takes an unexpected direction. The goal is to avoid putting Baltimore's offense in difficult field position, especially when a punt could end up inside the five-yard line.

"What we don't want is our offense starting inside the 5-yard line or starting at the 1-yard line," Levine said.

That creates a difficult balance for the returner. Catching a ball near the five-yard line might prevent a worse outcome, but it can also leave the coaching staff and fans wondering whether allowing it to bounce would have been the better decision. Levine wants Wester to make sound decisions while recognizing how unpredictable the football can be once it hits the ground. Baltimore also needs better blocking and more consistent execution if it hopes to generate meaningful returns. Levine believes the unit can improve, but the responsibility starts with everyone involved doing a better job.

#2781. 7 former Seahawks chosen in the 2027 UFL Draft

The 2027 UFL Draft wrapped up Thursday, with six players who previously spent time with the Seattle Seahawks selected across the 15-round event.

The group includes a former seventh-round NFL draft pick, a former fifth-round Los Angeles Rams selection, several undrafted free agents and players who spent time with Seattle during training camp or on the practice squad. Not all of them appeared in a regular-season game for the Seahawks, but each had a connection to the organization.

Here is a closer look at their time in Seattle and where they are headed next.

Edge rusher | No. 11 overall | Second round

Jones joined Seattle as an undrafted free agent in May 2026 after finishing his college career at Oklahoma.

He spent time with the team during the offseason and eventually earned another opportunity on the practice squad in August. His second stint didn't last long, as Seattle released him on September 5.

Dallas made Jones one of its earliest selections, taking him 11th overall in the second round.

Offensive tackle | No. 13 overall | Second round

The Tulane offensive tackle originally signed with the Houston Texans as an undrafted free agent in June 2026. After leaving Houston, he received an opportunity with the Seahawks.

Seattle signed him on August 25, but released him just four days later. He never made it to a regular-season game with the team.

Edge rusher | No. 14 overall | Second round

Gaines joined Seattle as an undrafted free agent in May 2025 after playing at Illinois State.

He quickly made an impression during his first preseason game against the Las Vegas Raiders. With the game tied 23-23 and time expiring, Gaines blocked Daniel Carlson's 55-yard field goal attempt, preserving the tie and denying Pete Carroll a victory in his return to Lumen Field.

That wasn't his only encouraging moment. Gaines continued to flash during training camp, showing some pass-rush ability and the kind of athleticism that made him an intriguing developmental prospect. He eventually spent time on the practice squad before signing a future contract with Seattle in February 2026. The Seahawks gave him another opportunity, but he couldn't secure a permanent roster spot.

Linebacker | No. 18 overall | Third round

Paul Jr. arrived in Seattle with an interesting background. The Los Angeles Rams selected him in the fifth round of the 2025 NFL Draft, 172nd overall, before waiving him.

The former Ole Miss linebacker had a strong final college season, recording 88 tackles, 11 tackles for loss and 3.5 sacks in 2024. He earned All-American recognition and was a Butkus Award finalist.

There was reason to believe Paul could develop into a useful NFL linebacker. He joined Seattle in 2026 and showed some of that potential during the preseason. His best performance came against the Tennessee Titans in Week 2 of this year. Paul recorded eight total tackles, six of them solo, and added a tackle for loss. He was one of Seattle's more productive defensive players that night.

Unfortunately, his opportunity came to an abrupt end. Paul was waived with an injury designation on August 27, following the Titans game. He never got the chance to establish himself in Seattle's regular-season defense.

Defensive tackle | No. 46 overall | Sixth round

Singleton joined Seattle as an undrafted free agent after the 2025 NFL Draft, coming out of Iowa State.

He spent time with the Seahawks during training camp and the preseason, showing flashes as an interior defensive lineman. His ability to compete along the defensive front made him an interesting developmental option, even if he wasn't able to turn those moments into a permanent roster spot.

Seattle continued to give him opportunities during its offseason roster-building process, but Singleton ultimately couldn't establish himself as a long-term option.

Running back | No. 60 overall | Eighth round

Martinez is probably the most recognizable name on this list for Seahawks fans.

Seattle selected the RB with the 223rd overall pick in the seventh round of the 2025 NFL Draft. Martinez entered the league after a productive college career at Oregon State and Miami, finishing his final season with 1,002 rushing yards and 10 touchdowns.

He entered training camp competing for a place in Seattle's running back room but couldn't secure a spot on the initial 53-man roster. The Seahawks brought him back on the practice squad after roster cuts.

His time in Seattle eventually came to an end, and he was most recently with the Green Bay Packers practice squad.

Wide receiver | 84th overall pick | 11th round

Brenden Rice is another notable name on this list. The son of legendary wide receiver Jerry Rice, who also played for Seattle late in his career, Brenden began his professional journey after being selected by the Los Angeles Chargers in the fifth round of the 2024 NFL Draft.

He appeared in three games during his rookie season, primarily contributing on special teams, before ending the year on injured reserve. The Chargers released him in August 2025, and he subsequently spent time on the New England Patriots' practice squad.

The Seahawks signed Rice to their practice squad on November 18, 2025. His time in Seattle was short-lived, however, as the team released him on December 2 without appearing in a regular-season game.

Rice will now get another opportunity with the Colorado Stampede.

The seven players selected in the 2027 UFL Draft aren't the only former Seahawks looking to continue their football careers in spring football. Several other players with Seattle ties are already on UFL rosters for the upcoming season.

Here are some additional names worth keeping an eye on.

Mike Novitsky, C: Novitsky signed with Seattle as an undrafted free agent in 2024 out of Kansas. He spent time on the practice squad and signed a future contract before being released in April 2025.

Raiqwon O'Neal, OT: O'Neal had multiple stints with Seattle, including time on the active roster in 2023 and the practice squad in 2024. The Seahawks originally acquired him after he spent time with Tampa Bay.

Cam Bright, LB: An undrafted free agent out of Washington in 2023, Bright spent part of the offseason with Seattle before being released.

Sal Cannella, TE: Cannella signed with Seattle in August 2023 after an impressive season with the XFL's Arlington Renegades. His stay with the Seahawks lasted just six days, but he went on to establish himself as one of spring football's more productive tight ends. He has earned All-UFL recognition and is now back with St. Louis.

Easop Winston Jr., WR: Winston spent time with Seattle in 2023 and was part of the Seahawks' initial 53-man roster. He also returned to the organization on a future contract and was part of the practice squad.

Walter Palmore, DT: Palmore spent time with Seattle during the 2021 offseason after signing in May. He also had opportunities with other NFL teams before building a career in spring football. He's been in spring football since 2022.

Jalen McKenzie, OL: McKenzie spent time on Seattle's practice squad in 2022 and signed a future contract with the Seahawks in January 2023. He later moved on to other NFL organizations before joining the UFL.

John Rhys Plumlee, QB: Plumlee joined Seattle's practice squad late in the 2024 season and was promoted to the active roster in January 2025. The former Ole Miss and UCF quarterback was also an intriguing athlete because of his ability to contribute at quarterback and receiver.

DeVere Levelston, DT: Levelston signed with Seattle as an undrafted free agent in 2024 after playing at SMU. He spent time on the practice squad before moving on to the UFL, where he continued his professional career.

Ty Scott, WR: Scott is another interesting case. He originally played for the DC Defenders before earning an NFL opportunity with Seattle. The Seahawks brought him in for training camp in 2024 and later signed him to the practice squad. He returned to spring football and is now back with DC.

The list shows that Seattle's connections to spring football go well beyond the players selected in this year's draft. Some were drafted by the Seahawks, others were undrafted free agents, and several had brief practice squad stints.

For players still chasing an NFL opportunity, the UFL remains a valuable place to keep competing and get noticed.

The UFL and its predecessor leagues, the USFL and XFL, have increasingly become opportunities for players to showcase their skills and earn another shot at the NFL.

Jake Bates is one of the clearest examples. After standing out with the Michigan Panthers in the USFL, he earned an opportunity with the Detroit Lions and established himself as an NFL kicker. He made 27 field goals in the 2025 season.

KaVontae Turpin followed a similar path. The former New Jersey Generals standout won the 2022 USFL MVP award before joining the Dallas Cowboys. He has since become one of the league's most dangerous return specialists, earning two Pro Bowl selections.

Brandon Aubrey and Andre Szmyt are other examples of kickers who used spring football as part of their path to the NFL.

For Martinez, Paul, Gaines, Graham, Singleton and Jones, the UFL represents another chance to keep their professional careers moving forward. And while the road back to the NFL won't be easy, the league has already shown that the opportunity is there.

#2780. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2778. The Phoenix Suns’ core four are getting better, with more runway to grow

The Phoenix Suns are 7-7 overall after a 1-5 start to the season. We were hoping for a much quicker start to the season than last year, but the difficulty of opponents, combined with the addition of Miles Bridges and Oso Ighodaro's injury, meant the Suns were not at their best to start the season.

The Suns are now 6-2 since Ighodaro was inserted into the starting lineup. Devin Booker is back to playing at a near All-NBA level this season. Jordan Ott is learning the right rotations. Dillon Brooks looks like he is in full villain mode on both ends of the floor after an up-and-down week in November that culminated in a 1-point performance in a loss to the Lakers. His move in the rotation to be the go-to scorer with the second unit to begin the second and fourth quarters appears to have unlocked him.

Miles Bridges is starting to find his lanes and facilitate an offense that needs to keep moving. His defense and rebounding are getting better as well.

Even Jalen Green, who finds himself in trade chatter, in the last two games, has had inspiring second halves to show what Brian Gregory's vision of this team is supposed to look like. Green's 18-point, seven-assist and seven-rebound night was a glimpse into who the Suns need him to be more consistently as one of the best athletes and downhill threats on this team. Combine that with the energy he played with against the Nuggets in that second half, where he had multiple steals, and maybe, just maybe, this backcourt pairing might work between him and Booker. The fit will never be perfect, but if Green can play this way more consistently, it will quiet a lot of the noise around him for the time being.

Regardless of the level of opponent, the Suns offense was crisp and flowing all night long against the Kings. The ball movement, spacing, and unselfishness jumped off the television screen. All four of the Suns starters had over five assists against the Kings; Ighodaro only had two. But that level of effort and commitment to making each other better on both ends of the floor started against the Nuggets in a win Monday night.

In back-to-back games, the core four have all scored in double figures, and the only occurrence of someone scoring below 15 points was Bridges against the Kings; he scored 13 points. Against the Nuggets, the core four combined for 67 points, and against the Kings they combined for 80 points.

The numbers also back it up as well. Before the Suns played the Magic on November 5, the core four had a -59 over the first seven games of the season. Since then, it is only a -2 in eight games, and the group continues to play better. The eye test also shows that they are playing better as well.

This group still has a long way to go, and it still has yet to put it together against a high-quality opponent like the Thunder or Spurs, but the good news is the next seven games on the schedule are: at Utah Jazz, at New Orleans Pelicans, at Houston Rockets, home vs Dallas Mavericks, at Utah Jazz, home vs Los Angeles Clippers, and home vs Sacramento. The Suns should realistically finish this stretch 5-2 or better.

However, it is even deeper than the record over the next seven games. The Suns need to continue to prove that how they have played the last two games is who they are. They are still building winning habits and are still working through defensive and rebounding lapses that have plagued them all season.

Does the 3-point shooting efficiency continue for Booker? Can Green play with the defensive intensity and playmaking? Can Brooks sustain the energy to be the emotional leader night in and night out? Does Miles Bridges continue to do the little things like rebounding and defending regardless of his shot attempts? And as a group, can this core four show up and put teams away without sleepwalking through quarters that give the lesser teams life?

This team still has flaws that might be too difficult to overcome, but if the Suns answer yes to most of these questions over the next two weeks, then they will be right back up into the top eight in the Western Conference when the calendar turns to December.
