#2777. Broncos vs Raiders 5 questions: How is Raider Nation feeling about Fernando Mendoza?

The Fernando Mendoza era is officially underway in Las Vegas.

The rookie quarterback made his first career NFL start for the Las Vegas Raiders against the Seattle Seahawks. Now he gets a taste of the historic rivalry against the Denver Broncos this Sunday.

For the first time in close to two decades, it appears that there is legitimate excitement over the future of the Raiders. But is that really the case?

To get some answers, we go "behind enemy lines" with Matt Holder from Silver and Black Pride.

Matt: Ultimately, Las Vegas' 3-0 start proved to be fool's gold. The Raiders were expected to beat the Dolphins, but no one really saw the Chargers being as bad as they are, and the Saints have been a big disappointment this year. Those three teams have a combined record of 5-22 and are currently slated to pick second, third, and 11th in the draft, according to Tankathon. The only real tangible difference between the start of the season and the last month is that the defense was doing a better job of creating turnovers, with nine turnovers in the first three weeks and seven in the last seven. For good measure, the one win in the last seven weeks was against the 2-8 Jets, who hold the fourth pick in the draft.

That being said, Vegas is a team that had the No. 1 pick last April, an "award" for finishing in last place. So, the Raiders are making progress by separating themselves from the bottom of the league, and this was always supposed to be year one of a two-year rebuild. Technically, they're still in the Wild Card hunt, but they aren't a legitimate postseason contender until they can beat another team in that category.

Matt: Raider Nation is pretty excited to see what Mendoza can do for the rest of the year. A lot of people were sad to see Kirk Cousins go because he certainly gave the Raiders a better chance to win than a rookie quarterback, given how well Cousins has been playing this year. However, the rest of the team just wasn't ready to compete for a playoff spot, so it was time to pivot to the long-term plan and give Mendoza reps.

The No. 1 pick did a good job of protecting the football, using his athleticism to scramble or run the ball, and was good at getting through his reads to find his checkdowns last week. A lot of that may seem trivial, but going up against the Seahawks' defense with mad scientist Mike Macdonald calling the plays is probably the worst draw a rookie quarterback can have in his first start. Moving forward, I'd like to see Mendoza be more aggressive pushing the ball down the field — he missed a few opportunities last week — and show a better feel for pressure. The latter was the biggest issue last week, as he took six sacks, and that will be a point of emphasis against the Broncos' pass rush this Sunday.

If anyone is interested/curious, I wrote an article breaking down a few plays that I felt told the story of Mendoza's starting debut, good and bad.

Matt: Losing six of the last seven games has definitely put a damper on the mood within the fanbase. A big part of people's frustration is that a lot of general manager John Spytek's draft picks and free-agent signings aren't yielding high returns on the organization's investments right now. However, we've only seen one game from this past year's top pick, and there are a few offseason additions who are making an impact, like safety Treydan Stukes, linebacker Nakobe Dean, and guard Trey Zuhn III, to name a few. So, there's definitely a good amount of optimism surrounding the future of the Raiders, but how much definitely depends on who you ask.

Matt: Defensively, they have to get pressure from someone other than Maxx Crosby. Bo Nix has been one of the worst quarterbacks in the NFL under pressure this season, but the Raiders don't have a respectable pass rusher outside of Crosby. That's led to opponents sliding the protection to him and/or double teaming/chip blocking him throughout the game, essentially forcing someone else to beat them. No. 2 edge rusher Malcolm Koonce was answering the call in the first five games of the year, but that was primarily against backup-quality tackles. The competition level rose over the last five weeks, and Koonce's numbers have gone way down. And don't even ask me about the defensive tackles; they're terrible.

Offensively, it goes back to what I brought up a couple of questions ago: protect Mendoza. I've given up on the offense's ability to run the ball because the answers in that department will have to be solved in the offseason. Rookie quarterback or not, the Raiders are a passing offense. The problem is that Mendoza doesn't have a good feel for pressure; that was one of his biggest weaknesses as a prospect. So, the offensive line has to be at their best to keep him upright, which, of course, is easier said than done with Nik Bonitto and Zach Allen on the other side of the trenches.

Matt: As crazy as it sounds, I actually think Mendoza can have a decent game and take a step forward in Denver. He was good at making week-to-week adjustments in college, and as good as the Broncos' defense is, they do rank 27th in yards allowed per game (355.0). Of course, Brock Bowers' status is a big factor, and that's up in the air at the time of writing, but I think the Raiders will be able to move the ball. However, I have zero confidence in the defense. They've been a total mess on that side of the ball, to the point where I can't trust them enough to pull off a 9.5-point upset. However, I'm willing to take the points and say Vegas will cover: 31-24 Broncos.

#2774. Knicks 102, Timberwolves 99: “3 straight on the road, what’s up…”

LaMelo Ball hit one of his patented three-pointers from the left elbow early in the third quarter against the New York Knicks last night and as the crowd cheered, he proceeded to jog back on defense. Of course, the only not totally broken Ball brother couldn't let the moment pass without completely indulging himself into a thoroughly scripted "ice in the veins"-gesture that feels as original these days as a two-handed set shot. Just a moment later Josh Hart rained on the parade, running directly by Vanilla Ball's D and finishing an easy backdoor cut with a simple layup. And just like that the Knicks were up 14 again, ignoring the protocol of how cutting a deficit to 12 in a game where your team got handsomely dominated up to that point needs to be celebrated.

It feels good to root for a professional team, doesn't it? It will allow you to say things like Real Clydes Wear Plaid shared in the Postgame Thread and which I unapologetically stole for the headline of this recap. The Knicks won their third game in a row at Minnesota last night and they probably made it a lot harder than it needed to be. Their opponents certainly had something to do with it, no matter how ill-advised some individual emotions might have been. The Timberwolves can play tremendous defense, are as long as those trees in their logo and have an aggression you could certainly link to that name-giving animal of them. They got a good albeit cranky coach, a proven system, years of winning experience. Yet in the end they also got LaMelo Ball now.

We get that he is a talented, at times iconic passer; we also get that he has found his footing fairly well on the frozen tundra near the Great Lakes so far. But we really can't get convinced that you can ever really win big with a "talent" like that. His play can remind one of the game young kids play before they really get a hang of Dr. Naismith's rules. They also take two steps before every dribble, then four after they pick the ball up. They also couldn't care less about a repetitive shooting motion or dribbling the ball without palming it every time. With the kids it's okay and fun, we let them discover themselves as players and excuse it. But Lamborghini LaMelo should be held to a different standard, he is supposed to be a professional NBA player after all.

Luckily for the Knicks, they got plenty of real pros on their roster, guys who truly care about winning and treat their profession like it means something – not only to them but to others. It certainly seemed that way when they played most of the game last night with a level of calmness and concentration that has been a hallmark of theirs ever since they went on that beautiful championship run last year. But despite all their dominance over that two-month stretch in the playoffs, you can't ignore that they are a team with plenty of cracks in their armor, many of which showed themselves last night as well. It's the kind of weakness that are often the reason for the Bockers falling behind big only to have the opportunity to stage their beloved monumental comebacks later on.

Yesterday the Knicks offense completely bogged down late when Minnesota went to more switching on D (raise your hand if you've seen that before), neutralizing all the beautiful team basketball that helped the Gotham Gang run up an almost 20-point lead earlier. Not even Karl-Anthony Towns, once again mesmerizing for most of the night against a traditional five at his old stomping grounds, couldn't regain his first-half form. Maybe he rode the pine a little long, Mr. Brown? Well, you can't play him all 48, we get it. A lineup that included Jose Alvarado, Andre Drummond and Josh Hart was still an interesting choice, to say the least. For all the individual chops it's quite a load for Jalen Brunson to carry that group offensively, it almost feels like him heaving big AD up K2 or some other majestic mountain. It might get you to the summit against certain defenses but considering some defenses are as long and physical as the Wolf Pack, it can also get cold rather quickly. Especially when Brunson still hasn't found his touch inside the paint yet.

That New York could still pull it out in the end is a testament to timely plays and a gritty, opportunistic defense that at no point in the game relented to the physically imposing Wolves coming at them. When LaMelo Ball couldn't find someone open downtown, the canines' only plan was to ram their oversized combo forwards ahead. It worked here or there but never consistently. Watch out, there's an extended arm coming at you – boom, another offensive foul! It's an interesting yet understandable choice by the league to make the off arm a point of emphasis this year (sorry, SGA). Why didn't they do the same for palming the basketball or taking more steps than a dressage horse? Your guess is as good as mine.

For the moment, though, let us not worry about it – there is a win to be celebrated. For all we know though, our guys are probably watching some film right now and preparing for their next opponent (Portland on Saturday). Maybe they are also speeding race cars through some busy pedestrian zone or practice their one-legged step-back fadeaway jumper that has netted them less than 42 percent shooting for their career?

Nah, we leave that to the guy with ice in his veins.

#2772. Carolina Panthers 2026 fan mailbag: Wide receiver concerns, injury review, Thanksgiving, 007, and more!

Hello CSR! Welcome to Brian Answers, part two of your weekly Panthers fan mailbag for everyone. The Panthers season is well on its way as they still control their own destiny. Thanksgiving is around the corner and I'm happy football is still meaningful at this juncture. Let's dive right into all your questions!

RealityDan: So question… according to a quick google search, the Panthers have two "return from IR designations". One seems to be locked in for Horn, do we use the other one on Thomas Incoom or do we hold onto it and loose Incoom for the rest of the season?

I believe you are correct in that Jaycee Horn is earmarked for one of those designations, unless they decide it isn't worth bringing him back. I don't know what his injury situation looks like since he didn't get surgery and is rehabbing it instead, so it is definitely possible he doesn't come back at all. For the last spot, I suspect at this point in the season they will still hold one. Remember, they only have to be in injured/reserve for 4 weeks to qualify for that designation. We still have 8 games left, so lots of runway.

schrodingersblackcat: Brian, what was your favorite part of the game on Sunday? Beating the Saints in NO? Chuba going into full-on superhero mode? Our recovering DEF showing up and looking like they're could soon become more-than-respectable? Freeling and Hunter showing us signs that they're the future of this franchise? The 15 minute mindless turducken conversation that let you completely switch off and dissociate just long enough to forget how boring the first half was? Which aspect of this victory isn't being celebrated enough?

Also: Brad Idzik gets a visit from the Ghost of Offensive Drives Past. What does the ghost show and tell him?

I don't care how ugly the victory is, a win against the Saints in New Orleans will always be a massive plus in my book. Carolina also hasn't beaten the Saints in two whole seasons, so we'll take it. I would also say seeing the defense play hard and fast. They are certainly still motivated which gives me hope this team could still make the playoffs and be somewhat competitive, at least in the wild card.

I would imagine the ghost shows him that having Bryce Young take the easy throws is sometimes the right call. I know that many have detracted from the win on Sunday since Bryce was hitting Chuba Hubbard out of the backfield, but Brad Idzik's offense is definitely taking a lot more shots down field. WHICH IS GOOD! But some weeks, you just got to take what the defense is giving you rather than pushing the ball down the field when it isn't as necessary. The NFL now knows Carolina isn't going to hesitate to throw the deep balls, that does open things up in the short game in itself.

@WTMealey: What NFC wildcard contender playoff teams do you think we can beat? At least have a decent chance even if we're not favored.

I think even with our current losing record the goal is a playoff W. That would look like progress.

I'd say the Lions and Packers are teams the Panthers can beat. They already beat the Lions and I think the Packers game goes a bit differently in round two. I'd also go with the Rams and Seahawks, just because the Rams aren't a dream team and I think they played Seattle well enough last season that they could make a jump. I'm not expecting the playoffs right now but if they do make it, I think there's a real chance they could win at home against some of these teams.

TXPanther: What should be my 3rd side choice for our Thanksgiving order? We are going with Mashed Sweet Potatoes and Fire Roasted Brussels Sprouts. The last option comes down to Mac & Cheese, Green Bean Casserole, or Mashed Potatoes with poblano mushroom sauce. There's a cornbread stuffing option but we didn't like it last year.

I'm very partial to Green Bean Casserole, though it was one of my favorite recipes growing up that had a lot more fixings in it that I think most recipes have as a standard. Mashed Potatoes with that mushroom sauce sound very good as well though. If I were coming to your Thanksgiving I'd be excited to try them.

TXPanther: How many penalties/penalty yards will the Panthers have this week?

25 yards on 2 penalties, this is the get right game. Book it, you heard it here first.

Brazilian Panther: Give us three players you want to see resigned and other three dudes you want to see released or traded at the end of the season Brian.

The list to bring back is pretty easy for me, OT Ikem Ekwonu, CB Mike Jackson, and TE Tommy Tremble. I think the Panthers are in a much better situation if the first two are healthy this season, and bringing back Jackson allows them to play a slower game with upgrading the cornerback situation. And Tommy Tremble just deserves it with how far along he has come. He's an important piece in the passing game now and has always been an important piece in the run blocking attack.

Based on your question I assume we're not talking about players that are simply going to be free agents in 2027. I'm going to preface this question by saying I almost never vote for players to lose their jobs. But, if I had to pick, I think you need to let OG Robert Hunt go, DT Terk Wharton go, and maybe QB Kenny Pickett. For the first two, it would be purely for cap reasons as compared to performance. But I wouldn't be upset if they both stay. As for Pickett, I think his ceiling is fairly capped if he ever needs to come in for a long period. I'd bring in another veteran with higher upside or see what you really have in Haynes King.

Bull123: just took a quick look at tampas schedule…notwithstanding lions this week, they have chargers, ravens, saints twice, falcons, rams and us

they can easily be 9-8…i see no path for us without beating them on the Monday night game

After the beating they put on the Panthers, not only do I think they need to beat them to push any tie-breakers, but I think the Panthers have to beat them to prove they deserve to be in the wild card. Every season teams have bad games, but that was a fundamental beating you need to really bounce back from in game 2.

Irishboy: Brian, I thought the Panther's offense was completely out of sink most of the game against the Saints. While I thought this could be a get right game for them, only for Chuba, we would have been in trouble. I know the saints have a decent front 7, but their secondary wasn't.

As I am someone you wouldn't have a strong grasp on schematics, why was our offense basically bad?

As schrodingersblackcat pointed out in the comments, the Saints did play a lot of man against the Panthers, and that has generally been their formula playing against the Dave Canales/Brad Idzik offense. While I love Jalen Coker and Tetairoa McMillan, both guys just aren't as strong against man coverage because they aren't the fastest guys. Both can win jump balls and 50/50 passes for sure, but in man they are more likely to have a guy in their hip pocket which forces tighter window throws. I think this is why losing Chris Brazzell for the season was a bigger deal than people realize, the offense just doesn't have that speed option that can beat the breaks off a guy who just wants to run with them. Couple that with Idzik trying to push the ball down the field more and the margin for error is just much lower. All in my opinion, but I've seen several analysts this week share the same sentiment.

schrodingersblackcat: Who was the best James Bond, and why was it Sean Connery?

Sean Connery is a strong one. I have more of a connection to Daniel Craig but that was because Connery was a bit before my time. I will say, my out of left field answer, Patrick Gibson as a young James Bond in the First Light video game actually really hit with me for some reason. Definitely worth checking out if you are a 007 fan and play modern day games.

That's all for this week, Panthers fans. Enjoy this week and hopefully another victory for the team. KEEP POUNDING!

#2771. Chop Robinson’s Pressure Rate Proves The Doubters Wrong

The critics who said Chop Robinson could not handle the pressure have been proven wrong. Yahoo Sports reports he currently tops the NFL in pressure rate, applying it on 26.2 percent of his snaps. This stat is not a small number. It shows he is getting to the quarterback faster than anyone else in the league. The Dolphins edge rusher has 5 sacks and 20 tackles so far this season. He is also up to his first-round expectations after a shaky start to his career.

Robinson knows how fast the hype can turn. He refuses to let one good stretch change his approach. "One game doesn't define me, and what I've been doing doesn't define me," Robinson said. He is not going to get carried away by the praise. His focus stays on the work he puts in every single day. "So at the end of the day, I'm just trying to get better no matter what," he added. This humility is rare for a player who just took the top spot in a major category.

Coaches see the change in his daily habits too. Miami defensive coordinator Sean Duggan noted that "His practice habits have gotten really, really good." Duggan also praised his versatility, saying he can play multiple spots on the line. The team sees a player who knows his mistakes and fixes them quickly. This growth is exactly what the Dolphins needed from their young pass rusher.

The impact of this defense is now so strong that even the opposing quarterback is taking notice. Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen praised the unit during his weekly media session. "You turn on the tape of that defense, they're doing some fantastic things, and I'm not just not just saying that," Allen said. He called their scheme "freaking awesome" and noted how sticky the players are in coverage. A perennial MVP candidate does not hand out compliments like that unless he sees real trouble.

The Dolphins face a tough test on Sunday, Nov. 22, when they travel to Highmark Stadium to play the Bills. The game will kick off at 1 p.m. on CBS.

#2770. Bucks vs. Trail Blazers Player Grades: Ament drops career high, Rollins returns with a vengeance

On yet another night when the Milwaukee Bucks matched up against a high-profile former player (or two), they couldn't get it done, losing to the Portland Trail Blazers 124-114. The Blazers gave the Bucks chances early, looking like they were the ones on the second night of a back-to-back, not the Bucks. Unfortunately, the Bucks failed to capitalise on those chances and fell at the mercy of two former star Milwaukee point guards, Damian Lillard and Jrue Holiday, who taught the young Bucks a lesson down the stretch. Read our full summary of the game here and catch a six-minute audio recap on the Bucks+ podcast, Bucks In Six Minutes, below.

31 minutes, 19 points, 4 rebounds, 3 assists, 1 steal, 4 turnovers, 7/13 FG, 4/7 3P, 1/3 FT, -16

Herro's counting stats look fine, but it felt like he played a lot worse. Herro started the game on autopilot, and his turnovers all felt like pick-sixes, especially the one in the fourth quarter where he got ripped trying to bring the ball up against Holiday. I generally don't lean too much into single-game plus/minus, but this one feels dead on. All things being equal—which they may not have been—Herro should not have closed the game.

21 minutes, 15 points, 3 rebounds, 6 assists, 4 steals, 3 turnovers, 5/11 FG, 1/5 3P, 4/6 FT, +5

You can basically take everything I said about Herro and flip it for Rollins. His impact on the game was monumental, and most of it came on defence. Even more impressive, he did this while coming off an illness. Rollins deserved more minutes than he got (assuming he wasn't on a minutes restriction).

22 minutes, 9 points, 1 rebounds, 2 assists, 1 steal, 1 turnover, 3/11 FG, 1/4 3P, -5

Jaquez was bad. He contributed virtually nothing on offence, and with Avdija out, there wasn't really a defensive matchup for him. I especially hate the possessions where Jaquez dribbles aimlessly without gaining any advantage on his defender; it feels like they always end in a turnover.

25 minutes, 11 points, 5 rebounds, 2 steals, 4/8 FG, 2/4 3P, -5

Ware was… decent? Like, the three-ball is coming back, and he continues to show stuff defensively, but you know what I loved? That monster offensive rebound and putback he had in the fourth quarter. That showed a level of emotion and care factor we have rarely seen from Ware. Inject it into my veins!

28 minutes, 14 points, 3 rebounds, 3 assists, 2 steals, 3 turnovers, 5/13 FG, 2/5 3P, -11

A bit of a rookie game for Burries, with a bunch of good stuff and some not-so-good stuff. He's got that floater going left on lock, so that's good. His defence felt really impactful, and the play where he prevented Scott Henderson from even crossing half court was stupendous. I will say that Burries' release is going to have to speed up in the future; guys are getting to his shots starting from far away. All in all, I thought the rook played better than what his stat line would suggest.

22 minutes, 18 points, 3 rebounds, 2 assists, 1 steal, 2 turnovers, 6/11 FG, 3/6 3P, 3/5 FT, -6

A third really solid game in a row from Jakucionis, who should have closed over Herro. At this point, it's basically become a theme that he comes into the game, makes stuff happen, and, most importantly, brings energy. Now, some silly stuff is going to come with that, but you take the good with the bad, because there is undoubtedly more good. Finally, love that he's not even hesitating on his three-ball right now.

35 minutes, 18 points, 9 rebounds, 0 turnovers, 6/11 FG, 2/5 3P, 4/4 FT, -7

On balance, this was Ament's best game of his young NBA career, and it showed in the number of minutes he played. I truly think his shot has a high chance of going in every time he shoots, and that's a great sign for the future. I also love that Ament is attacking rebounds more and more, especially on the offensive glass; his game is becoming more multifaceted with each passing week. Plus, no turnovers! My only negative—and it is a big one—is that his off-ball defence remains a wreck; overhelping was a major issue last night.

27 minutes, 7 points, 3 rebounds, 3 assists, 1 block, 0 turnovers, 3/8 FG, 1/5 3P, +8

I know it's become a bit of a cliché to say that "good things happen when Nance is on the floor," but it's true! His line isn't impressive, but the offence just flows when the two-way big is on the court in a way it doesn't necessarily with other players. Just wait until that three-ball starts dropping. More please!

11 minutes, 3 points, 3 rebounds, 1/2 FG, 0

I considered leaving LeVert off, but I couldn't ignore his impact as a rebounder in the fourth. He obviously had that ridiculous and-one over Clingan, but LeVert grabbed like three O-boards in one possession; unfortunately, the Bucks couldn't pay it off with a bucket.

I've already alluded to Jenkins making what I believed was the wrong call closing with Herro over Jakucionis, but he also brought back Rollins—who was making a wildly positive impact—too late. Then there are the tough decisions that aren't entirely based on the now, like closing with Ament. You had to close with the rookie given the game he had played, but Lillard and Holiday kinda feasted on him late. That's the push-and-pull of coaching a rebuilding side. On the other hand, I loved the move to start Nance.

DNP-CD: AJ Green, Kam Jones, Bogoljub Markovic, Cormac Ryan

Inactive: Myles Turner, Kyle Kuzma, Ousmane Dieng

The veterans are not necessarily needed for this team to compete.

I found it ironic that Dame complained about a foul call where Ament hooked his arm and then drew a shooting foul. That's Dame's signature move! LOL.

Jrue was coaching up Brayden after the game. What a guy.

Speaking of sneaky foul-drawing, Jakucionis has the "drive hard at the hip, throw it up, and pray to the gods they call a foul" move on lock. What worries me is that, like it or not, those calls are generally reserved for guys with stature. Therefore, there will be—and have been—times when KJ does that, it doesn't get called, and he throws up a shot that is basically a turnover.

Gary Trent Jr.'s stint was absolutely diabolical. Exactly why I don't necessarily buy the idea that high steal numbers are a sign of a good defender.

Former Wisconsin Badger John Tonje was in the Blazers rotation.

Nate Ament spoke glowingly of Jrue Holiday in his postgame presser, highlighting his two-way impact.

The Bucks are back in action on Saturday afternoon against the Philadelphia 76ers in Philly. Tip-off is at 12:00 p.m. CST—watch on MY24.

#2768. 5 keys to a Jaguars victory over the Giants in Week 11

The Jacksonville Jaguars will look to extend their winning streak to four games Sunday when they face the New York Giants at MetLife Stadium for Week 11. Jacksonville enters the game with a 7-2 record and a firm hold on first place in the AFC South, while the 5-3-1 Giants lead the NFC East under head coach John Harbaugh.

The Jaguars have scored at least 30 points in four consecutive games, but extending that streak will be difficult against a New York defense that ranks among the NFL's best against the pass.

Here are five keys to a Jacksonville victory on Sunday.

The Giants have been one of the NFL's toughest teams to throw against, allowing just 184.1 passing yards per game. However, their rushing defense has been significantly less effective, giving up 121.6 yards per contest.

That gives Jacksonville an opportunity to establish its ground game early and take pressure off Trevor Lawrence.

Bhayshul Tuten has been particularly productive recently, rushing for 104 yards against Indianapolis and another 88 against Tennessee. However, his availability will be worth monitoring after he missed Thursday's practice with an ankle and foot injury, so Chris Rodriguez might be called upon to play a bigger role on Sunday.

Regardless of who carries the ball, though, Jacksonville must find ways to get the run game going early. A successful rushing attack would help keep the offense out of obvious passing situations and potentially open opportunities for Lawrence through play-action.

The Giants have consistently brought additional pressure this season, blitzing on nearly 40 percent of opposing passing plays. That presents a major challenge for Jacksonville, particularly with starting center Robert Hainsey ruled out due to a knee injury. Jonah Monheim will be the starting center on Sunday instead, and being able to communicate protection assignments will be essential.

Lawrence has been effective against pressure this season, but New York's aggressive approach could test an offensive line already dealing with multiple injuries.

Quick passes, effective protection adjustments, and a balanced rushing attack could help neutralize the Giants' pressure packages. Jacksonville cannot afford to let New York dictate the pace of the game by forcing Lawrence into hurried decisions.

The Giants' rushing attack has become increasingly productive with running back Cam Skattebo playing alongside quarterback J.J. McCarthy. In their last two games together, Skattebo has rushed for 202 yards and three touchdowns, while averaging 5.8 yards per carry. His physical running style makes him particularly difficult to bring down once he gets moving.

Jacksonville has been strong against the run throughout the season, allowing just 91 rushing yards per game, and the expected debut of defensive tackle Jordan Davis should provide another strong presence along the interior. But stopping Skattebo will require more than simply winning at the line of scrimmage. The Jaguars struggled with missed tackles against Tennessee, allowing Tony Pollard to turn a short reception into a 30-yard touchdown.

Jacksonville must tackle cleanly and prevent Skattebo from turning routine gains into explosive plays.

Although McCarthy has only recently taken over as the Giants' starting quarterback, he has already demonstrated the ability to push the ball downfield. He enters Sunday averaging 8.8 yards per passing attempt, one of the highest marks in the NFL. New York also has dangerous receiving threats in Malik Nabers and tight end Isaiah Likely, who is coming off a 127-yard performance against Washington.

The Jaguars have been effective defensively overall, but occasional breakdowns in coverage and tackling have allowed opponents to produce big gains. With safety Jessie Bates making his Jacksonville debut, the secondary will have an opportunity to improve its communication and limit those mistakes.

The Jaguars cannot allow New York to make explosive plays, especially if the Giants struggle to establish the run. Forcing McCarthy to move the ball methodically downfield would give Jacksonville more opportunities to create stops and turnovers.

The Jaguars lead the NFL with a plus-nine turnover differential, having forced 16 takeaways while committing just seven turnovers. New York, meanwhile, has committed 14 turnovers and has a minus-two differential.

That advantage will be especially important against a Giants defense that excels at forcing opponents off the field. New York has forced three-and-outs on 33.7 percent of opposing drives, the highest rate in the NFL. Jacksonville, however, has gone three-and-out on just 14 percent of its possessions, the second-lowest rate in the league.

That creates one of the game's most important battles. The Jaguars must continue sustaining drives, converting manageable third downs, and avoiding the mistakes that give the Giants additional possessions. If Jacksonville can protect the football and maintain its offensive efficiency, it will be in a strong position to extend its winning streak and remain atop the AFC South.
